q: מטופל מאושפז עקב מצב רפואי חד הגורם לפגיעה זמנית בכושר הנהיגה. לפי החוזר, מה נדרש מהרופא המטפל בתקופה שעד התייצבות המצב?
o: להפנות להליך רישוי קבוע בגלל הפגיעה הזמנית עצמה
להתריע על הימנעות מנהיגה עד התייצבות המצב
לאפשר נהיגה קצרה כדי לבדוק בפועל את התאוששותו
לדחות הדרכה על נהיגה עד שיופיע אירוע נוסף בכביש
explanation:
במצב רפואי חד עלולה להיות **פגיעה זמנית בנהיגה**. החוזר דורש להתריע בפני המטופל להימנע מנהיגה עד להתייצבות מצבו, ולציין במכתב השחרור המלצות מותאמות; משך ההימנעות אינו נקבע כאן כמספר חודשים אחיד (עמ׳ 3).
"נדרש להתריע בפני המטופל שעליו להימנע מנהיגה עד להתייצבות מצבו הרפואי, בהתאם לנהלים הרגילים המקובלים בכל תחום רפואי." (עמ׳ 3).
"ככלל, אין צורך בדיווח למרב"ד לגבי מצבים רפואיים זמניים." (עמ׳ 3).

**א. להפנות להליך רישוי קבוע בגלל הפגיעה הזמנית עצמה.** שגויה, החוזר מבחין בין מצבים קבועים לזמניים ומציין שככלל אין צורך בדיווח בשל מצב זמני; ההדרכה המיידית היא להימנע מנהיגה עד להתייצבות (עמ׳ 3).
**ב. להתריע על הימנעות מנהיגה עד התייצבות המצב.** נכונה, זו ההנחיה המפורשת לרופא בעת אשפוז בגלל מצב רפואי חד (עמ׳ 3).
**ג. לאפשר נהיגה קצרה כדי לבדוק בפועל את התאוששותו.** שגויה, נהיגת ניסיון אינה ההנחיה; החוזר דורש להתריע על הימנעות מנהיגה עד להתייצבות המצב (עמ׳ 3).
**ד. לדחות הדרכה על נהיגה עד שיופיע אירוע נוסף בכביש.** שגויה, החובה להתריע קיימת כבר בתקופת המחלה החדה, ולא מותנית באירוע נוסף בכביש (עמ׳ 3).

מקור: חוזר משרד הבריאות: הגדרה מחדש של חובת הדיווח, סעיף 9, עמ׳ 3.
ref: חוזר מנכ"ל משרד הבריאות 6/2023 — כשירות רפואית לנהיגה

q: נהג בן 68 החל טיפול באינסולין. לפי החוזר העוסק בדיווח על כשירות לנהיגה, מה יש להסביר לו לגבי הטיפול התרופתי?
o: יש לצמצם נהיגה לנסיעות קצרות כתחליף להדרכה על התרופה
יש להדריך על תופעות לוואי ועל בטיחות הנהיגה
יש להסתפק בהדרכה על מינון התרופה ולהפריד אותה מנהיגה
יש להמתין לאירוע בכביש לפני הדרכה על תופעות הלוואי
explanation:
חוזר משרד הבריאות מחייב **הדרכה על תופעות לוואי** העלולות להשפיע על הנהיגה ועל מצבים זמניים מסכנים. לכן ההדרכה בתחילת טיפול צריכה לכלול את השלכותיו האפשריות על כושר הנהיגה; זו החלת ההנחיה הכללית על המקרה, ולא אישור נהיגה אוטומטי בשל ניטור סוכר (עמ׳ 3).
"יש להזהיר את החולה בדבר תופעות לוואי של תרופות העלולות להשפיע על כושר הנהיגה, הערנות, וכן על מצבים זמניים העשויים לסכן בנהיגה" (עמ׳ 3).

**א. יש לצמצם נהיגה לנסיעות קצרות כתחליף להדרכה על התרופה.** שגויה, החוזר דורש הדרכה על תופעות לוואי ומצבים מסכנים; הגבלת מרחק הנסיעה אינה מחליפה אותה (עמ׳ 3).
**ב. יש להדריך על תופעות לוואי ועל בטיחות הנהיגה.** נכונה, זו הדרישה המפורשת בחוזר ומטרתה ליידע על השפעות הטיפול הרלוונטיות לנהיגה (עמ׳ 3).
**ג. יש להסתפק בהדרכה על מינון התרופה ולהפריד אותה מנהיגה.** שגויה, החוזר קושר במפורש בין הדרכת התרופות לבין כושר הנהיגה, ולכן הפרדה כזאת מחמיצה מידע נדרש (עמ׳ 3).
**ד. יש להמתין לאירוע בכביש לפני הדרכה על תופעות הלוואי.** שגויה, ההנחיה היא להזהיר את המטופל על הסיכון ולא להמתין לאירוע בכביש (עמ׳ 3).

מקור: חוזר משרד הבריאות: הגדרה מחדש של חובת הדיווח, סעיף 7.2, עמ׳ 3.

q: מהו ההבדל המשמעותי ביותר בין ייפוי כוח מתמשך לאפוטרופסות?
o: ייפוי כוח מתמשך ניתן על ידי בית המשפט לפי גילו של האדם; אפוטרופסות נבחרת מראש בחתימתו
ייפוי כוח ניתן על ידי האדם עצמו מראש, אפוטרופסות ממונה על ידי בית משפט
ייפוי כוח מתמשך ניתן בידי האפוטרופוס הכללי; אפוטרופסות נערכת אצל עורך דין לפי בחירת האדם
בשני ההסדרים בני המשפחה ממנים את הנציג בחתימתם, ללא בחירת האדם וללא מינוי של בית משפט
explanation:
**ייפוי כוח מתמשך** מבטא בחירה מראש של האדם, בשלב שבו הוא מסוגל לקבל החלטות. לעומתו, מינוי **אפוטרופוס** נעשה בצו שיפוטי; ההבדל הוא בזהות הגורם הבוחר והממנה, ולא בגיל לבדו (מדריך לממנה, עמ׳ 4; חוזר מינוי אפוטרופוס, עמ׳ 2).
"ייפוי כוח מתמשך הינו הסדר משפטי המבוסס על בחירה אישית של הממנה" (עמ׳ 4).

**א. ייפוי כוח מתמשך ניתן על ידי בית המשפט לפי גילו של האדם; אפוטרופסות נבחרת מראש בחתימתו.** שגויה, האפשרות מייחסת לבית המשפט את הבחירה בייפוי הכוח ולאדם את המינוי השיפוטי; בכך היא מחליפה את מקורות הסמכות של שני ההסדרים (מדריך עמ׳ 4; חוזר עמ׳ 2).
**ב. ייפוי כוח ניתן על ידי האדם עצמו מראש, אפוטרופסות ממונה על ידי בית משפט.** נכונה, האדם בוחר מראש מי ידאג לענייניו בייפוי הכוח, ואפוטרופוס מתמנה בצו בית משפט או בית דין (מדריך עמ׳ 4; חוזר עמ׳ 2).
**ג. ייפוי כוח מתמשך ניתן בידי האפוטרופוס הכללי; אפוטרופסות נערכת אצל עורך דין לפי בחירת האדם.** שגויה, הגורם הבוחר בייפוי הכוח הוא הממנה, לא האפוטרופוס הכללי; עריכה אצל עורך דין אינה מחליפה את הצו הנדרש למינוי אפוטרופוס (מדריך עמ׳ 4; חוזר עמ׳ 2).
**ד. בשני ההסדרים בני המשפחה ממנים את הנציג בחתימתם, ללא בחירת האדם וללא מינוי של בית משפט.** שגויה, קשר משפחתי אינו תחליף לבחירה אישית בייפוי הכוח או לצו שיפוטי באפוטרופסות (יישום מדריך עמ׳ 4 וחוזר עמ׳ 2).

מקור: משרד המשפטים, מדריך לממנה, עמ׳ 4; חוזר מינוי אפוטרופוס במסגרת אשפוז ממושך, עמ׳ 2.

q: מהו תומך בקבלת החלטות לפי חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות?
o: אפוטרופוס המקבל החלטות במקום האדם מכוח מינוי שיפוטי ובהתאם לסמכויות שנקבעו
אדם הממונה לסייע בקבלת החלטות מבלי להחליף את שיקול דעתו של האדם
עורך דין שמחליט במקום האדם על הטיפול הרפואי משום שהוא מייצג אותו בהליך המשפטי
עובד סוציאלי שמקבל את ההחלטה הסופית במקום האדם לאחר שהסביר לו את החלופות
explanation:
**תמיכה בקבלת החלטות** מסייעת לקבל מידע, להבין חלופות ולממש החלטות, אך **ההחלטה נשארת בידי האדם** (סעיף 67ב, עמ׳ 61 ו־62 בקובץ). בית המשפט רשאי למנות תומך לבגיר שיכול לקבל החלטות בעצמו בעזרת תמיכה; הסיוע אינו מעביר לתומך את שיקול הדעת (סעיף 67ב(ד), עמ׳ 62).
"תומך בקבלת החלטות לא יקבל החלטות בשמו של האדם שהוא מסייע לו." (עמ׳ 62 (PDF)).

**א. אפוטרופוס המקבל החלטות במקום האדם מכוח מינוי שיפוטי ובהתאם לסמכויות שנקבעו.** שגויה, קבלת החלטות במקום האדם היא תפקיד מחליף, ואילו לתומך נאסר לקבל החלטות בשם האדם (סעיף 67ב(ג), עמ׳ 62).
**ב. אדם הממונה לסייע בקבלת החלטות מבלי להחליף את שיקול דעתו של האדם.** נכונה, התומך מסייע בהבנת המידע ובמימוש ההחלטות בלי להפוך לבעל ההחלטה; זה המבנה שנקבע בחוק (סעיף 67ב, עמ׳ 61 ו־62).
**ג. עורך דין שמחליט במקום האדם על הטיפול הרפואי משום שהוא מייצג אותו בהליך המשפטי.** שגויה, ייצוג מקצועי אינו מתיר לתומך להחליט במקום האדם; כיישום האיסור, הוא חל גם אם התומך הוא עורך דין (סעיף 67ב(ג), עמ׳ 62).
**ד. עובד סוציאלי שמקבל את ההחלטה הסופית במקום האדם לאחר שהסביר לו את החלופות.** שגויה, הסבר חלופות הוא סיוע מתאים, אך החלטה סופית במקום האדם חורגת מתפקיד התומך (סעיף 67ב(א) ו־(ג), עמ׳ 61 ו־62).

מקור: חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ_ב-1962.pdf עמ׳ 61 בקובץ; חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ_ב-1962.pdf עמ׳ 62 בקובץ.
ref: חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ״ב-1962 · §67ב; PDF pp61–62
label: Source: חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ״ב-1962 · §67ב; PDF pp61–62

q: במחלקה מכינים תיק בקשה למינוי אפוטרופוס למטופל באשפוז ממושך. לפי רשימת המסמכים שבסעיף 9.3 לנוהל, איזה דו״ח נכלל לצד תעודת רופא מומחה והסכמות המועמד ובני המשפחה?
o: דו״ח סיעודי שמכין צוות האחיות במחלקה.
דו״ח סוציאלי שמכין העובד הסוציאלי המטפל.
דו״ח תפקודי שמכין הפיזיותרפיסט המטפל במחלקה.
דו״ח תרופתי שמכין הרוקח הקליני במחלקה.
explanation:
**דו״ח סוציאלי** הוא אחד המסמכים המנויים בסעיף 9.3 לצד תעודת רופא מומחה והסכמות. הוא משלים את החומר שמכינים להליך המינוי; עם זאת, הנוהל מאפשר לבן משפחה או לצד מעוניין להגיש בקשה גם בלעדיו, ובית המשפט יורה בדרך כלל על קבלת תסקיר (עמ׳ 4–5).
"דו״ח סוציאלי (נספח 2);" (עמ׳ 4).

**א. דו״ח סיעודי שמכין צוות האחיות במחלקה.** שגויה, דו״ח סיעודי אינו הדו״ח הנוסף המנוי ברשימת סעיף 9.3. לצד התעודה הרפואית מופיע דו״ח סוציאלי, ולכן מסמך זה אינו תחליף לו ברשימה הנשאלת (עמ׳ 4).
**ב. דו״ח סוציאלי שמכין העובד הסוציאלי המטפל.** נכונה, זהו הדו״ח שהסעיף מונה במפורש לצד תעודת המומחה וההסכמות. בהמשך מפורטים אופן הכנתו והאפשרות לפתוח הליך גם כאשר טרם הוגש (עמ׳ 4–5).
**ג. דו״ח תפקודי שמכין הפיזיותרפיסט המטפל במחלקה.** שגויה, הערכת פיזיותרפיה אינה הדו״ח המנוי בסעיף. השאלה עוסקת בתיק הבקשה המשפטית המתואר, ולא בהערכה התפקודית השיקומית (עמ׳ 4).
**ד. דו״ח תרופתי שמכין הרוקח הקליני במחלקה.** שגויה, סקירת תרופות אינה הדו״ח הנוסף שברשימת המסמכים. גם אם היא מועילה לטיפול, היא אינה ממלאת את מקומו של הדו״ח הסוציאלי ברשימה (עמ׳ 4).

מקור: נוהל מינוי אפוטרופוס במסגרת אשפוז ממושך, סעיפים 9.3 ו־9.3.3, עמ׳ 4–5.
ref: מינוי אפוטרופוס על גופו של אדם ו/או רכושו במסגרת אשפוז ממושך · §§7.1,9.3; PDF pp3–5
label: Source: מינוי אפוטרופוס על גופו של אדם ו/או רכושו במסגרת אשפוז ממושך · §§7.1,9.3; PDF pp3–5

q: An 88-year-old woman with severe dementia and advanced heart failure is receiving care focused on comfort and quality of life. Her family asks about reducing medications. Which principle should guide the medication review?
o: Base medication continuation on separate guidelines for each chronic condition
Base medication selection on care goals and expected current benefit
Base the order of drug withdrawal on the date each medication was started
Base deprescribing on prioritizing prevention over relief of current symptoms
explanation:
**Medication review** should connect indications and expected benefits to the patient's goals of care, not just disease guidelines. With increasing frailty and a focus on quality of life, deprescribing seeks to avoid adverse effects and drugs unlikely to provide meaningful benefit while preserving symptom control (pp. 314, 1080).
"take into consideration the patient’s goals of care and sociodemographic/sociocultural factors." (p. 314).
"especially when the focus becomes more on quality of life and symptom control and avoiding side effects and medications that are unlikely to contribute any meaningful effect." (p. 1080).

**A. Base medication continuation on separate guidelines for each chronic condition.** Wrong, the source explicitly requires goals of care to supplement clinical guidelines (p. 314).
**B. Base medication selection on care goals and expected current benefit.** Correct, this aligns the review with the stated comfort goal and the expected meaningful benefit of each medicine (pp. 314, 1080).
**C. Base the order of drug withdrawal on the date each medication was started.** Wrong, start dates help identify prescribing cascades, but they do not substitute for assessing indication, benefit and goals when deciding what to stop (p. 314).
**D. Base deprescribing on prioritizing prevention over relief of current symptoms.** Wrong, prioritizing prevention regardless of current symptoms conflicts with the stated emphasis on quality of life and symptom control (p. 1080).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 314, 1080.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 314, 1080

q: איזה תיאור תואם הנחיות רפואיות מקדימות לפי סעיף 31 לחוק החולה הנוטה למות?
o: הוראות של רופא בדבר הטיפול המתוכנן למטופל בעת אשפוזו הנוכחי
הוראות אדם כשיר לטיפול עתידי כשיהיה נוטה למות וחסר כשירות
הוראות של בני משפחה בדבר הטיפול הרצוי בקרובם אם יאבד כשירות
הוראות של ועדה מוסדית בדבר הטיפול בחולה כשמתעוררת מחלוקת
explanation:
**הנחיות רפואיות מקדימות** מבטאות את רצונו של האדם עצמו בעודו בעל כשירות. הן מתייחסות לטיפול עתידי אם ייקבע שהוא חולה הנוטה למות שאינו בעל כשירות; סעיף 30 מדגיש שהבעת הרצון צריכה להיות חופשית ועצמאית (סעיפים 30–31, עמ׳ PDF 16).
"אדם בעל כשירות רשאי לתת הנחיות רפואיות מקדימות שבהן יפרט את רצונו לגבי טיפול רפואי עתידי בו" (עמ׳ 16).
"אם ייקבע לגביו כי הוא חולה הנוטה למות שאינו בעל כשירות, הכל לפי הוראות חוק זה." (עמ׳ 16).

**א. הוראות של רופא בדבר הטיפול המתוכנן למטופל בעת אשפוזו הנוכחי.** שגויה, זהו תיאור של הוראות טיפול של רופא, ואילו סעיף 31 מגדיר הנחיות שבהן האדם הכשיר עצמו מפרט את רצונו לגבי טיפול עתידי (סעיף 31, עמ׳ PDF 16).
**ב. הוראות אדם כשיר לטיפול עתידי כשיהיה נוטה למות וחסר כשירות.** נכונה, התיאור כולל את נותן ההנחיות ואת המצב העתידי שבו הן נועדו לשמש: אדם כשיר המפרט רצון לקראת מצב של חולה הנוטה למות שאינו כשיר (סעיף 31, עמ׳ PDF 16).
**ג. הוראות של בני משפחה בדבר הטיפול הרצוי בקרובם אם יאבד כשירות.** שגויה, רצון המשפחה אינו ההנחיות של האדם עצמו. החוק מעמיד במרכז את רצונו החופשי של נותן ההנחיות, ולא הוראות שהמשפחה יוצרת במקומו (סעיפים 30–31, עמ׳ PDF 16).
**ד. הוראות של ועדה מוסדית בדבר הטיפול בחולה כשמתעוררת מחלוקת.** שגויה, החלטת ועדה במחלוקת אינה מסמך רצון עתידי שנותן אדם בעל כשירות, ולכן אינה ההגדרה שבסעיף 31 (עמ׳ PDF 16).

מקור: חוק החולה הנוטה למות, תשס״ו–2005, סעיפים 30–31, עמ׳ PDF 16.
label: Source: A_dying-patient-law_nevo-consolidated.htm · §31; corroborated PDF p16

q: מטופלת בת 82 מגיעה לבית חולים עם שברים חוזרים שאינם מוסברים היטב. לפי נוהל משרד הבריאות לטיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, מהי הגישה המתאימה?
o: לברר את החשד לאחר קבלת הוכחה לזהותו של הגורם לשברים
לברר את החשד ביחידות ובשיתוף עובד סוציאלי
לברר את החשד לאחר הגשת תלונה רשמית של המטופלת למשטרה
לברר את החשד בנוכחות המלווה ובאמצעות תשאול משותף
explanation:
**שברים בלתי מוסברים או חוזרים** נמנים בנוהל עם סימנים מחשידים לפגיעה פיזית. הם מצדיקים בירור, ואינם כשלעצמם הוכחה לזהות הפוגע. הנוהל מורה על בדיקה בסודיות וביחידות ועל זימון עובד סוציאלי כאשר קיים חשד (עמ׳ 6; נספח 1, עמ׳ PDF 8).
"שברים לא מוסברים, שברים חוזרים באיזורים שונים בגוף" (נספח 1, עמ׳ PDF 8).
"בכל מקרה בו קיים חשד להתעמרות יוזמן מיד רופא לבדיקת הנפגע." (עמ׳ 6, סעיף 8.1).

**א. לברר את החשד לאחר קבלת הוכחה לזהותו של הגורם לשברים.** שגויה, הנוהל מפעיל את הבירור כבר בחשד; הוא אינו דורש הוכחת זהות הפוגע כתנאי לבדיקה, עמ׳ 6.
**ב. לברר את החשד ביחידות ובשיתוף עובד סוציאלי.** נכונה, הבדיקה ביחידות וההערכה הסוציאלית תואמות את דרך הבירור שנקבעה כאשר קיים חשד, עמ׳ 6.
**ג. לברר את החשד לאחר הגשת תלונה רשמית של המטופלת למשטרה.** שגויה, הנוהל מורה להזמין רופא מיד עם החשד, ולא להמתין לתלונה במשטרה, עמ׳ 6.
**ד. לברר את החשד בנוכחות המלווה ובאמצעות תשאול משותף.** שגויה, הנוהל קובע בדיקה בסודיות וביחידות ללא מלווים, לפי שיקול המטפל; תשאול משותף אינו ממלא את מתכונת הבירור הזאת, עמ׳ 6.

מקור: משרד הבריאות, נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, עמ׳ 6 ונספח 1, עמ׳ PDF 8.

q: רופא בבית חולים חושד בהזנחה של מטופל קשיש על ידי המטפל העיקרי. מה חובתו?
o: לדווח למשטרה ולהשלים בכך את הטיפול, בלי לערב עובד סוציאלי ובלי לתעד את החשד
לערב עובד סוציאלי ולתעד; בחשד לפי תנאי החוק, לדווח לפקיד סעד או למשטרה
לבקש מן המטפל לשנות את התנהגותו ולהמתין להוכחה מלאה לפני בירור ותיעוד של החשד
לשחרר את המטופל לטיפולו של אותו מטפל ולהסתפק בהמלצה כללית למעקב בקהילה
explanation:
**חשד להזנחה** מחייב בירור, תיעוד והערכת סיכון, ואינו מסתיים בפנייה למשטרה בלבד. הנוהל דורש לערב עובד סוציאלי ולתעד את השיחה; חובת הדיווח חלה כאשר מתקיימים התנאים החוקיים של חשד סביר לעבירה בחסר ישע בידי האחראי עליו (עמ׳ 2 ו־6).
"בכל מקרה לגביו קיים חשד להתעמרות יזומן לבדיקה עובד סוציאלי." (סעיף 8.2, עמ׳ 6).

**א. לדווח למשטרה ולהשלים בכך את הטיפול, בלי לערב עובד סוציאלי ובלי לתעד את החשד.** שגויה, דיווח אינו מחליף את הזמנת העובד הסוציאלי, השיחה המתועדת והערכת הסיכון להמשך הפגיעה (סעיפים 8.2 עד 8.5, עמ׳ 6).
**ב. לערב עובד סוציאלי ולתעד; בחשד לפי תנאי החוק, לדווח לפקיד סעד או למשטרה.** נכונה, האפשרות משלבת את הבירור והתיעוד עם דיווח כאשר מתקיימת החובה, ולכן אינה מדלגת על הערכת הפגיעה והמשך הסיכון (סעיפים 1.2 ו־8.2 עד 8.5, עמ׳ 2 ו־6).
**ג. לבקש מן המטפל לשנות את התנהגותו ולהמתין להוכחה מלאה לפני בירור ותיעוד של החשד.** שגויה, הרף בנוהל הוא חשד, ובתנאי חובת הדיווח יסוד סביר לחשוב שנעברה עבירה; אין להמתין להוכחה מלאה לפני בירור ותיעוד (עמ׳ 2 ו־6).
**ד. לשחרר את המטופל לטיפולו של אותו מטפל ולהסתפק בהמלצה כללית למעקב בקהילה.** שגויה, הנוהל דורש הגנה על הנפגע ותכנון שחרור בתיאום עם פקיד הסעד והצוות. החזרה ללא בירור לאותו מטפל מתעלמת מהחשד ומהסיכון להמשך פגיעה (סעיפים 8.4, 9 ו־10.1, עמ׳ 6).

מקור: נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, סעיפים 1.2, 8, 9 ו־10, עמ׳ 2 ו־6.
ref: נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות · §1.2,§8.2–8.5; PDF pp2,6
label: Source: נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות · §1.2,§8.2–8.5; PDF pp2,6

q: In Hazzard's discussion of the free-radical theory of aging, which process links free-radical production to damage of cellular macromolecules?
o: Lipid peroxidation damages cellular proteins and nucleic acids
Lipid peroxidation protects cellular proteins against oxidative injury
Free-radical production reduces lipid peroxidation within aging cells
Free-radical production preserves nucleic acids by increasing caloric intake
explanation:
**Lipid peroxidation** is the main consequence of free-radical production described in this discussion (p. 1274). "The main consequence of free radical production is lipid peroxidation, which results in damage to cellular proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids." (p. 1274). The source presents increased caloric intake as a proposed driver of increased free-radical production and accelerated aging damage (p. 1274).

**A. Lipid peroxidation damages cellular proteins and nucleic acids.** Correct, this is the stated sequence: free-radical production, lipid peroxidation, and damage to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (p. 1274).
**B. Lipid peroxidation protects cellular proteins against oxidative injury.** Wrong, the source assigns a damaging effect to lipid peroxidation, rather than a protective effect on proteins (p. 1274).
**C. Free-radical production reduces lipid peroxidation within aging cells.** Wrong, free-radical production promotes lipid peroxidation in this account rather than reducing it (p. 1274).
**D. Free-radical production preserves nucleic acids by increasing caloric intake.** Wrong, the source links increased caloric intake to increased free-radical production and accelerated damage, rather than preservation of nucleic acids (p. 1274).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1274.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1274

q: What does the Hayflick limit describe in the discussion of cellular aging in Hazzard?
o: Limited cell replication in culture associated with telomere erosion
Estimation of biological age from patterns of DNA methylation
Calculation of predicted age from combined biochemical measurements
Estimation of coronary risk from the measured LDL cholesterol level
explanation:
**Telomere erosion limits cellular replication in vitro**. Hazzard calls this the Hayflick limit and distinguishes it from methylation clocks, composite age estimates, and disease-specific biomarkers (p. 602). "The gradual erosion of telomeres limits the replicative capacity of a cell in vitro, known as the Hayflick limit" (p. 602).

**A. Limited cell replication in culture associated with telomere erosion.** Correct, This matches the limit on a cultured cell's replicative capacity described by the source (p. 602).
**B. Estimation of biological age from patterns of DNA methylation.** Wrong, DNA methylation patterns underlie epigenetic age clocks, rather than the replication limit being defined here (p. 602).
**C. Calculation of predicted age from combined biochemical measurements.** Wrong, Composite biochemical age estimation is a biomarker strategy, not the telomere-related cell replication limit (p. 602).
**D. Estimation of coronary risk from the measured LDL cholesterol level.** Wrong, LDL cholesterol is discussed as a coronary-disease biomarker; it does not measure the defined in-vitro replication limit (p. 602).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 602.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 602, Aging biomarkers

q: Which statement matches the experimental evidence about the TOR pathway and longevity?
o: Inhibition by rapamycin can extend longevity in rodents and invertebrates
Inhibition by rapamycin can shorten longevity in rodents and invertebrates
Activation by rapamycin can extend longevity in rodents and invertebrates
Activation by rapamycin can shorten longevity in rodents and invertebrates
explanation:
**TOR** is a nutrient-sensing pathway that regulates protein translation in response to nutrient supply, stress, and hormonal signals. Rapamycin inhibits TOR; the longevity experiments described report extension of lifespan with this inhibition (p. 8).
"inhibition of TOR function by the drug rapamycin can extend longevity in rodents and invertebrates" (p. 8).
"TOR plays a major role in regulating protein translation rates and other key target pathways" (p. 8).

**A. Inhibition by rapamycin can extend longevity in rodents and invertebrates.** Correct, The source identifies rapamycin as an inhibitor and reports longer life in these experimental organisms (p. 8).
**B. Inhibition by rapamycin can shorten longevity in rodents and invertebrates.** Wrong, The reported direction is extension of longevity after TOR inhibition, not shortening (p. 8).
**C. Activation by rapamycin can extend longevity in rodents and invertebrates.** Wrong, Rapamycin acts through inhibition of TOR in the cited experiments, so the proposed activation mechanism is incorrect (p. 8).
**D. Activation by rapamycin can shorten longevity in rodents and invertebrates.** Wrong, This misstates both the inhibitory action of rapamycin and the extension of longevity reported (p. 8).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 8.
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: Which description of mammalian sirtuins is supported by Hazzard?
o: NAD+-consuming protein deacylases that regulate gene expression, DNA repair, and metabolism.
ATP-consuming protein kinases that regulate these processes by phosphorylating target proteins.
NAD+-consuming protein proteases that regulate these processes by degrading target proteins.
ATP-consuming DNA polymerases that regulate these processes by elongating telomeres.
explanation:
**Sirtuins** link a metabolic cofactor to protein modification: "The sirtuins are a family of protein deacylases that consume the metabolic cofactor NAD+ during catalysis" (p. 9). Their substrates are modified through deacetylation or removal of other posttranslational modifications, regulating gene expression, DNA repair, metabolism, and other processes (p. 10).

**A. NAD+-consuming protein deacylases that regulate gene expression, DNA repair, and metabolism.** Correct, the cofactor and enzyme class match the source, and the listed regulatory processes are explicitly described (pp. 9-10).
**B. ATP-consuming protein kinases that regulate these processes by phosphorylating target proteins.** Wrong, the source describes NAD+-dependent deacylation, not ATP-dependent phosphorylation, as the defining activity (pp. 9-10).
**C. NAD+-consuming protein proteases that regulate these processes by degrading target proteins.** Wrong, the described action removes modifications from protein substrates rather than degrading those substrates as a protease (pp. 9-10).
**D. ATP-consuming DNA polymerases that regulate these processes by elongating telomeres.** Wrong, sirtuins act on protein modifications; the source does not describe them as ATP-dependent DNA polymerases (pp. 9-10).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 9, 10.
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: According to Hazzard, which effect of dietary restriction has been described in rodents without establishing it as the mechanism of lifespan extension?
o: Increased efficiency of the mitochondrial electron transport chain
Slower mitochondrial respiration throughout the tissues of the animal
Increased damage from reactive oxygen species in liver tissue
Reduced adiposity through a global reduction in metabolic rate
explanation:
**Dietary restriction** increases mitochondrial electron transport efficiency and reduces oxidative damage in some tissues. Reduced adiposity is not simply due to a lower overall metabolic rate, and the mechanisms of lifespan extension remain uncertain (p. 6). "DR does, however, increase the efficiency of the mitochondrial electron transport chain," (p. 6).

**A. Increased efficiency of the mitochondrial electron transport chain.** Correct, the reported increase in electron transport efficiency is an observed effect, not proof of the longevity mechanism (p. 6).
**B. Slower mitochondrial respiration throughout the tissues of the animal.** Wrong, mitochondrial respiration actually increases in some tissues, which contradicts slowing throughout the tissues (p. 6).
**C. Increased damage from reactive oxygen species in liver tissue.** Wrong, the described change is reduced damage attributable to reactive oxygen species in tissues such as the liver (p. 6).
**D. Reduced adiposity through a global reduction in metabolic rate.** Wrong, the text explicitly rejects a simple global reduction in metabolic rate as the explanation for lower adiposity (p. 6).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 6.
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: Which description of cellular senescence is supported by Hazzard?
o: Nondividing cells persisting with secretion of inflammatory cytokines
Acceleration of cell division with suppression of inflammatory cytokines
Death and removal of cells following progressive telomere shortening
Resumption of cell division following activation of telomerase
explanation:
**Cellular senescence** involves cessation of proliferation while cells remain alive. Senescent cells express secreted enzymes and inflammatory cytokines; Hazzard describes their possible contribution to tissue aging without establishing a universal causal pathway to chronic inflammation (p. 13).
"after which the remaining cells survive indefinitely in a healthy but nondividing state." (p. 13).
"Senescent cells in vitro express a suite of secreted enzymes and inflammatory cytokines" (p. 13).

**A. Nondividing cells persisting with secretion of inflammatory cytokines.** Correct, cells can survive in a nondividing state, and senescent cells express inflammatory cytokines (p. 13).
**B. Acceleration of cell division with suppression of inflammatory cytokines.** Wrong, proliferation halts rather than accelerates, and the secretory phenotype includes inflammatory cytokines (p. 13).
**C. Death and removal of cells following progressive telomere shortening.** Wrong, cell death is distinguished from senescence: critically shortened telomeres can lead to either outcome, while senescent cells remain alive (p. 13).
**D. Resumption of cell division following activation of telomerase.** Wrong, resumed division is inconsistent with the cessation of proliferation that defines the senescent state (p. 13).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 13.
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: What does the term inflammaging describe in Hazzard?
o: A chronic, mild proinflammatory state associated with aging
An acute inflammatory response during a bacterial infection
An allergic inflammatory response following repeated allergen exposure
A chronic reduction in inflammatory cytokines during immune aging
explanation:
**Inflammaging** is the chronic, mild proinflammatory state associated with aging (p. 624). Hazzard describes "elevated levels of serum proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor" and notes its presence even in people free of disease and disability (p. 624). The definition does not require an acute infectious or allergic episode.

**A. A chronic, mild proinflammatory state associated with aging.** Correct, This captures the chronic, low-level proinflammatory pattern described by the source (p. 624).
**B. An acute inflammatory response during a bacterial infection.** Wrong, An acute infection is not the age-associated chronic state, which can be present in disease-free individuals (p. 624).
**C. An allergic inflammatory response following repeated allergen exposure.** Wrong, An allergen-triggered reaction is not the chronic age-associated pattern being defined (p. 624).
**D. A chronic reduction in inflammatory cytokines during immune aging.** Wrong, The source describes elevated, not reduced, proinflammatory cytokines (p. 624).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 624.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.624, 1386

q: Which description matches a stage 3 pressure injury in Hazzard?
o: Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat but no exposed tendon, muscle, or bone
Partial-thickness skin loss with a pink moist bed and exposed dermis but no visible fat
Full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed bone or muscle in the wound bed
Intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema and no loss of skin or visible fat
explanation:
**Stage 3 pressure injury** involves full-thickness skin loss with visible adipose tissue, without exposure of deeper structures such as muscle, tendon, or bone. Depth and the tissues exposed distinguish this stage from partial-thickness loss, intact erythematous skin, and stage 4 tissue loss (pp. 687-688).
"Full-thickness loss of skin, in which adipose (fat) is visible in the ulcer" (p. 687).
"Fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage, and/or bone are not exposed." (p. 687).

**A. Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat but no exposed tendon, muscle, or bone.** Correct, it combines the visible adipose tissue and absence of exposed deeper structures specified for stage 3 (p. 687).
**B. Partial-thickness skin loss with a pink moist bed and exposed dermis but no visible fat.** Wrong, partial-thickness loss and exposed dermis describe stage 2; stage 3 has full-thickness skin loss and visible fat (p. 687).
**C. Full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed bone or muscle in the wound bed.** Wrong, exposure of muscle or bone indicates the deeper tissue loss described for stage 4, exceeding stage 3 (pp. 687-688).
**D. Intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema and no loss of skin or visible fat.** Wrong, intact skin with nonblanchable erythema describes stage 1; stage 3 requires full-thickness skin loss (p. 687).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 687, 688.

q: A bedbound woman cannot reposition herself and is at risk for pressure injury. How should repositioning be planned?
o: Schedule repositioning according to the patient and support surface
Defer repositioning until a skin wound becomes apparent
Use risk assessment in place of a repositioning program
Stop repositioning after an appropriate support surface is installed
explanation:
Patients at risk who cannot move independently need **scheduled repositioning**. The schedule depends on the patient’s profile and the support surface; a support surface may affect frequency without replacing the program (p. 683). "Patients at risk for PI who are unable to move independently should be placed on scheduled repositioning programs." (p. 683).

**A. Schedule repositioning according to the patient and support surface.** Correct, this uses the patient profile and support surface to determine the repositioning schedule (p. 683).
**B. Defer repositioning until a skin wound becomes apparent.** Wrong, the recommendation applies to patients at risk, so waiting for a wound misses the preventive purpose (p. 683).
**C. Use risk assessment in place of a repositioning program.** Wrong, recognizing risk does not carry out the scheduled repositioning recommended for patients unable to move independently (p. 683).
**D. Stop repositioning after an appropriate support surface is installed.** Wrong, support surfaces affect the schedule; they do not cancel the recommendation for a repositioning program in this immobile patient (p. 683).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 683.

q: Which appearance is characteristic of deep tissue pressure injury (DTPI) in Hazzard's staging figure?
o: Persistent maroon or purple discoloration, or epidermal separation revealing a blood-filled blister
Localized nonblanchable erythema of intact skin without deep maroon or purple discoloration
Partial-thickness skin loss with moist pink exposed dermis and a serum-filled blister
Full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat and granulation but no exposed muscle
explanation:
**Deep tissue pressure injury** reflects intense or prolonged pressure and shear at the bone–muscle interface. The figure describes persistent deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, or epidermal separation revealing a dark wound bed or blood-filled blister, and distinguishes it from the other appearances listed (pp. 687–688). "This injury results from intense and/or prolonged pressure and shear forces at the bone-muscle interface." (p. 688)

**A. Persistent maroon or purple discoloration, or epidermal separation revealing a blood-filled blister.** Correct, This matches the characteristic deep discoloration or blood-filled blister described for DTPI (p. 688).
**B. Localized nonblanchable erythema of intact skin without deep maroon or purple discoloration.** Wrong, This is the stage 1 appearance; the figure explicitly distinguishes purple or maroon changes as potentially indicating DTPI (p. 687).
**C. Partial-thickness skin loss with moist pink exposed dermis and a serum-filled blister.** Wrong, Exposed viable pink dermis with a serum-filled blister describes stage 2, rather than the deep discoloration or blood-filled blister characteristic of DTPI (pp. 687–688).
**D. Full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat and granulation but no exposed muscle.** Wrong, Visible fat and granulation describe full-thickness stage 3 loss; the DTPI definition directs such visible tissue loss to full-thickness staging (pp. 687–688).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 688, 687.

q: Which mechanism explains pressure injury development?
o: Prolonged pressure compresses tissues and compromises their circulation
Surface friction produces hyperkeratosis while deep tissues remain unloaded
Improved tissue perfusion reduces oxygen requirements and causes tissue injury
Accumulated fat shields tissues from deformation and thereby causes tissue injury
explanation:
**Pressure injury** results from intense or prolonged pressure, sometimes combined with shear (p. 679). Sustained loading can deform cells directly and impair circulation (p. 681). Hazzard states: "If pressure is not relieved, the blood vessels collapse and thrombose"; tissues are then deprived of oxygen, nutrients, and waste removal (p. 681).

**A. Prolonged pressure compresses tissues and compromises their circulation.** Correct, This describes the mechanical loading and circulatory compromise in the source (pp. 679, 681).
**B. Surface friction produces hyperkeratosis while deep tissues remain unloaded.** Wrong, Surface friction without deep pressure does not describe the pressure-induced tissue compression and injury mechanism (pp. 679, 681).
**C. Improved tissue perfusion reduces oxygen requirements and causes tissue injury.** Wrong, The source describes compromised circulation and oxygen deprivation, not improved perfusion, as injurious (p. 681).
**D. Accumulated fat shields tissues from deformation and thereby causes tissue injury.** Wrong, The source describes tissue deformation as a key damaging factor; protection from deformation does not explain that mechanism (p. 681).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 679, 681.

q: A nursing team uses a structured tool such as Braden to assess pressure-injury risk at admission. What is the purpose of using the result according to Hazzard?
o: Direct preventive measures toward risks found during assessment
Replace the prevention plan with documentation of the resulting score
Schedule reassessment after a pressure injury becomes clinically apparent
Reduce support-surface use when the assessment identifies high risk
explanation:
**Pressure-injury risk assessment** is intended to direct prevention resources and interventions toward identified risks. The source also calls for assessment at admission and periodic reassessment, so the score informs ongoing care rather than replacing preventive action (p. 683).
"This tool is scored in six areas of risk and provides direction to target interventions to those specific risk factors." (p. 683).

**A. Direct preventive measures toward risks found during assessment.** Correct, the Braden tool is described as directing interventions to specific risk factors (p. 683).
**B. Replace the prevention plan with documentation of the resulting score.** Wrong, documentation does not substitute for prevention: identified risks should lead to interventions that reduce them (p. 683).
**C. Schedule reassessment after a pressure injury becomes clinically apparent.** Wrong, risk should be reassessed periodically after admission, rather than waiting for an injury to appear (p. 683).
**D. Reduce support-surface use when the assessment identifies high risk.** Wrong, support surfaces are part of prevention for at-risk patients; recognizing high risk is a reason to apply prevention, not reduce it (p. 683).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 683.

q: A patient has a stage 4 pressure injury over the sacrum. Which description matches this stage?
o: Full-thickness loss with exposed deep structures and osteomyelitis risk
Intact skin with nonblanchable erythema and preserved deeper tissue
Partial-thickness loss with a moist wound bed and a serum-filled blister
Visible subcutaneous fat with granulation and covered bone and tendon
explanation:
A **stage 4 pressure injury** exposes deep structures such as bone, muscle, or tendon. Hazzard describes osteomyelitis as a common outcome when bone is exposed; this distinguishes it from the shallower tissue involvement in earlier stages (pp. 686–687).
"Full-thickness loss of skin with exposure of bone, muscle, tendon, ligament, or cartilage." (p. 686).
"Osteomyelitis is a common outcome when there is exposure of bone and should be considered the cause of nonhealing in any stage 4 PI." (p. 686).

**A. Full-thickness loss with exposed deep structures and osteomyelitis risk.** Correct, This captures the deep exposure of stage 4 and the source-described risk when bone is exposed (p. 686).
**B. Intact skin with nonblanchable erythema and preserved deeper tissue.** Wrong, Intact skin with nonblanchable erythema describes stage 1, not the full-thickness deep exposure of stage 4 (pp. 686–687).
**C. Partial-thickness loss with a moist wound bed and a serum-filled blister.** Wrong, Partial-thickness loss and a serum-filled blister describe stage 2 rather than exposed deep structures (pp. 686–687).
**D. Visible subcutaneous fat with granulation and covered bone and tendon.** Wrong, Stage 3 can expose fat, but the source explicitly excludes exposed muscle, tendon, or bone from that stage (pp. 686–687).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 686, 687.

q: What is the principle of moist wound healing in the treatment of pressure injuries?
o: A moist environment facilitates cellular migration and promotes wound healing.
A dry environment with air exposure facilitates epithelial migration and wound healing.
A moist environment inhibits epithelial migration and slows superficial wound closure.
A dry gauze dressing promotes healing better than a moisture-retentive dressing.
explanation:
**Moist wound healing** maintains fluid beneath the dressing to facilitate epithelial migration. Hazzard describes trial and comparative-study support for moisture-retentive dressings over dry gauze and more rapid re-epithelialization than with air exposure (p. 693). "These dressings are changed every 3 to 5 days, which allows wound fluid to gather underneath the dressing, facilitating epithelial migration." (p. 693).

**A. A moist environment facilitates cellular migration and promotes wound healing.** Correct, retaining wound fluid facilitates epithelial migration, which supports wound closure (p. 693).
**B. A dry environment with air exposure facilitates epithelial migration and wound healing.** Wrong, the source reports faster re-epithelialization in a moist environment than in wounds left open to air (p. 693).
**C. A moist environment inhibits epithelial migration and slows superficial wound closure.** Wrong, the described effect of retained wound fluid is facilitation, not inhibition, of epithelial migration (p. 693).
**D. A dry gauze dressing promotes healing better than a moisture-retentive dressing.** Wrong, the comparative evidence described supports moist dressings over dry gauze, not a healing advantage for dry gauze (p. 693).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 693.

q: When adequate wound perfusion has been confirmed, which pressure-injury finding supports debridement to remove devitalized tissue?
o: Devitalized tissue forming yellow slough within the wound bed
Stable dry adherent eschar covering skin over the heel
Intact skin showing localized nonblanchable erythema over a prominence
Viable pink moist dermis exposed within the wound bed
explanation:
**Debridement** targets nonviable tissue: Hazzard states, "It reduces devitalized or necrotic tissue, decreases risk for infection, and promotes granulation tissue formation." (p. 695). Adequate perfusion is required; stable heel eschar is specifically protected from removal (pp. 688, 696). Intact skin and viable dermis are different tissue states from the slough targeted here (p. 687).

**A. Devitalized tissue forming yellow slough within the wound bed.** Correct, slough is devitalized material targeted by debridement, and adequate perfusion addresses the prerequisite given in the stem (pp. 695–696).
**B. Stable dry adherent eschar covering skin over the heel.** Wrong, stable heel eschar should not be removed; the source defines stability by dryness, adherence and intactness without erythema or fluctuance (p. 688).
**C. Intact skin showing localized nonblanchable erythema over a prominence.** Wrong, intact skin with nonblanchable erythema is the stage-one description, not a wound bed containing devitalized tissue for removal (pp. 687, 695).
**D. Viable pink moist dermis exposed within the wound bed.** Wrong, the stage-two description identifies viable, pink or red, moist dermis without slough or eschar; this does not supply the devitalized tissue targeted by the question (pp. 687, 695).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th edition, pp. 687, 688, 695, 696.

q: An ambulant older adult has chronic constipation and can drink adequate fluids. There is no fecal impaction or rectal evacuation disorder. Which initial medication regimen follows Table 87-11 in Hazzard?
o: Give senna together with lactulose as the starting daily regimen
Give psyllium with adequate fluids as the starting daily regimen
Give daily oil-retention enemas as the starting evacuation regimen
Give regular glycerin suppositories as the starting evacuation regimen
explanation:
A **bulk laxative** is the starting point in the table for ambulant older people with adequate fluid intake. The stepwise approach separates uncomplicated chronic constipation from high-risk patients, impaction, and rectal outlet delay (p. 1378).
"Bulk laxative (psyllium) 1–3 times daily with fluids as required" (p. 1378).
"Senna 2–3 tablets at bedtime and sorbitol or lactulose 30 mL daily, titrating upward as needed" (p. 1378).

**A. Give senna together with lactulose as the starting daily regimen.** Wrong, the table places the senna-plus-lactulose regimen in the high-risk pathway, rather than as the starting step for this ambulant patient (p. 1378).
**B. Give psyllium with adequate fluids as the starting daily regimen.** Correct, psyllium with fluids is the initial regimen in the ambulant chronic-constipation pathway (p. 1378).
**C. Give daily oil-retention enemas as the starting evacuation regimen.** Wrong, oil-retention enemas belong to the impaction-with-obstruction pathway, which the stem does not describe (p. 1378).
**D. Give regular glycerin suppositories as the starting evacuation regimen.** Wrong, regular glycerin suppositories belong to the rectal-outlet-delay pathway, not the starting step specified here (p. 1378).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1378.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1378, Table 87-11

q: A 78-year-old patient with advanced dementia takes oxycodone for chronic pain and has severe constipation. Which treatment sequence is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Use laxatives such as PEG, then consider methylnaltrexone if refractory
Use methylnaltrexone first, then consider laxatives if refractory
Use regular docusate first, then consider magnesium citrate if refractory
Use magnesium citrate first, then consider regular docusate if refractory
explanation:
**Opioid-induced constipation** results from enteric opioid effects that reduce bowel tone and contractility and increase fluid absorption and anal sphincter tone (pp. 1377-1378). The source suggests "nonpharmacologic interventions and laxatives as first-line therapy" and recommends peripheral opioid antagonists for refractory constipation (p. 1378).

**A. Use laxatives such as PEG, then consider methylnaltrexone if refractory.** Correct, The sequence starts with the recommended first-line approach and reserves methylnaltrexone, a peripheral opioid antagonist, for refractory constipation (pp. 1376, 1378).
**B. Use methylnaltrexone first, then consider laxatives if refractory.** Wrong, The source places laxatives before peripheral opioid antagonists rather than reserving laxatives for failure of methylnaltrexone (p. 1378).
**C. Use regular docusate first, then consider magnesium citrate if refractory.** Wrong, Docusate is ineffective in older people, and magnesium citrate is not recommended because of adverse-effect risk (p. 1376).
**D. Use magnesium citrate first, then consider regular docusate if refractory.** Wrong, Magnesium citrate is not recommended in older people, and docusate is ineffective for their constipation (p. 1376).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376, 1377, 1378.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 1376–1378

q: An older adult with constipation takes verapamil, amitriptyline, and oral ferrous sulfate. Which assessment of these medications agrees with Table 87-5?
o: Consider contributions from verapamil, the tricyclic antidepressant, and the iron supplement
Consider verapamil and the tricyclic antidepressant; regard the iron supplement as protective
Consider the tricyclic antidepressant and iron supplement; regard verapamil as protective
Consider verapamil and the iron supplement; regard the tricyclic antidepressant as protective
explanation:
**Medication review** should consider multiple constipating agents. Table 87-5 lists anticholinergic drugs including tricyclics, iron supplements, and calcium channel antagonists including verapamil (p. 1359). The accompanying text explains that "Calcium channel antagonists impair lower gut motility" (p. 1359).

**A. Consider contributions from verapamil, the tricyclic antidepressant, and the iron supplement.** Correct, each of these medication groups appears among the source’s risk factors for constipation (p. 1359).
**B. Consider verapamil and the tricyclic antidepressant; regard the iron supplement as protective.** Wrong, iron supplements are listed as a risk factor, not a protective influence (Table 87-5, p. 1359).
**C. Consider the tricyclic antidepressant and iron supplement; regard verapamil as protective.** Wrong, verapamil is explicitly listed, and calcium channel antagonists impair lower gut motility (p. 1359).
**D. Consider verapamil and the iron supplement; regard the tricyclic antidepressant as protective.** Wrong, anticholinergic drugs, including tricyclics, are listed as risk factors rather than protective agents (p. 1359).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1359.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1359, Table 87-5

q: An older adult reports constipation despite having a bowel movement daily. For at least 12 weeks in the last year, straining has occurred with more than one quarter of bowel movements. Loose stools do not occur without laxatives, and criteria for irritable bowel syndrome are insufficient. According to Table 87-1, which additional symptom occurring with more than one quarter of bowel movements supplies a second listed symptom?
o: A sensation of incomplete evacuation after a bowel movement
A sensation of marked abdominal bloating after finishing a meal
A sensation of early satiety while eating a usual meal
Recurrent abdominal pain appearing after finishing a usual meal
explanation:
**Constipation symptoms** in Table 87-1 extend beyond stool frequency: the list includes straining and "Sensation of incomplete evacuation" (p. 1354). Thus daily bowel movements do not prevent the two-symptom requirement from being met. The question uses the duration and frequency stated in that table.

**A. A sensation of incomplete evacuation after a bowel movement.** Correct, incomplete evacuation is a listed symptom distinct from the straining already described (p. 1354).
**B. A sensation of marked abdominal bloating after finishing a meal.** Wrong, post-meal bloating is not one of the table’s enumerated qualifying symptoms (p. 1354).
**C. A sensation of early satiety while eating a usual meal.** Wrong, early satiety is not one of the table’s enumerated qualifying symptoms (p. 1354).
**D. Recurrent abdominal pain appearing after finishing a usual meal.** Wrong, post-meal abdominal pain is not one of the table’s enumerated qualifying symptoms; it does not supply the second symptom requested (p. 1354).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1354.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · Table 87-1, p. 1354

q: An 85-year-old woman has severe constipation and fecal incontinence. Rectal examination finds a firm, large mass of stool. What initial treatment sequence agrees with Hazzard?
o: Manually evacuate before inserting an enema or suppository.
Insert a soapsuds enema before attempting to remove the impaction.
Insert a suppository before attempting to remove the impacted stool.
Begin oral docusate and await passage of the impacted stool.
explanation:
For a **firm, large rectal impaction**, Hazzard specifies manual evacuation before insertion of an enema or suppository. Docusate is ineffective for constipation or rectal outlet delay in older people, and soapsuds enemas should not be used in this population (p. 1376).
"In patients who have a firm and large rectal impaction, manual evacuation should be performed before inserting enemas or suppositories," (p. 1376).

**A. Manually evacuate before inserting an enema or suppository.** Correct, manual clearance before rectal medication is the recommended sequence for this examination finding (p. 1376).
**B. Insert a soapsuds enema before attempting to remove the impaction.** Wrong, soapsuds enemas should not be administered to older patients, and the large firm impaction calls for manual evacuation first (p. 1376).
**C. Insert a suppository before attempting to remove the impacted stool.** Wrong, suppository insertion should follow manual evacuation for a firm, large rectal impaction (p. 1376).
**D. Begin oral docusate and await passage of the impacted stool.** Wrong, docusate is not effective for this constipation or outlet problem and does not supply the recommended initial evacuation (p. 1376).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1374,1378 (Tables 87-9,87-11)

q: How do stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl differ from osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol and lactulose?
o: Stimulants promote intestinal motility; osmotic agents increase fluid within the intestinal lumen.
Stimulants mainly draw in fluid osmotically; osmotic agents primarily stimulate the myenteric plexus.
Stimulants lubricate stool with an oily layer; osmotic agents antagonize intestinal opioid receptors.
Stimulants and osmotic agents activate a shared receptor; their distinction is the route of administration.
explanation:
**Stimulant and osmotic laxatives** differ in their mechanisms. Hazzard describes senna as stimulating the myenteric plexus and increasing motility, bisacodyl as having secretory and prokinetic effects, and PEG as increasing intraluminal fluid osmotically (Table 87-9, pp. 1373–1374). "Osmotically increases intraluminal fluids" (p. 1373).

**A. Stimulants promote intestinal motility; osmotic agents increase fluid within the intestinal lumen.** Correct, the distinction captures the motility-promoting action of stimulants and the luminal-fluid effect of osmotic agents (pp. 1373–1374).
**B. Stimulants mainly draw in fluid osmotically; osmotic agents primarily stimulate the myenteric plexus.** Wrong, the table attributes the osmotic fluid effect to PEG and the myenteric-plexus stimulation to senna, so these assigned mechanisms do not fit the named classes (pp. 1373–1374).
**C. Stimulants lubricate stool with an oily layer; osmotic agents antagonize intestinal opioid receptors.** Wrong, neither proposed mechanism describes senna or PEG in the table: senna stimulates motility and PEG increases intraluminal fluid osmotically (pp. 1373–1374).
**D. Stimulants and osmotic agents activate a shared receptor; their distinction is the route of administration.** Wrong, the table distinguishes their mechanisms, including neural stimulation for senna and an osmotic fluid effect for PEG; a shared receptor does not explain that distinction (pp. 1373–1374).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1373, 1374.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · Table 87-9, pp. 1373–1374

q: A 90-year-old patient with severe dementia has chronic constipation despite trials of polyethylene glycol and lactulose. Which additional laxative is supported by Hazzard?
o: Add a stimulant laxative such as bisacodyl or senna
Add a stool-softening laxative such as oral docusate
Add a magnesium salt such as oral magnesium citrate
Add an irritant laxative such as oral castor oil
explanation:
**Stimulant laxatives** are among the treatment options for constipation in older people (p. 1375). Hazzard states: "Bisacodyl is a useful alternative stimulant laxative to Senna" and reports improved stool frequency and consistency in a trial (p. 1375).

**A. Add a stimulant laxative such as bisacodyl or senna.** Correct, Bisacodyl is a supported stimulant alternative to senna, with trial evidence of improved stool frequency and consistency (p. 1375).
**B. Add a stool-softening laxative such as oral docusate.** Wrong, The source finds docusate ineffective for constipation in older people (p. 1376).
**C. Add a magnesium salt such as oral magnesium citrate.** Wrong, Magnesium citrate has greater adverse-effect risk, including colonic pseudo-obstruction, and is not recommended in older people (p. 1376).
**D. Add an irritant laxative such as oral castor oil.** Wrong, Castor oil should not be used in older people because of its high risk of adverse effects (p. 1375).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1375, 1376.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 1372, 1375, 1378

q: What does overflow fecal incontinence that resembles diarrhea represent, and what finding should guide its treatment?
o: Watery leakage around impacted stool, calling for clearance of the impaction
Watery leakage indicating an empty colon, calling for reduced laxative use
Watery leakage indicating rapid transit, calling for suppression of bowel movements
Watery leakage excluding stool retention, calling for deferral of rectal assessment
explanation:
**Overflow fecal incontinence** can be mistaken for diarrhea even though retained stool is the underlying problem. Hazzard states, "Fecal impaction must be ruled out in the presence of fecal soiling or incontinence"; a large, firm rectal impaction is manually evacuated before enemas or suppositories (pp. 1363, 1376).

**A. Watery leakage around impacted stool, calling for clearance of the impaction.** Correct, The source links watery leakage to overflow and requires evaluation for impaction; identified impaction needs clearance (pp. 1363, 1376).
**B. Watery leakage indicating an empty colon, calling for reduced laxative use.** Wrong, Watery leakage does not establish an empty colon; it is specifically described as a presentation in which impaction must be excluded (p. 1363).
**C. Watery leakage indicating rapid transit, calling for suppression of bowel movements.** Wrong, Inference from the impaction treatment: suppressing bowel movements does not address the retained mass that requires evacuation (pp. 1363, 1376).
**D. Watery leakage excluding stool retention, calling for deferral of rectal assessment.** Wrong, The source directs assessment for fecal impaction when leakage is present, rather than treating leakage as evidence against retention (p. 1363).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1363, 1376.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 1363, 1376

q: Which description of lactulose matches the source table that lists flatulence and abdominal cramps among its adverse effects?
o: Colonic bacteria metabolize the nonabsorbable disaccharide
Stool lubrication by mineral oil is its principal action
Direct blockade of intestinal chloride channels causes fluid loss
Systemic absorption replaces an intestinal osmotic effect
explanation:
**Lactulose** is listed as a hyperosmolar agent with the same adverse effects as sorbitol, including transient abdominal cramps and flatulence. The table describes these nonabsorbable disaccharides as being metabolized by colonic bacteria to acetic acid and other short-chain fatty acids (p. 1373).
"Nonabsorbable disaccharides metabolized by colonic bacteria into acetic acid and other short-chain fatty acids" (p. 1373).
"Sweet tasting, transient abdominal cramps, flatulence" (p. 1373).

**A. Colonic bacteria metabolize the nonabsorbable disaccharide.** Correct, The table identifies bacterial metabolism of nonabsorbable disaccharides, alongside cramps and flatulence, supporting this explanation (p. 1373).
**B. Stool lubrication by mineral oil is its principal action.** Wrong, The table identifies a hyperosmolar disaccharide mechanism, not lubrication with mineral oil (p. 1373).
**C. Direct blockade of intestinal chloride channels causes fluid loss.** Wrong, The stated mechanism is bacterial metabolism of a nonabsorbable disaccharide; chloride-channel blockade is not that mechanism (p. 1373).
**D. Systemic absorption replaces an intestinal osmotic effect.** Wrong, The table expressly calls the disaccharides nonabsorbable and classifies them as hyperosmolar agents, contradicting systemic absorption as their action (p. 1373).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1373.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 1373, 1376

q: מהו הקו הראשון בטיפול באינסומניה כרונית בקשישים?
o: CBT-I (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia)
Zolpidem כטיפול התחלתי לפני ניסיון טיפול התנהגותי
Lorazepam כטיפול התחלתי לפני ניסיון טיפול התנהגותי
Zaleplon כטיפול התחלתי לפני ניסיון טיפול התנהגותי
explanation:
CBT-I מומלץ כקו ראשון; טיפול תרופתי נשקל במצב חד או לאחר כישלון טיפול התנהגותי (p 659)
Zolpidem כטיפול התחלתי לפני ניסיון טיפול התנהגותי — הספר מעדיף CBT-I כקו ראשון ולא התחלה שגרתית בתרופה (p 659)
Lorazepam כטיפול התחלתי לפני ניסיון טיפול התנהגותי — תרופות שינה כרוכות בתופעות לוואי; הן אינן קודמות ל-CBT-I (p 659)
Zaleplon כטיפול התחלתי לפני ניסיון טיפול התנהגותי — הקו הראשון המומלץ הוא CBT-I ולא התחלה במשרה שינה (p 659)

q: Which benefit-risk profile does the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria describe for zolpidem in older adults?
o: Minimal improvement in sleep, with a risk of delirium and falls.
Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in fall risk.
Minimal improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.
Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.
explanation:
**Zolpidem** belongs to the nonbenzodiazepine benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics listed in Beers (p. 2060). The criteria describe "minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration" alongside adverse events including delirium, falls, and fractures, supporting the recommendation to avoid these agents in older adults (p. 2060).

**A. Minimal improvement in sleep, with a risk of delirium and falls.** Correct, the limited sleep benefit and the stated adverse events match the source (p. 2060).
**B. Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in fall risk.** Wrong, the source describes minimal benefit and falls as an adverse event, not substantial benefit with fall protection (p. 2060).
**C. Minimal improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.** Wrong, although the benefit is described as minimal, delirium is a listed adverse event rather than a risk reduced by treatment (p. 2060).
**D. Substantial improvement in sleep, with a reduction in delirium risk.** Wrong, both parts conflict with the source: benefit is minimal, and delirium is an adverse event (p. 2060).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2060.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: Which mechanism describes obstructive sleep apnea, a sleep-disordered breathing condition that can present with daytime sleepiness and nocturia?
o: Upper-airway obstruction despite continuing respiratory effort
Lower-airway obstruction despite continuing respiratory effort
Failure of the respiratory center to send a breathing signal
Primary nocturnal urine production with maintained airway patency
explanation:
**Obstructive sleep apnea** involves upper-airway obstruction despite respiratory effort. Hazzard distinguishes this from central events caused by failure of the respiratory controller to signal breathing; daytime sleepiness and nocturia are relevant symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing (p. 646).
"Obstructive events occur from anatomic obstruction of the upper airway despite respiratory effort." (p. 646).
"Central events result from a failure of the respiratory control center to send a signal to breathe." (p. 646).

**A. Upper-airway obstruction despite continuing respiratory effort.** Correct, This is the mechanism stated for obstructive events (p. 646).
**B. Lower-airway obstruction despite continuing respiratory effort.** Wrong, The obstruction described for OSA is in the upper airway, not the lower airway (p. 646).
**C. Failure of the respiratory center to send a breathing signal.** Wrong, Failure of the central breathing signal defines central events, whereas obstructive events occur despite respiratory effort (p. 646).
**D. Primary nocturnal urine production with maintained airway patency.** Wrong, Nocturia is a symptom that can accompany sleep-disordered breathing; it does not replace the upper-airway obstruction that defines the obstructive event (p. 646).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 646.

q: Which combination defines REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) according to Hazzard?
o: Dream enactment during REM sleep with loss of normal muscle atonia
Complex movements during NREM sleep with normal muscle atonia during REM
Threatening dreams during REM sleep with preserved normal muscle atonia
Complex movements during wakefulness with normal muscle tone during sleep
explanation:
**RBD combines dream enactment with REM sleep without atonia**. Normal REM sleep includes skeletal muscle atonia, whereas its absence permits the motor behavior described in RBD; the source also links RBD with synucleinopathies (p. 654). "However, in RBD there is REM sleep without atonia, which is required for the diagnosis of RBD, in addition to dream enactment behavior." (p. 654)

**A. Dream enactment during REM sleep with loss of normal muscle atonia.** Correct, This includes both features required by the source: dream enactment and REM sleep without atonia (p. 654).
**B. Complex movements during NREM sleep with normal muscle atonia during REM.** Wrong, NREM movements with preserved REM atonia do not meet the required REM-without-atonia component (p. 654).
**C. Threatening dreams during REM sleep with preserved normal muscle atonia.** Wrong, Threatening dream content alone does not satisfy dream enactment plus loss of REM atonia (p. 654).
**D. Complex movements during wakefulness with normal muscle tone during sleep.** Wrong, Wakeful movements do not meet the required occurrence during REM sleep without atonia (p. 654).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 654.

q: Which pattern of sleep architecture and efficiency is described with aging?
o: Less N3 sleep, more sleep fragmentation, and lower sleep efficiency.
More N3 sleep, less sleep fragmentation, and higher sleep efficiency.
Less N3 sleep, less sleep fragmentation, and higher sleep efficiency.
More N3 sleep, more sleep fragmentation, and higher sleep efficiency.
explanation:
**Aging sleep** includes less deep N3 sleep, greater fragmentation, and reduced sleep efficiency. Sleep efficiency is the time actually asleep divided by time spent in bed, distinguishing sleep quantity from time in bed (p. 643). "Longer time to initiate sleep and more fragmented sleep occur with aging." (p. 643).

**A. Less N3 sleep, more sleep fragmentation, and lower sleep efficiency.** Correct, all three changes match the source's description (p. 643).
**B. More N3 sleep, less sleep fragmentation, and higher sleep efficiency.** Wrong, N3 and efficiency decrease, while fragmentation increases; this proposed improvement in continuity is not the described pattern (p. 643).
**C. Less N3 sleep, less sleep fragmentation, and higher sleep efficiency.** Wrong, the N3 direction matches, but fragmentation increases and efficiency decreases (p. 643).
**D. More N3 sleep, more sleep fragmentation, and higher sleep efficiency.** Wrong, the fragmentation direction matches, but N3 and efficiency decrease rather than increase (p. 643).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 643.
label: Source: hazzard marked .pdf · 643

q: An 80-year-old woman reports restless legs in the evening. Which laboratory test does Hazzard recommend to evaluate iron deficiency as a contributor?
o: Measure the serum ferritin concentration
Measure the serum thyroid-stimulating hormone
Measure the blood glycated hemoglobin
Measure the morning serum cortisol
explanation:
**Serum ferritin** is part of the evaluation of restless legs syndrome (RLS): "Patients with RLS or PLMD should have a serum ferritin measured to rule out any degree of iron deficiency contributing to these conditions." (p. 652). The proposed pathophysiology involves disturbed iron regulation and consequent dopamine dysfunction, although the exact mechanisms are not known (p. 652).

**A. Measure the serum ferritin concentration.** Correct, this is the measurement explicitly recommended to look for iron deficiency contributing to the leg symptoms (p. 652).
**B. Measure the serum thyroid-stimulating hormone.** Wrong, this does not supply the ferritin measurement specified for evaluating the iron-deficiency contribution to RLS (p. 652).
**C. Measure the blood glycated hemoglobin.** Wrong, this does not provide the ferritin result on which the chapter bases assessment of iron deficiency and consideration of iron replacement (p. 652).
**D. Measure the morning serum cortisol.** Wrong, a morning cortisol measurement does not supply the serum ferritin result required for the iron-focused evaluation described (p. 652).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th edition, pp. 652.

q: An older patient has symptomatic osteoarthritis confined to one knee and has not yet tried pharmacological treatment. There is no contraindication to topical treatment. Which initial drug treatment does Hazzard recommend?
o: Diclofenac gel applied locally to the knee
Celecoxib tablets at a standard oral dose
Tramadol tablets taken by the oral route
Triamcinolone injected into the knee joint
explanation:
**Topical NSAIDs** are recommended before oral NSAIDs for knee osteoarthritis because of their pain relief and favorable adverse-effect profile (p. 787). Hazzard describes them as "first-line pharmacological therapy to treat hand and knee OA prior to starting oral NSAIDs" (p. 787).

**A. Diclofenac gel applied locally to the knee.** Correct, diclofenac gel is the named example of the recommended topical first-line approach (p. 787).
**B. Celecoxib tablets at a standard oral dose.** Wrong, oral NSAIDs follow topical treatment in this localized, previously untreated presentation (p. 787).
**C. Tramadol tablets taken by the oral route.** Wrong, tramadol is reserved for contraindications or inadequate responses to other treatments, rather than this initial topical-treatment opportunity (p. 788).
**D. Triamcinolone injected into the knee joint.** Wrong, intra-articular glucocorticoids are discussed for continuing symptoms after other measures, whereas topical NSAIDs are the first-line treatment here (pp. 787–789).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 787, 788, 789.
label: Source: hazzard marked .pdf · 787

q: Why do oral NSAIDs require particular caution in older adults with osteoarthritis?
o: They increase gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular risks
They increase gastrointestinal risk while improving renal function
They increase renal risk while improving heart-failure congestion
They increase gastrointestinal risk while improving hypertension
explanation:
**Oral NSAID toxicity** involves more than gastrointestinal bleeding: Hazzard also describes nephrotoxicity and cardiovascular adverse effects (pp. 787–788). NSAIDs can worsen heart failure "by impairing renal sodium and water excretion and contributing to intravascular volume overload" (p. 1173). They can also exacerbate hypertension rather than treating it (p. 1074).

**A. They increase gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular risks.** Correct, bleeding, nephrotoxicity, and cardiovascular complications are all source-described concerns in older patients with OA and comorbidities (pp. 787–788, 1173).
**B. They increase gastrointestinal risk while improving renal function.** Wrong, nephrotoxicity is a stated adverse effect; improved renal function is not the renal effect described here (p. 788).
**C. They increase renal risk while improving heart-failure congestion.** Wrong, impaired sodium and water excretion can worsen congestion and heart failure, rather than improve it (p. 1173).
**D. They increase gastrointestinal risk while improving hypertension.** Wrong, NSAIDs can exacerbate hypertension; the proposed blood-pressure benefit conflicts with the source (p. 1074).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 787, 788, 1173, 1074.
ref: AGS Beers Criteria 2023 — Tables 2–3, pp 2062–2063, 2065 (IMA P005 required article 1)

q: After accounting for study bias, how does Hazzard summarize evidence for intra-articular hyaluronic acid injections in osteoarthritis?
o: Meta-analyses found no clear benefit for osteoarthritis symptoms
Meta-analyses found a clearer benefit for hip osteoarthritis
Meta-analyses found consistent benefit after correction for study bias
Meta-analyses found superiority supporting use as first-line treatment
explanation:
**Viscosupplementation** has a biological rationale because hyaluronic acid is a constituent of synovial fluid, but that does not establish clinical benefit. Meta-analyses found "no clear benefit of intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection for the treatment of OA symptoms" after addressing bias, especially in hip osteoarthritis (p. 789). The source still allows that selected patients may benefit from a trial after other options fail.

**A. Meta-analyses found no clear benefit for osteoarthritis symptoms.** Correct, This reflects the bias-adjusted evidence summary, without asserting that no individual could benefit (p. 789).
**B. Meta-analyses found a clearer benefit for hip osteoarthritis.** Wrong, Hip osteoarthritis is specifically emphasized in the finding of no clear benefit, not stronger benefit (p. 789).
**C. Meta-analyses found consistent benefit after correction for study bias.** Wrong, The absence of clear benefit persisted when study bias was addressed (p. 789).
**D. Meta-analyses found superiority supporting use as first-line treatment.** Wrong, The cited guidelines do not recommend viscosupplementation on the available evidence; the possible individual trial described follows failure of other options (p. 789).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 789.
ref: Hazzard Ch 52 — OSTEOARTHRITIS · Harrison Ch 382 — Approach to Articular and Musculoskeletal Disease

q: Which situation supports considering total knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis in a patient healthy enough to undergo surgery?
o: Persistent pain and substantial functional loss despite maximal conservative treatment
Radiographic joint changes before a trial of treatment in a person without symptoms
Mild pain controlled by conservative treatment in a person seeking less physical activity
Persistent pain with preserved function before adequate trials of conservative treatment
explanation:
**Joint replacement** is considered when severe osteoarthritis causes persistent pain and loss of function despite conservative treatment. Fitness for surgery matters; age and comorbidities inform shared decisions rather than automatically preventing an offer of surgery (p. 789).
"Surgical intervention should be considered in OA patients who continue to have significant pain and disability despite maximal use of nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic therapies." (p. 789).
"Patients must also be healthy enough to withstand surgery." (p. 789).

**A. Persistent pain and substantial functional loss despite maximal conservative treatment.** Correct, this combines failed conservative treatment with the persistent pain and functional loss described as indications (p. 789).
**B. Radiographic joint changes before a trial of treatment in a person without symptoms.** Wrong, radiographic changes without symptoms or a conservative-treatment trial do not meet those clinical indications (p. 789).
**C. Mild pain controlled by conservative treatment in a person seeking less physical activity.** Wrong, controlled mild pain does not meet the criterion of persistent significant symptoms despite treatment (p. 789).
**D. Persistent pain with preserved function before adequate trials of conservative treatment.** Wrong, this omits both failed conservative treatment and the associated functional loss specified for replacement (p. 789).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 789.
ref: Hazzard Ch 52 — OSTEOARTHRITIS · Harrison Ch 382 — Approach to Articular and Musculoskeletal Disease

q: A hand radiograph is being assessed for osteoarthritis. Which pattern is described in Hazzard as supporting this diagnosis?
o: Asymmetric joint-space narrowing with osteophytes
Uniform symmetric joint-space narrowing without osteophytes
Widening of the joint space with osteophytes
Widening of the joint space without bony change
explanation:
**Hand osteoarthritis** typically produces nonuniform, asymmetric joint-space loss. Osteophytes are among its radiographic features, although radiographs are not required for a clinical diagnosis (p. 782). "Joint space loss is typically nonuniform and asymmetric." (p. 782).

**A. Asymmetric joint-space narrowing with osteophytes.** Correct, Asymmetric joint-space loss and osteophytes match the described radiographic pattern (p. 782).
**B. Uniform symmetric joint-space narrowing without osteophytes.** Wrong, Uniform symmetric loss does not match the characteristic nonuniform, asymmetric pattern described for hand osteoarthritis (p. 782).
**C. Widening of the joint space with osteophytes.** Wrong, The described change is narrowing from joint-space loss, not widening (p. 782).
**D. Widening of the joint space without bony change.** Wrong, Widening without bony change does not represent the described combination of joint-space loss and osteophyte formation (p. 782).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 782.
ref: Hazzard Ch 52 — OSTEOARTHRITIS · Harrison Ch 382 — Approach to Articular and Musculoskeletal Disease

q: Which description identifies crepitus on examination of a joint affected by osteoarthritis?
o: A crackling or grating sensation felt on palpation
An enlargement at the distal interphalangeal joint
A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee joint
A reduction in the joint's range of motion
explanation:
**Crepitus** is a crackling, crinkly, or grating feeling on palpation and may also be audible. It is a typical examination finding in osteoarthritis, distinct from bony enlargement, a popliteal cyst, or reduced motion (p. 782). "crepitus (ie, a peculiar crackling, crinkly, or grating feeling on palpation, which may also be audible)" (p. 782).

**A. A crackling or grating sensation felt on palpation.** Correct, this is the source's definition of crepitus (p. 782).
**B. An enlargement at the distal interphalangeal joint.** Wrong, this describes a bony enlargement such as a Heberden node rather than the palpated grating sensation (p. 782).
**C. A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee joint.** Wrong, this describes a popliteal or Baker's cyst rather than crepitus (p. 782).
**D. A reduction in the joint's range of motion.** Wrong, reduced motion can occur as osteoarthritis progresses, but it is distinct from the crackling or grating sensation (p. 782).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 782.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.781–782

q: For a patient older than 80 receiving levothyroxine, Hazzard suggests targeting TSH toward the upper end of the normal range. Which consideration explains cautious titration?
o: Overreplacement carries risks of atrial fibrillation and bone loss
TSH suppression provides cardiac protection during replacement treatment
Adding T3 reduces cardiac adverse effects during replacement treatment
Faster hormone clearance supports rapid increases in replacement dose
explanation:
**Thyroid hormone replacement has a narrow therapeutic window**, and iatrogenic hyperthyroidism should be avoided (p. 1552). Hazzard identifies the risks "most notably atrial fibrillation and bone loss." (p. 1552). Careful titration and subsequent monitoring are intended to reduce overreplacement risk (p. 1552).

**A. Overreplacement carries risks of atrial fibrillation and bone loss.** Correct, these are the adverse outcomes explicitly associated with iatrogenic hyperthyroidism, explaining the caution about excess replacement (p. 1552).
**B. TSH suppression provides cardiac protection during replacement treatment.** Wrong, a low TSH can reflect overreplacement; the source describes cardiac risk from iatrogenic hyperthyroidism rather than cardiac protection (p. 1552).
**C. Adding T3 reduces cardiac adverse effects during replacement treatment.** Wrong, the source advises against T3 replacement in older people because supraphysiologic T3 concentrations can have adverse cardiac effects (p. 1552).
**D. Faster hormone clearance supports rapid increases in replacement dose.** Wrong, the source describes lower thyroid-hormone clearance in older people and potentially longer time to steady state, not faster clearance (p. 1552).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1552.
label: Source: hazzard marked .pdf · 1552

q: An asymptomatic 82-year-old woman has a first TSH result of 8 mU/L with normal free T4. Which next step follows Hazzard's approach to confirming subclinical hypothyroidism?
o: Begin annual TSH surveillance on the basis of this first result
Repeat TSH and free T4 in 1–3 months for confirmation
Start levothyroxine treatment on the basis of this first result
Classify thyroid function as normal on the basis of absent symptoms
explanation:
**Persistent subclinical hypothyroidism** should be confirmed before treatment decisions are made. Hazzard notes that TSH elevations can be transient and recommends repeat testing in one to three months for this initial TSH range (pp. 1553–1554). Figure 98-4 specifies: “Initial thyrotropin level 4.5–14.9 mU/L, repeat measurement and document normal free thyroxine level in 1–3 months” (p. 1554).

**A. Begin annual TSH surveillance on the basis of this first result.** Wrong, Annual surveillance skips the initial confirmation step; the source first requires repeat testing to determine persistence (pp. 1553–1554).
**B. Repeat TSH and free T4 in 1–3 months for confirmation.** Correct, This confirms whether the TSH elevation persists while free T4 remains normal, following the algorithm for the initial result given (pp. 1553–1554).
**C. Start levothyroxine treatment on the basis of this first result.** Wrong, Treatment considerations follow confirmation of persistent subclinical hypothyroidism; the first result has not yet met that requirement (pp. 1553–1554).
**D. Classify thyroid function as normal on the basis of absent symptoms.** Wrong, Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined biochemically by elevated TSH and normal free T4; absent symptoms do not establish normal thyroid function (p. 1553).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1553, 1554.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1553–1554, Figure 98-4

q: Which pair of adverse effects is particularly associated with levothyroxine overreplacement in older adults?
o: Atrial fibrillation and loss of bone
Bradycardia and loss of bone
Atrial fibrillation and increased bone mass
Bradycardia and increased bone mass
explanation:
**Iatrogenic hyperthyroidism** is a risk of excessive thyroid hormone replacement (p. 1552). Its adverse effects parallel endogenous hyperthyroidism, "most notably atrial fibrillation and bone loss"; careful titration and monitoring reduce overreplacement risk (p. 1552).
