q: During an advance care planning discussion, equivalent outcomes are presented first as gains and then as losses. According to the prospect-theory example in Hazzard, which pattern of decision making is expected?
o: Greater risk seeking with gains and greater risk aversion with losses
Greater risk aversion with gains and greater risk seeking with losses
Greater risk seeking with gains and greater risk seeking with losses
Greater risk aversion with gains and greater risk aversion with losses
explanation:
**Framing** influences decisions even when the underlying outcomes are equivalent. The prospect-theory example describes risk aversion when outcomes are framed as gains and risk seeking when they are framed as losses (p. 110).
"when options are presented as gains, people tend to be risk averse, and when options are presented as losses, people tend to be risk seeking." (p. 110).

**A. Greater risk seeking with gains and greater risk aversion with losses.** Wrong, The source describes risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses, so both proposed responses have the wrong direction (p. 110).
**B. Greater risk aversion with gains and greater risk seeking with losses.** Correct, This is the gain-versus-loss pattern described in the example of framing equivalent outcomes (p. 110).
**C. Greater risk seeking with gains and greater risk seeking with losses.** Wrong, Risk seeking fits the loss frame, but the gain frame elicits risk aversion in the source example (p. 110).
**D. Greater risk aversion with gains and greater risk aversion with losses.** Wrong, Risk aversion fits the gain frame, but the loss frame elicits risk seeking in the source example (p. 110).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 110.
ref: Hazzard Ch 7 — DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST
chapterTitle: DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: A 77-year-old man with heart failure and diabetes reports fatigue, dizziness, and sleep problems. His daughter requests extensive testing to find the cause of everything. Which approach follows Hazzard's discussion of clinical decision-making in older adults with multimorbidity?
o: Organize evaluation around separate disease diagnoses before considering symptom goals.
Organize evaluation and symptom management around the patient's functional goals.
Organize evaluation around age-based expectations before considering individual goals.
Organize evaluation around separate specialist priorities before considering shared goals.
explanation:
**Symptoms in multimorbidity** may reflect accumulated physical, psychological, social, and environmental influences rather than a single disease (p. 110). A disease-by-disease approach can produce inconclusive testing and interventions misaligned with patient preferences: "A clinical focus solely on diagnosing and treating discrete diseases may lead to expensive diagnostic testing with inconclusive results" (p. 110). The source therefore supports symptom-focused treatment guided by the patient's priorities.

**A. Organize evaluation around separate disease diagnoses before considering symptom goals.** Wrong, This puts discrete diagnoses ahead of the patient's priorities, despite the source's warning that symptoms may have multiple accumulated causes and testing may be inconclusive (p. 110).
**B. Organize evaluation and symptom management around the patient's functional goals.** Correct, Comfort and function are often primary goals in multimorbidity, and patient priorities should guide evaluation and management; the proposed approach applies those principles (p. 110).
**C. Organize evaluation around age-based expectations before considering individual goals.** Wrong, The source calls for eliciting this patient's priorities, not substituting age-based expectations for them (p. 110).
**D. Organize evaluation around separate specialist priorities before considering shared goals.** Wrong, Separate disease priorities do not establish the patient's preferred outcomes; the source directs evaluation and management toward those outcomes (p. 110).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 110.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: אישה בת 84 עם דמנציה מתונה מתגוררת בבית אבות. בנה, המתגורר רחוק, מתעקש שהיא הייתה רוצה 'שיעשו הכל' ומבקש העברה ל-ICU למעקב צמוד על pneumonia שלה. צוות הסיעוד מדווח שהיא הביעה שוב ושוב שהיא 'רק רוצה להרגיש בנוח' ו'לא רוצה יותר בתי חולים.' בתה, המבקרת אותה באופן קבוע, תומכת בטיפול הממוקד ב-comfort. איזה עיקרון אתי צריך להנחות בעיקר את קבלת ההחלטות במצב זה?
o: סמכות הבן כילד הבכור והקרוב משפחה החוקי
העדפותיה האישיות של המטופלת שהביעה שוב ושוב בעצמה
המלצת צוות הסיעוד לטיפול ממוקד comfort
גישת פשרה המאזנת בין נקודות המבט של שני הילדים
explanation:
**רצון המטופלת והסכמה מדעת** הם נקודת המוצא לבירור מטרות הטיפול. החוק דורש למסור מידע באופן המאפשר הבנה ובחירה מרצון; מכאן, כהסקה אתית, ההעדפות שהביעה בעצמה חשובות יותר מהעדפת בן משפחה או מהסכמה בין בני המשפחה (סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8). יש לברר את הבנתה ביחס להחלטה המסוימת, ואין להסיק כשירות או היעדרה מתווית הדמנציה בלבד.
"לא יינתן טיפול רפואי למטופל אלא אם כן נתן לכך המטופל הסכמה מדעת לפי הוראות פרק זה." (סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8)

**א. סמכות הבן כילד הבכור והקרוב משפחה החוקי.** שגויה, מעמדו כבן בכור אינו מענה לשאלת העיקרון המנחה ואינו מחליף את בירור הבנתה ורצונה; זו הסקה מעקרון ההסכמה מדעת (סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
**ב. העדפותיה האישיות של המטופלת שהביעה שוב ושוב בעצמה.** נכונה, העדפותיה הן הבסיס לשיחה מותאמת עמה על הטיפול, תוך בירור הבנה ובחירה מרצון; זו החלת העיקרון על הסיפור (סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
**ג. המלצת צוות הסיעוד לטיפול ממוקד comfort.** שגויה, הצוות מספק מידע חשוב על דבריה, אך העיקרון הוא בחירת המטופלת ולא העדפת המטפלים כשלעצמה; זו הסקה (סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
**ד. גישת פשרה המאזנת בין נקודות המבט של שני הילדים.** שגויה, פשרה בין הילדים אינה מבטיחה החלטה המשקפת את רצונה; יש לחזור לשיחה המאפשרת הבנה ובחירה עצמאית ככל האפשר, כהסקה מהחוק (סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).

מקור: חוק זכויות החולה, תשנ״ו–1996, סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8 בקובץ המקור.

q: An 82-year-old woman reports weakness, difficulty rising from a chair, and falls. Her SARC-F screen is positive. In the stepwise approach described in Hazzard, which parameter should be measured first?
o: Serum albumin concentration to assess nutritional status
Standardized handgrip strength to assess muscle strength
DXA bone density to assess skeletal mineralization
Peripheral nerve conduction velocity to assess nerve function
explanation:
**Muscle strength**, usually assessed by handgrip strength, is the first recommended measurement after clinical suspicion or a positive SARC-F. Grip strength can serve as a proxy because its relationship with leg strength is sufficiently consistent; leg-strength measurement also requires expensive equipment (p. 734).
"The recommended first parameter to be measured when sarcopenia is suspected clinically or by a positive SARC-F is muscle strength, usually through handgrip strength." (p. 734).
"the link between leg strength and grip strength is consistent enough to use the latter as a proxy." (p. 734).

**A. Serum albumin concentration to assess nutritional status.** Wrong, albumin does not provide the first muscle-strength measurement specified in this diagnostic sequence (p. 734).
**B. Standardized handgrip strength to assess muscle strength.** Correct, standardized grip-strength testing measures the first parameter recommended after a positive screen (p. 734).
**C. DXA bone density to assess skeletal mineralization.** Wrong, bone density does not measure the muscle strength required at this first step (p. 734).
**D. Peripheral nerve conduction velocity to assess nerve function.** Wrong, nerve conduction is not the first strength parameter specified in the source (p. 734).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 734.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 78-year-old man screens positive on SARC-F and reports difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, and a recent fall. In the EWGSOP2 approach described by Hazzard, which measurement comes next?
o: Estimate muscle mass using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry
Assess physical performance using a standardized gait-speed test
Measure handgrip strength using a validated dynamometer protocol
Measure serum vitamin D and testosterone concentrations
explanation:
**Muscle strength** is the first parameter assessed after clinical suspicion or a positive SARC-F screen. Hazzard states that it is measured "usually through handgrip strength" (p. 734). Muscle mass assessment is a subsequent step, and physical performance measures assess broader whole-body function (p. 735).

**A. Estimate muscle mass using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry.** Wrong, Muscle mass estimation may be the second step; it does not replace the initial strength measurement after a positive screen (pp. 734–735).
**B. Assess physical performance using a standardized gait-speed test.** Wrong, Gait speed assesses physical performance, whereas the specified next parameter in this sequence is muscle strength (pp. 734–735).
**C. Measure handgrip strength using a validated dynamometer protocol.** Correct, This directly measures the first parameter specified after a positive SARC-F screen, using the standardized approach described (p. 734).
**D. Measure serum vitamin D and testosterone concentrations.** Wrong, Laboratory concentrations do not measure the muscle-strength parameter that the source places first in the diagnostic sequence (p. 734).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 734, 735.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 75-year-old woman is evaluated for sarcopenia. Grip strength is low and DXA documents low muscle mass, but physical performance is preserved. Using the EWGSOP2 approach described in Hazzard, how should these findings be interpreted?
o: The findings do not meet the criteria for sarcopenia
The findings indicate suspected sarcopenia awaiting confirmation by measurement
The findings confirm sarcopenia without evidence of severe disease
The findings indicate severe sarcopenia under the specified definition
explanation:
**EWGSOP2** uses muscle strength first and muscle mass to confirm muscle involvement in strength loss (p. 732). Low physical performance is a marker of severity, a separate role from confirmation: "muscle mass used as confirmation of the involvement of muscle in strength loss." (p. 732)

**A. The findings do not meet the criteria for sarcopenia.** Wrong, preserved performance does not negate the combination of low strength and low muscle mass used for confirmation in this approach (p. 732).
**B. The findings indicate suspected sarcopenia awaiting confirmation by measurement.** Wrong, the source uses suspected sarcopenia when strength is low and mass has not been measured; mass is already documented as low in this vignette (p. 732).
**C. The findings confirm sarcopenia without evidence of severe disease.** Correct, low mass confirms muscle involvement in the documented strength loss, while preserved performance supplies no performance-based marker of severe disease (p. 732).
**D. The findings indicate severe sarcopenia under the specified definition.** Wrong, the source identifies low physical performance as a severity marker; the stem explicitly states preserved performance (p. 732).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 732.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: An 84-year-old man has had progressive weakness for a year, unintentional weight loss of 10 kg, and three falls in six months. Examination shows marked muscle wasting and fat infiltration in the limbs. Thyroid function and vitamin levels are normal. Which age-related muscle change specifically describes the fat infiltration?
o: Loss of motor units within the aging muscle
Myosteatosis with intra- and intermuscular fat
Preferential loss of type I rather than type II fibers
Impaired energy processing within muscle mitochondria
explanation:
**Myosteatosis** describes the infiltration of aging muscle by fat, rather than the loss of muscle fibers or altered intracellular energy processing. Hazzard states: "Extracellular fat increases with aging, as do intra- and intermuscular fat, infiltrating muscles in a process named myosteatosis" (p. 734).

**A. Loss of motor units within the aging muscle.** Wrong, Neurologic signaling changes contribute to sarcopenia, but they do not describe the fat infiltration asked about here (p. 734).
**B. Myosteatosis with intra- and intermuscular fat.** Correct, This term identifies the intra- and intermuscular fat infiltration described in the stem (p. 734).
**C. Preferential loss of type I rather than type II fibers.** Wrong, The source describes preferential involvement of type II fibers, and fiber loss is a different change from fat infiltration (p. 734).
**D. Impaired energy processing within muscle mitochondria.** Wrong, Altered mitochondrial integrity concerns intracellular energy processes, not the accumulation of fat between and within muscles (p. 734).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 734.
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: A 79-year-old woman with sarcopenia is receiving nutritional advice and asks what to add to improve muscle strength and function. Which intervention is the evidence-supported cornerstone described by Hazzard?
o: A regular aerobic walking program as the main exercise component
A regular resistance exercise program started with expert professional supervision
Vitamin D supplementation for muscle function without severe vitamin deficiency
Growth hormone treatment to increase the amount of skeletal muscle
explanation:
**Resistance exercise** has compelling evidence for improving muscle function and mass in sarcopenia (p. 737). Repetitive movements using weights or elastic bands target muscle strength and power: "Including resistance exercise is key to improve muscle function." (p. 737)

**A. A regular aerobic walking program as the main exercise component.** Wrong, the source distinguishes usual cardiovascular activities such as walking from the resistance component required to improve muscle function in sarcopenia (p. 737).
**B. A regular resistance exercise program started with expert professional supervision.** Correct, resistance exercise targets the function being treated; the source advises starting under expert exercise or physical-therapy supervision to teach correct performance and avoid injury (p. 737).
**C. Vitamin D supplementation for muscle function without severe vitamin deficiency.** Wrong, vitamin D has not been shown to improve muscle function in sarcopenic patients, with possible benefit described in severe deficiency rather than the situation proposed (p. 737).
**D. Growth hormone treatment to increase the amount of skeletal muscle.** Wrong, growth hormone is among the hormonal treatments whose trials showed negative results; it is not the source’s evidence-supported treatment cornerstone (p. 737).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 737.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 73-year-old man with sarcopenia and osteoporosis sustains a hip fracture after a fall. His family asks about the relationship between his bone and muscle conditions. Which description of osteosarcopenia agrees with Hazzard?
o: Coexisting bone and muscle loss without evidence of endocrine communication between the tissues
Coexisting bone and muscle loss with evidence of endocrine communication between the tissues
Bone loss defined by a prior fracture that subsequently produces muscle weakness through immobilization
Muscle loss defined by recurrent falls that subsequently produce osteoporosis through fractures
explanation:
**Osteosarcopenia** describes coexisting osteoporosis and sarcopenia. Hazzard reports "evidence of cross-talk between muscle and bone through endocrine factors" but also states that its relevance to sarcopenia pathogenesis has not been established (p. 734). The concept does not establish a particular causal sequence in this patient.

**A. Coexisting bone and muscle loss without evidence of endocrine communication between the tissues.** Wrong, The source describes evidence of endocrine cross-talk, so describing the coexisting conditions as lacking that evidence is inaccurate (p. 734).
**B. Coexisting bone and muscle loss with evidence of endocrine communication between the tissues.** Correct, This states coexistence and the observed endocrine communication without claiming that the communication proves the cause of his conditions (p. 734).
**C. Bone loss defined by a prior fracture that subsequently produces muscle weakness through immobilization.** Wrong, The definition is coexistence, not a required sequence from fracture through immobilization to muscle weakness (p. 734).
**D. Muscle loss defined by recurrent falls that subsequently produce osteoporosis through fractures.** Wrong, The definition does not require falls to cause osteoporosis; it describes osteoporosis and sarcopenia occurring together (p. 734).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 734.

q: In aging muscle with sarcopenia, which pattern of muscle-fiber change is described in Hazzard?
o: Preferential involvement of type I fibers, with a partial transition from type I to type II
Preferential involvement of type II fibers, with a partial transition from type I to type II
Preferential involvement of type II fibers, with a partial transition from type II to type I
Preferential involvement of type I fibers, with a partial transition from type II to type I
explanation:
**Sarcopenia** involves loss of muscle-fiber size and number, particularly in type II fibers. The accompanying partial transition is toward type I; these are distinct features of the cellular changes described (p. 734).
"a reduction in the size and number of myofibers, particularly affecting type II fibers, with a partial transition of muscle fibers from type II to type I." (p. 734).

**A. Preferential involvement of type I fibers, with a partial transition from type I to type II.** Wrong, Type II fibers are preferentially affected, and the transition is toward type I, so both components misidentify the pattern (p. 734).
**B. Preferential involvement of type II fibers, with a partial transition from type I to type II.** Wrong, The preferential involvement is correct, but the source describes transition toward type I, not toward type II (p. 734).
**C. Preferential involvement of type II fibers, with a partial transition from type II to type I.** Correct, Both the preferential involvement of type II fibers and the partial transition toward type I match the source (p. 734).
**D. Preferential involvement of type I fibers, with a partial transition from type II to type I.** Wrong, The transition is correctly directed, but the preferentially affected fibers are type II (p. 734).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 734.
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: A 76-year-old man with sarcopenia reports little improvement in weakness despite six months of a protein-rich diet and nutritional supplements. His geriatrician recommends structured exercise. Which pair of pathways is named in Hazzard’s explanation of exercise as a treatment for sarcopenia?
o: Muscular and vascular pathways
Neural and skeletal pathways
Muscular and neural pathways
Vascular and endocrine pathways
explanation:
**Exercise** acts through both muscular and neural pathways and is described as the best-established treatment for sarcopenia. The source suggests that mixed results from nutritional interventions may reflect their failure to improve neural mechanisms; it does not establish why this particular patient failed to improve (p. 734).
"Physical exercise, the best-established treatment for sarcopenia, has been shown to act through both muscular and neural pathways." (p. 734).
"such interventions would not improve neural mechanisms" (p. 734).

**A. Muscular and vascular pathways.** Wrong, the source names muscular and neural pathways; substituting vascular effects omits the neural component of the stated explanation (p. 734).
**B. Neural and skeletal pathways.** Wrong, the source names muscular and neural pathways; substituting skeletal effects omits the muscular component of that statement (p. 734).
**C. Muscular and neural pathways.** Correct, this is the pair explicitly named in the source’s explanation of exercise treatment (p. 734).
**D. Vascular and endocrine pathways.** Wrong, this does not identify either of the two pathways named in that statement (p. 734).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 734.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 734, Exercise

q: How does Hazzard describe the relationship between sarcopenia and physical frailty?
o: One syndrome identified using the same diagnostic measures
Separate syndromes with unrelated physical components
Distinct syndromes with overlapping physical components
One syndrome identified using cognitive diagnostic measures
explanation:
**Sarcopenia and physical frailty** overlap because muscle loss, weakness, and slow walking contribute to both constructs. They remain distinct: physical frailty can arise from nonmuscular disease, and mild sarcopenia need not produce frailty (p. 736). "Thus, they are distinct but overlapping constructs." (p. 736).

**A. One syndrome identified using the same diagnostic measures.** Wrong, the source explicitly calls them distinct constructs, so it does not treat them as a single diagnosis with identical criteria (p. 736).
**B. Separate syndromes with unrelated physical components.** Wrong, the physical components overlap, including muscle loss, weakness, and slow walking (p. 736).
**C. Distinct syndromes with overlapping physical components.** Correct, this preserves both their overlap and the distinction described in the source (p. 736).
**D. One syndrome identified using cognitive diagnostic measures.** Wrong, the cited relationship concerns muscle and physical function, and the source describes distinct constructs rather than one cognitive syndrome (p. 736).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 736.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 77-year-old man reports weakness and slow walking. Grip strength is below the reference values for his sex and population, but estimated muscle mass is not low. Which approach is appropriate according to Hazzard?
o: Confirm sarcopenia from the normal muscle-mass estimate
Defer intervention until a repeat test shows low muscle mass
Consider sarcopenia and other causes, and address weakness
Favor hand osteoarthritis before considering other causes
explanation:
**Low grip strength** warrants attention even when the muscle-mass estimate is not low. Hazzard recommends considering sarcopenia and a broad differential, and states that weakness merits intervention because it predicts adverse outcomes irrespective of cause (p. 735).
"sarcopenia should be suspected, as it is the most frequent reason of muscle weakness." (p. 735).
"the differential diagnosis is wide and other potential causes for low muscle strength should be considered" (p. 735).

**A. Confirm sarcopenia from the normal muscle-mass estimate.** Wrong, a normal mass estimate does not confirm sarcopenia; muscle-mass estimates have limitations and must be interpreted with strength and other findings (p. 735).
**B. Defer intervention until a repeat test shows low muscle mass.** Wrong, low grip strength itself merits intervention, even when further diagnostic testing is unavailable (p. 735).
**C. Consider sarcopenia and other causes, and address weakness.** Correct, this preserves the differential diagnosis while acting on clinically important weakness (p. 735).
**D. Favor hand osteoarthritis before considering other causes.** Wrong, hand osteoarthritis is one possible cause, but the source calls for a broad differential rather than preferring it without additional evidence (p. 735).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 735.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 78-year-old woman attends routine follow-up. She reports unintentional loss of 4 kg in six months, increased exhaustion, and difficulty walking to her mailbox without resting. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and osteoarthritis. Examination finds reduced grip strength and slow gait. Her medication regimen is stable, and she has no acute medical illness. Which interpretation follows Hazzard's description of the Fried frailty phenotype?
o: The combination warrants assessment of a multisystem frailty syndrome
The weak grip establishes frailty independently of the other clinical findings
The chronic diagnoses establish frailty independently of the physical features
The absence of an acute precipitant makes a frailty assessment unnecessary
explanation:
**Physical frailty** is a multisystem syndrome characterized by weight loss, weakness, exhaustion, slowness, and low activity. The combination in this vignette warrants formal assessment; a single feature is insufficient, and an acute precipitant is not required for the associated risk of disability (p. 619).
"the phenotype of frailty was defined by five characteristics (Table 42-2): unintentional weight loss, weakness, exhaustion, slowness, and low activity." (p. 619).
"the presence of one criterion alone may constitute a risk factor but does not represent frailty itself, because frailty is considered a multisystemic syndrome." (p. 619).

**A. The combination warrants assessment of a multisystem frailty syndrome.** Correct, several reported features correspond to the physical phenotype, supporting assessment of the syndrome rather than reliance on one finding (p. 619).
**B. The weak grip establishes frailty independently of the other clinical findings.** Wrong, Hazzard states that one criterion alone may be a risk factor but does not represent frailty itself (p. 619).
**C. The chronic diagnoses establish frailty independently of the physical features.** Wrong, multimorbidity is associated with frailty risk, but the Fried phenotype is defined by physical characteristics rather than the diagnoses alone (p. 619).
**D. The absence of an acute precipitant makes a frailty assessment unnecessary.** Wrong, frailty-related disability and loss of independence can occur without an acute precipitant (p. 619).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 619.

q: An 82-year-old man is scheduled for elective hip replacement. He has congestive heart failure, diabetes, and mild cognitive impairment. Preoperative assessment identifies slow walking, weak grip, low energy, and loss of 3 kg during the past year. What does assessment for frailty contribute to the surgical discussion?
o: Evidence of preserved physiologic reserve and a lower likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes
Evidence of reduced physiologic reserve and an increased likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes
Evidence of reduced physiologic reserve and a lower likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes
Evidence of preserved physiologic reserve despite an increased likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes
explanation:
**Frailty assessment** addresses physiologic vulnerability beyond individual organ diagnoses (pp. 372, 627). Hazzard identifies "increased vulnerability or frailty, which is an important predictor of adverse surgical outcomes" (p. 372). The surgical-risk discussion relates this vulnerability to reduced functional reserve across multiple systems, so the findings warrant assessing that reserve rather than assuming it is preserved (p. 627; application).

**A. Evidence of preserved physiologic reserve and a lower likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes.** Wrong, preserved reserve and lower risk do not describe the vulnerability associated with frailty (pp. 372, 627).
**B. Evidence of reduced physiologic reserve and an increased likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes.** Correct, this combines the reduced reserve and higher adverse-outcome risk described in the source (p. 627).
**C. Evidence of reduced physiologic reserve and a lower likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes.** Wrong, reduced reserve in frailty is associated with increased, not decreased, postoperative risk (p. 627).
**D. Evidence of preserved physiologic reserve despite an increased likelihood of adverse surgical outcomes.** Wrong, the source relates frailty to reduced reserve across systems, rather than preserved reserve despite increased risk (p. 627).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 372, 627.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 372

q: A 75-year-old woman with COPD, osteoporosis, and depression has not returned to her previous function two months after hospitalization for pneumonia. She remains weak, has reduced appetite, and now uses a walker although she previously walked independently. Which physiologic concept in Hazzard's frailty model explains vulnerability to stress and impaired recovery?
o: The number of chronic diagnoses as a measure of disease burden
Loss of conditioning from inactivity during the hospital admission
Reduced physiologic reserve and impaired responses to stressors
Progression of pulmonary disease as the explanation for systemic decline
explanation:
**Frailty involves reduced reserve and resilience**. Dysregulated stress-response systems reduce homeostatic capacity and the ability to recover after a perturbation (pp. 618–619). "some homeostatic mechanisms/stress response systems are impaired, show low reserve and reduced ability to respond to perturbation" (p. 618). This is the model being tested, rather than a claim that other contributors to her decline have been excluded.

**A. The number of chronic diagnoses as a measure of disease burden.** Wrong, Comorbidity is associated with frailty, but counting diagnoses does not express the stress-response and resilience mechanism in the question (pp. 618–619).
**B. Loss of conditioning from inactivity during the hospital admission.** Wrong, Inactivity can be relevant to the history, but the question asks for the frailty model's broader physiologic mechanism of impaired stress response (pp. 618–619).
**C. Reduced physiologic reserve and impaired responses to stressors.** Correct, Reduced reserve and stress-response dysregulation are the model's explanation for vulnerability and impaired recovery (pp. 618–619).
**D. Progression of pulmonary disease as the explanation for systemic decline.** Wrong, The source describes a multisystem syndrome; the stem does not establish COPD progression as the explanation for the decline (pp. 618–619).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 618, 619.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 618–619, Frailty phenotype

q: A 69-year-old man attends an annual visit. He reports less energy and avoids social activities because walking has become difficult. Hypertension and hyperlipidemia are controlled. Examination shows slow gait and mild weakness; laboratory tests are normal. What approach accords with Hazzard's discussion of functional change and frailty?
o: Consider the changes to be normal aging and defer evaluation of the functional decline
Consider underlying disease and defer interventions directed at muscle strength and function
Consider early frailty, assess function, and begin appropriate preventive interventions
Consider depression to be established and start an antidepressant without assessing function
explanation:
**Functional change** should prompt evaluation and intervention, and frailty describes heightened physiologic vulnerability (p. 123). "Therefore, changes in functional status should prompt further diagnostic evaluation and intervention." (p. 123). Preventive strategies include maintaining muscle mass and strength; applying these principles does not require assuming that the cause of this patient?s symptoms is already established (p. 123).

**A. Consider the changes to be normal aging and defer evaluation of the functional decline.** Wrong, deferring evaluation because of age conflicts with the instruction to investigate and intervene when function changes (p. 123).
**B. Consider underlying disease and defer interventions directed at muscle strength and function.** Wrong, investigating underlying disease can be appropriate, but deferring function-directed care omits the intervention component described in the source (p. 123; application).
**C. Consider early frailty, assess function, and begin appropriate preventive interventions.** Correct, it treats the findings as a reason for assessment and prevention, consistent with the frailty and functional-assessment discussion (p. 123).
**D. Consider depression to be established and start an antidepressant without assessing function.** Wrong, the source describes screening and further assessment of mood; these symptoms do not establish depression or replace assessment of the reported functional change (p. 123; application).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 123.

q: An 85-year-old woman with heart failure, diabetes, and arthritis is evaluated after a fall. Her family reports progressive unsteadiness, weight loss, and increased confusion. Examination shows slowness and weak grip. Which feature fits the physical frailty phenotype described by Hazzard?
o: The count of chronic diagnoses considered apart from physical performance
The acute confusion considered apart from weakness and loss of weight
The cluster of weight loss, weakness, and slowness considered together
The single fall considered apart from the other functional findings
explanation:
**Physical frailty** is a syndrome rather than one isolated event or a diagnosis count. Its defining characteristics include "unintentional weight loss, weakness, exhaustion, slowness, and low activity." (p. 619). Considering weight loss, weak grip, and slowness together fits this phenotype; it does not explain away the separate acute cognitive change.

**A. The count of chronic diagnoses considered apart from physical performance.** Wrong, a diagnosis count is not the cluster of physical phenotype characteristics listed by the source (p. 619).
**B. The acute confusion considered apart from weakness and loss of weight.** Wrong, acute confusion is not one of the listed physical phenotype characteristics; the source notes that this model lacks a specific cognitive dimension (pp. 619–620).
**C. The cluster of weight loss, weakness, and slowness considered together.** Correct, these are three of the physical characteristics explicitly listed for the phenotype (p. 619).
**D. The single fall considered apart from the other functional findings.** Wrong, a single event does not represent the multisystem syndrome, and a fall is not itself one of the five defining characteristics (p. 619).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 619, 620.

q: A 72-year-old man has progressive fatigue and functional decline despite well-controlled hypertension, diabetes, and coronary disease. He has become less active, lost weight, and developed sarcopenia and slow gait. Which biological association does Hazzard describe in frailty?
o: Chronic inflammation associated with improved recovery from physiologic stress
Reduced inflammation associated with accumulating damage and exhausted resilience
Chronic inflammation associated with accumulating damage and failing resilience
Reduced inflammation associated with increased physiologic reserve and frailty
explanation:
**Frailty** involves decreased reserve and impaired response to stress rather than being defined by disease diagnoses alone (p. 616). The source states: "The failing of resilience and the accumulation of damage are associated with a chronic proinflammatory state." (p. 616). This is an association described in frailty, not proof of a specific cause of this patient’s decline.

**A. Chronic inflammation associated with improved recovery from physiologic stress.** Wrong, The source links chronic inflammation to failing resilience, not improved recovery from stress (p. 616).
**B. Reduced inflammation associated with accumulating damage and exhausted resilience.** Wrong, The stated association is with a proinflammatory state rather than reduced inflammation (p. 616).
**C. Chronic inflammation associated with accumulating damage and failing resilience.** Correct, This matches the described association among damage accumulation, failing resilience, and chronic inflammation (p. 616).
**D. Reduced inflammation associated with increased physiologic reserve and frailty.** Wrong, Frailty is characterized by decreased reserve and impaired stress response; increased reserve and reduced inflammation do not describe the stated association (p. 616).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 616.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 68-year-old woman with heart failure, COPD, and osteoarthritis is referred because she appears frail. Her physician requests help with prognosis and treatment planning. Which principle from Hazzard should guide assessment?
o: Use the count of diagnoses to characterize the patient's functional prognosis.
Use functional status to add prognosis beyond disease-specific assessment.
Use a biomarker panel to replace clinical characterization of frailty.
Use cognitive screening to represent the patient's physical functional status.
explanation:
**Functional status** provides prognostic information beyond disease labels in older adults (p. 616). Hazzard states that “functional status provides powerful prognostic information on multiple adverse health outcomes independent of disease status” (p. 616). Its frailty framework includes physical, cognitive, and mental-health domains, rather than substituting a single domain or a laboratory panel for clinical assessment (p. 617).

**A. Use the count of diagnoses to characterize the patient's functional prognosis.** Wrong, Disease diagnoses do not capture the prognostic information supplied by function; the source states that diagnosis is not enough to infer prognosis or treatment response (p. 616).
**B. Use functional status to add prognosis beyond disease-specific assessment.** Correct, This directly applies the source's account of functional status as prognostically informative independently of disease status (p. 616).
**C. Use a biomarker panel to replace clinical characterization of frailty.** Wrong, The source reports little agreement on a specific set of clinical measures and laboratory biomarkers useful for diagnosis, rather than a panel replacing clinical assessment (p. 617).
**D. Use cognitive screening to represent the patient's physical functional status.** Wrong, The described clinical layer includes physical function as well as cognition; assessing cognition alone omits a central component (p. 617).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 616, 617.

q: An 80-year-old man with several comorbidities has a prolonged recovery, complications, and a need for rehabilitation after hospitalization for pneumonia. His family asks why recovery remains difficult after the pneumonia has resolved. Which description captures the frailty concept in Hazzard?
o: Preserved resilience and homeostatic capacity with increased susceptibility to stressors.
Reduced resilience and enhanced homeostatic capacity with reduced susceptibility to stressors.
Reduced resilience and homeostatic capacity with increased susceptibility to stressors.
Enhanced resilience and homeostatic capacity with reduced susceptibility to stressors.
explanation:
**Frailty** involves reduced physiologic reserves, decreased resistance to stressors, and loss of resilience (p. 618). Hazzard describes "dysregulation of the stress response systems responsible for organismal resilience" with loss of homeostatic capabilities (p. 619). This explains the concept relevant to impaired recovery without proving the cause of each complication.

**A. Preserved resilience and homeostatic capacity with increased susceptibility to stressors.** Wrong, loss of resilience and homeostatic capacity, rather than their preservation, characterizes frailty (pp. 618-619).
**B. Reduced resilience and enhanced homeostatic capacity with reduced susceptibility to stressors.** Wrong, the source describes loss of homeostatic capabilities, not enhancement (p. 619).
**C. Reduced resilience and homeostatic capacity with increased susceptibility to stressors.** Correct, this combines the reduced resilience, loss of homeostasis, and increased susceptibility described (pp. 618-619).
**D. Enhanced resilience and homeostatic capacity with reduced susceptibility to stressors.** Wrong, decreased rather than improved resistance to stressors is a defining characteristic (p. 618).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 618, 619.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 618–619, Frailty and resilience

q: A 77-year-old woman has slowed over eighteen months. She has stable diabetes, hypertension, and mild heart failure, reports reduced energy, has unintentionally lost 4 kg, and now uses a cane for stability. Medications are unchanged and recent laboratory results are normal. Which conceptualization from Hazzard is relevant when assessing possible frailty?
o: Frailty represents the accumulation of diagnosed chronic diseases.
Frailty represents susceptibility associated with accelerated aging processes.
Frailty represents established disability in everyday functional activities.
Frailty represents loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength.
explanation:
**Frailty** is related to disease burden but is not exhaustively defined by multimorbidity, disability, or sarcopenia (pp. 616–617). Hazzard states that “Frailty can be conceptualized as a final common outcome of accelerated aging processes” (p. 616). This provides a framework for assessment; it does not prove accelerated aging in this individual or that her decline is reversible.

**A. Frailty represents the accumulation of diagnosed chronic diseases.** Wrong, The source says frailty cannot be exhaustively defined by multimorbidity, so counting diagnoses does not define the syndrome (p. 617).
**B. Frailty represents susceptibility associated with accelerated aging processes.** Correct, This expresses the source's conceptual link between a susceptibility state and accelerated aging, which is relevant to assessing her presentation (p. 616).
**C. Frailty represents established disability in everyday functional activities.** Wrong, The source distinguishes frailty from disability and states that their definitions should not overlap (p. 617).
**D. Frailty represents loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength.** Wrong, The source states that sarcopenia does not exhaustively define frailty; reduced muscle mass alone is not the syndrome (p. 617).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 616, 617.

q: A 74-year-old man is being considered for a complex cardiac procedure. Cardiac function is normal, but he walks slowly, appears to have lost muscle mass, and reports exhaustion with minimal exertion. His family describes reduced activity over the past year. How should frailty assessment contribute to procedural risk assessment?
o: Treat normal cardiac function as evidence against the need for frailty assessment
Use chronological age as the principal measure of physiological reserve
Combine frailty assessment with the other measures of procedural risk
Treat comorbidity counts as a replacement for assessment of physical function
explanation:
**Frailty** describes low physiological reserve and increased vulnerability; reserve varies between people of the same age (p. 372). Frailty instruments can "improve risk assessment particularly when used in combination with other risk-assessment tools" (p. 373).

**A. Treat normal cardiac function as evidence against the need for frailty assessment.** Wrong, normal cardiac function does not assess the wider physical and cognitive variation described in the source (pp. 372–373; application).
**B. Use chronological age as the principal measure of physiological reserve.** Wrong, chronological age cannot capture heterogeneous physiological reserve; the source explicitly rejects age alone for estimating risk (p. 372).
**C. Combine frailty assessment with the other measures of procedural risk.** Correct, combining frailty measures with other risk tools is the recommended use, rather than substituting a single measure (p. 373).
**D. Treat comorbidity counts as a replacement for assessment of physical function.** Wrong, replacing physical assessment with comorbidity counts omits the functional information the source identifies as important for postoperative risk (p. 373).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 372, 373.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 72-year-old woman with osteoporosis and a previous vertebral compression fracture has been sedentary for years because she fears falling. She has no cardiac symptoms, normal vital signs, and takes calcium and vitamin D. What is an appropriate initial approach to exercise?
o: Begin with high-intensity resistance exercise to maximize the initial training stimulus
Defer an exercise program because osteoporosis makes continued inactivity preferable
Begin an individualized low-intensity program with gradual progression and balance work
Defer moderate exercise until routine cardiac stress screening has been completed
explanation:
**Starting exercise** should be individualized to fitness, function, and chronic conditions. Hazzard applies "start low and go slow" and recommends balance exercises for people at risk of falling (p. 814). Asymptomatic people planning moderate-intensity exercise do not need screening before starting (pp. 813–814).

**A. Begin with high-intensity resistance exercise to maximize the initial training stimulus.** Wrong, The source recommends low initial intensity in deconditioned people, with progression tailored to tolerance; starting at high intensity does not follow that approach (pp. 813–814).
**B. Defer an exercise program because osteoporosis makes continued inactivity preferable.** Wrong, The recommendations emphasize avoiding sedentary behavior and being active as conditions allow, rather than using osteoporosis as a reason for continued inactivity (pp. 813–814).
**C. Begin an individualized low-intensity program with gradual progression and balance work.** Correct, Low initial intensity, individual progression, and balance exercises match the stated approach for a sedentary older person concerned about falling (pp. 813–814).
**D. Defer moderate exercise until routine cardiac stress screening has been completed.** Wrong, Routine screening before moderate exercise is not required for asymptomatic individuals in the cited guidance (pp. 813–814).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 813, 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 814, Starting exercise

q: A 78-year-old man with NYHA class II heart failure, diabetes, and mild cognitive impairment wants to begin exercising. He lives alone, has fallen twice in the past year, and takes metformin, lisinopril, and metoprolol. His daughter is concerned about safety. Which approach best applies Hazzard's exercise principles?
o: Defer physical exercise because of his combination of chronic conditions
Prescribe the general aerobic target without adapting it to his fitness
Tailor exercise and balance work to his abilities and conditions
Substitute cognitive exercises for physical activity because of his heart failure
explanation:
**Individualized exercise** matches activity to fitness, chronic conditions, and functional abilities. Hazzard recommends balance exercise for people at risk of falling and activity within the limits of chronic conditions; low intensity is appropriate when more intensive exercise is not tolerated (p. 814).
"Key to recommendations for exercise in older adults is the need to individualize the program of physical activity." (p. 814).

**A. Defer physical exercise because of his combination of chronic conditions.** Wrong, Chronic conditions call for adaptation to ability rather than deferral of physical exercise on that basis (p. 814).
**B. Prescribe the general aerobic target without adapting it to his fitness.** Wrong, The general activity target does not replace adjustment to fitness and chronic disease (p. 814).
**C. Tailor exercise and balance work to his abilities and conditions.** Correct, This combines individualized activity with balance work relevant to the reported falls (p. 814; application).
**D. Substitute cognitive exercises for physical activity because of his heart failure.** Wrong, Heart failure is among conditions for which lower-intensity exercise may be needed, rather than a reason to substitute cognitive activity for physical exercise (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 814, 1179, Exercise prescription

q: A 69-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease and hypertension takes several medications and plans to begin a walking program. What medication-related preparation does Hazzard recommend?
o: Plan dose increases as physical fitness improves
Plan dose reductions based on the intended walking time
Arrange a medication and dose review before starting exercise
Plan to replace medication with exercise once fitness improves
explanation:
Starting **exercise** should be individualized, including communication with the patient's health care provider. Medication or dose adjustments may be necessary, so review is appropriate without assuming a predetermined direction or magnitude of change (p. 814). "It is appropriate for patients to notify their health care providers of their intent to begin an exercise program, because adjustments in medications or dosages may be necessary." (p. 814).

**A. Plan dose increases as physical fitness improves.** Wrong, the source calls for review because adjustments may be needed, not a preplanned increase tied to fitness (p. 814).
**B. Plan dose reductions based on the intended walking time.** Wrong, the source does not prescribe reductions based on intended walking time; the need for adjustment should be reviewed individually (p. 814).
**C. Arrange a medication and dose review before starting exercise.** Correct, notifying the provider permits review of medication or dosage adjustments when beginning the program (p. 814).
**D. Plan to replace medication with exercise once fitness improves.** Wrong, the source discusses adjustments to medications and individualized exercise, not a plan to substitute exercise for prescribed treatment (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 814, Starting exercise

q: An 82-year-old man had a stroke six months ago and has mild residual left-sided weakness and fear of falling. He wants to improve strength and balance but worries about his limitations. His wife is supportive and also concerned about safety. Which program design follows the adherence strategies described by Hazzard?
o: Rapid increases in training intensity, emphasizing early strength gains
Flexible patient-set goals, family support, and personalized feedback
Fixed distance targets, emphasizing strict attainment at each session
Independent exercise sessions, avoiding family involvement in planning
explanation:
**Exercise adherence** is supported by gradual progression, personalized feedback, family involvement, and goals set by the participant. These strategies address continuation of the program as well as its exercise content (p. 814). The source recommends "flexible goals (time rather than distance) set by the participant" (p. 814).

**A. Rapid increases in training intensity, emphasizing early strength gains.** Wrong, rapid escalation conflicts with the source recommendation for slow progression to reduce early injuries (p. 814).
**B. Flexible patient-set goals, family support, and personalized feedback.** Correct, this combines the participant-set goals, family support, and individualized feedback explicitly described to reduce dropout (p. 814).
**C. Fixed distance targets, emphasizing strict attainment at each session.** Wrong, fixed distance targets do not follow the recommended flexible, time-based goals chosen by the participant (p. 814).
**D. Independent exercise sessions, avoiding family involvement in planning.** Wrong, excluding family involvement removes a source of support specifically recommended for participation (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 814.

q: A 76-year-old woman with diabetes, hypertension, and mild frailty has completed eight weeks of low-intensity exercise. Mood and sleep have improved, but strength gains have been small. Her daughter proposes more intensive exercise. Which principle should guide the discussion?
o: A limited strength response supports increasing intensity before reassessment
Continued lower-intensity activity offers benefits with individualization
A limited strength response supports ending the current exercise program
A limited strength response supports switching directly to intensive intervals
explanation:
**Exercise intensity** should be individualized to fitness and chronic conditions (p. 814). Hazzard notes that "significant cardiovascular and metabolic improvements can be obtained when less intense exercise is maintained over sufficiently long periods of time"; this does not promise a particular strength gain (p. 814).

**A. A limited strength response supports increasing intensity before reassessment.** Wrong, the source requires effort to be related to fitness and chronic conditions, not automatic escalation from a single outcome (p. 814).
**B. Continued lower-intensity activity offers benefits with individualization.** Correct, the source supports benefits from sustained lower-intensity exercise and individualized prescriptions (p. 814).
**C. A limited strength response supports ending the current exercise program.** Wrong, ending activity disregards the source’s statement that any amount provides some health benefits (p. 814).
**D. A limited strength response supports switching directly to intensive intervals.** Wrong, switching directly to intensive intervals bypasses the required assessment of fitness and the effects of chronic conditions on safe activity (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 814.

q: A 71-year-old man with COPD and osteoarthritis begins an individualized exercise program. The next day he reports severe muscle soreness and generalized fatigue. What should guide the next session?
o: The load was low, so exercise intensity should be increased
The load was appropriate, so the same exercise dose should be repeated
The load was excessive, so the exercise dose should be adjusted
The load was completed, so the exercise session should be lengthened
explanation:
**Postexercise monitoring** helps identify an excessive exercise dose (p. 825). "Severe muscle soreness and general body fatigue are signs that the exercise stress was excessive." Adjusting the next dose is the practical application of that finding (p. 825).

**A. The load was low, so exercise intensity should be increased.** Wrong, the symptoms indicate excessive stress, not a load that was too low (p. 825).
**B. The load was appropriate, so the same exercise dose should be repeated.** Wrong, repeating the same dose disregards the source’s signs of excessive stress (p. 825).
**C. The load was excessive, so the exercise dose should be adjusted.** Correct, recognizing excessive stress and adjusting the prescription follows the source’s monitoring principle (p. 825).
**D. The load was completed, so the exercise session should be lengthened.** Wrong, completing a session does not establish tolerability; the next-day symptoms indicate excessive stress (p. 825).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 825.

q: An 84-year-old woman has been sedentary for years because of arthritis pain. She wants to be stronger for her granddaughter's wedding in six months, has realistic expectations, and has family support. Which educational approach is supported for increasing activity?
o: Give general advice to increase activity and let her select the details
Provide a written exercise prescription with specific instructions
Suggest a general gym membership and let her select the exercises
Recommend postponing exercise until after the wedding to prevent injury
explanation:
**Specific exercise instructions** help previously sedentary adults translate a broad goal into a program. Hazzard favors a written prescription and gradual, individualized progression (p. 814). "Provision of written exercise prescriptions from health care providers increases activity levels among previously sedentary adults." (p. 814).

**A. Give general advice to increase activity and let her select the details.** Wrong, general advice is less helpful than specific instructions for older adults who find activity goals daunting (p. 814).
**B. Provide a written exercise prescription with specific instructions.** Correct, a written prescription supplies the specific guidance associated with increased activity among previously sedentary adults (p. 814).
**C. Suggest a general gym membership and let her select the exercises.** Wrong, an unguided membership does not provide the individualized instructions and support described in the source (p. 814; application to this option).
**D. Recommend postponing exercise until after the wedding to prevent injury.** Wrong, the source recommends starting at a low level and progressing slowly to address safety, rather than delaying an appropriate program because of general injury concerns (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 814, Adherence

q: A 79-year-old man with mild dementia (MMSE 24/30) lives with his family and attends a community exercise program. His daughter says he enjoys the social contact but sometimes forgets the routine between sessions. The program director asks how to support continued participation. Which approach matches Hazzard’s exercise-adherence recommendations?
o: Use fixed distance targets and advance the exercise pace quickly
Use music, enthusiastic leadership, and regular personalized praise
Use general activity advice and reduce individualized feedback
Use individual sessions and reduce family involvement in the program
explanation:
**Continued exercise participation** is supported by a tailored program and reinforcing social support. Hazzard lists “enthusiastic leadership”, “personalized feedback and praise”, and “distraction techniques such as music” among ways to reduce recidivism (p. 814). These are adherence recommendations; the passage does not claim that they restore memory in dementia.

**A. Use fixed distance targets and advance the exercise pace quickly.** Wrong, rapid progression and fixed distance targets do not match slow progression and flexible, participant-set time goals (p. 814).
**B. Use music, enthusiastic leadership, and regular personalized praise.** Correct, this combines three of the source’s listed strategies for sustaining participation (p. 814).
**C. Use general activity advice and reduce individualized feedback.** Wrong, specific instructions are more helpful than general advice, and regular personalized feedback is recommended (p. 814).
**D. Use individual sessions and reduce family involvement in the program.** Wrong, reducing family involvement removes a source-recommended form of support for participation (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.814

q: A 67-year-old woman with stable heart failure can walk for ten minutes at a time but becomes fatigued during longer sessions. She requests a plan suited to her current exercise tolerance. Which approach is consistent with the chapter?
o: Concentrate walking into a prolonged session to maintain continuous exercise
Increase walking intensity to compensate for the shorter exercise duration
Accumulate several short walking sessions suited to her current tolerance
Postpone walking sessions until prolonged exercise can be tolerated
explanation:
**Short exercise sessions** can be useful when more intensive or prolonged exercise is not tolerated. Hazzard describes benefit from multiple bouts lasting at least ten minutes, while preferring longer sessions when tolerated; applying the shorter-bout approach here is an inference from her stated tolerance (p. 814).
"While multiple short bouts of exercise (at least 10 minutes each) may be effective in improving certain outcome measures, longer sessions remain preferable if these can be tolerated." (p. 814).
"programs may be necessary in frail populations, such as those with stroke, heart failure, and chronic lung disease, in which more intensive exercise is not tolerated." (p. 814).

**A. Concentrate walking into a prolonged session to maintain continuous exercise.** Wrong, longer sessions are preferable only when tolerated, which this patient reports difficulty doing (p. 814).
**B. Increase walking intensity to compensate for the shorter exercise duration.** Wrong, the source supports adapting exercise when greater intensity is not tolerated, rather than requiring increased intensity to offset shorter duration (p. 814).
**C. Accumulate several short walking sessions suited to her current tolerance.** Correct, the source supports multiple short bouts when longer exercise is not tolerated (p. 814).
**D. Postpone walking sessions until prolonged exercise can be tolerated.** Wrong, the available short-bout approach allows exercise without waiting for tolerance of prolonged sessions (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.814, 824

q: An 88-year-old man after a stroke participates in supervised low-intensity exercise. He adheres to the program and reports functional improvement, but his illnesses limit vigorous activity. Which principle should guide continued exercise?
o: Set the effort level according to the usual target for his age group
Set the effort level according to his fitness and chronic conditions
Judge the expected benefit by attainment of high intensity at each session
Stop the program if he cannot reach the recommended weekly activity target
explanation:
**Individualizing exercise** means relating effort to fitness and chronic conditions. The source says low-intensity programs may be necessary after stroke when more intense exercise is not tolerated (p. 814). It also emphasizes that "any amount of physical activity provides some health benefits" (p. 814).

**A. Set the effort level according to the usual target for his age group.** Wrong, The source calls for effort relative to individual fitness, rather than an age-group target replacing individual assessment (p. 814).
**B. Set the effort level according to his fitness and chronic conditions.** Correct, This applies the stated fitness-based approach and accounts for chronic conditions that affect safe activity (p. 814).
**C. Judge the expected benefit by attainment of high intensity at each session.** Wrong, The source describes cardiovascular and metabolic benefits from sustained less-intense exercise, so high intensity is not the criterion for benefit (p. 814).
**D. Stop the program if he cannot reach the recommended weekly activity target.** Wrong, When the weekly target cannot be met because of chronic conditions, the source advises being as active as those conditions allow (p. 814).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 814.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 814, Exercise prescription

q: A 72-year-old woman with dementia and bilateral knee osteoarthritis cannot reliably report pain and has reduced sensation in both legs. She repeatedly removes heating pads. The rehabilitation team considers supervised aquatic therapy. Which description of this modality is supported by Hazzard?
o: Pool therapy combines heat and buoyancy to support upright activity
Pool therapy combines whole-body heating with peripheral vasoconstriction during upright activity
Pool therapy uses cold immersion to provide support during upright activity
Pool therapy uses whole-body heating to prevent postural hypotension after upright activity
explanation:
**Aquatic therapy** offers support for movement through warmth and buoyancy. "A therapeutic pool provides a combination of heat and buoyancy for support of upright activities." (p. 826). Impaired cognition or sensation calls for caution with modalities; pool therapy also requires attention to vasodilation, cardiac symptoms, and postural hypotension (p. 826).

**A. Pool therapy combines heat and buoyancy to support upright activity.** Correct, This is the source's stated combination for supporting upright movement in a therapeutic pool (p. 826).
**B. Pool therapy combines whole-body heating with peripheral vasoconstriction during upright activity.** Wrong, The source describes significant vasodilation from whole-body heating, not vasoconstriction (p. 826).
**C. Pool therapy uses cold immersion to provide support during upright activity.** Wrong, The therapeutic-pool description combines heat and buoyancy; cold-water immersion is listed as cryotherapy rather than this heating-and-support approach (p. 826).
**D. Pool therapy uses whole-body heating to prevent postural hypotension after upright activity.** Wrong, Whole-body heating produces vasodilation, and the source warns of possible postural hypotension on exiting the pool rather than prevention of it (p. 826).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 826.

q: An 82-year-old man with an MI six months ago and chronic heart failure (EF 35%) is considered for aquatic therapy after a hip fracture. He has mild chest discomfort with minimal exertion on land. Which concern about warm-water therapy is supported by Hazzard?
o: Increased weight bearing in water may worsen hip pain
Vasoconstriction on leaving the pool may cause hypertension
Whole-body heating may cause vasodilation and chest pain
Reduced buoyancy in warm water may limit support for walking
explanation:
**Aquatic therapy** combines warmth and buoyancy to support upright activity. Whole-body heating produces vasodilation, and patients with cardiac insufficiency may experience chest pain; leaving the pool also requires care because of postural hypotension (p. 826). "Because total body heating produces significant vasodilation, patients with cardiac insufficiency may experience chest pain." (p. 826).

**A. Increased weight bearing in water may worsen hip pain.** Wrong, the pool provides buoyant support and can permit walking when land movement is limited, rather than imposing the proposed increased loading (p. 826).
**B. Vasoconstriction on leaving the pool may cause hypertension.** Wrong, the source warns of postural hypotension when exiting, not vasoconstriction-related hypertension (p. 826).
**C. Whole-body heating may cause vasodilation and chest pain.** Correct, this is the mechanism and cardiac concern explicitly described for total-body heating (p. 826).
**D. Reduced buoyancy in warm water may limit support for walking.** Wrong, the therapeutic pool is described as providing heat together with buoyant support, not losing that support because it is warm (p. 826).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 826.
label: Source: hazzard marked .pdf · 826, Ch 55

q: אישה בת 78 עם neuropathy פריפרית סוכרתית וכיב רגל סוכרתי כרוני שלא הגיב לטיפול קונבנציונלי במשך 8 שבועות נשקלת לטיפול ב-electrical stimulation. הקוגניציה שלה תקינה אך אינה מרגישה מגע קל ברגליה. איזה מהמשפטים הבאים לגבי electrical stimulation לריפוי פצעים הוא נכון?
o: הטיפול אסור בגלל היעדר תחושה, מפני שהשפעתו על ריפוי פצעים תלויה בהרגשת כאב במהלך הגירוי
הוא מגביר סינתזת DNA וקולגן ומאושר על ידי Medicare לכיבים סוכרתיים
הטיפול מועיל רק כאשר המטופלת מרגישה את הזרם, מפני שתחושת הזרם היא שגורמת לייצור קולגן
הטיפול מיועד לפצעי לחץ בלבד ואינו מכוסה לטיפול בכיב סוכרתי שלא הגיב לטיפול המקובל
explanation: Electrical stimulation לריפוי פצעים מתאים ומועיל עבור מטופלת זו. לפי הספרות, electrical stimulation 'מאושר לכיסוי Medicare לטיפול ב-stasis, arterial pressure, וכיבים סוכרתיים שלא הגיבו לטיפול קונבנציונלי.' המנגנון כולל הגברת סינתזת DNA וקולגן, כוון migration של תאים, עיכוב פתוגנים בפצע, והגברת חוזק רקמת הצלקת. חשוב לציין: ה-contraindications הקשורים לפגיעה בתחושה מתייחסים ל-TENS לניהול כאב, ולא ל-electrical stimulation לריפוי פצעים. אופציה „הטיפול הוא contraindicated בשל הפגיעה בתחושה שלה“ שגויה כיוון שפגיעה בתחושה מהווה contraindication ל-TENS לניהול כאב, ולא ליישומי ריפוי פצעים. אופציה „יש להשתמש בו רק אם היא מסוגלת להרגיש את הזרם החשמלי“ שגויה מכיוון שהמטופלת אינה צריכה להרגיש את הזרם על מנת להפיק תועלת לריפוי הפצע — האפקטים החשמליים מתרחשים ברמה הסלולרית. אופציה „הוא אינו יעיל לכיבים סוכרתיים, אלא רק ל-pressure ulcers“ שגויה עובדתית, שכן הספרות מציינת במפורש את אישור Medicare לכיבים סוכרתיים, ואף שהעדויות החזקות ביותר קיימות ל-pressure ulcers, randomized controlled trials מדגימים יעילות למספר סוגי כיבים. ההבחנה בין יישומי electrical stimulation שונים קריטית בחולים גריאטריים שלהם לעיתים קרובות מספר אינדיקציות. Clinical Pearl: יש להבחין בין יישומי electrical stimulation — פגיעה בתחושה מהווה contraindication ל-TENS לכאב, אך לא ל-electrical stimulation לריפוי כיבים סוכרתיים.
