**C. Consider following pain symptoms in place of assessing bone mineral density.** Wrong, the source identifies bone mineral density testing as an assessment of bone health; pain follow-up does not perform that assessment (p. 1417).
**D. Consider androgen deprivation as protection against further bone loss.** Wrong, androgen suppression increases rather than protects against bone loss, so it is not a reason to withhold bone-directed treatment (p. 1417).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1417.
ref: Hazzard Ch 53 — HIP FRACTURES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: Biochemical recurrence is detected after radical prostatectomy. Which measure is useful for monitoring and deciding when to initiate treatment?
o: The passage of six months after surgery without new complaints
The PSA-doubling time assessed during follow-up after radical prostatectomy
The degree of recovery of urinary continence after surgery
The absence of local pain at a postoperative follow-up visit
explanation:
**PSA-doubling time** is useful for monitoring biochemical recurrence and deciding when treatment should start. Hazzard also describes treatment timing as dependent on PSA-doubling time, Gleason score, and patient preferences, rather than a single postoperative symptom or elapsed interval (p. 1416). "PSA-doubling time has been shown to be a useful parameter for monitoring patients and deciding when to initiate treatment after biochemical recurrence." (p. 1416).

**A. The passage of six months after surgery without new complaints.** Wrong, Elapsed postoperative time without new complaints does not provide the PSA-doubling information that the source uses for monitoring recurrence (p. 1416).
**B. The PSA-doubling time assessed during follow-up after radical prostatectomy.** Correct, The source explicitly identifies PSA-doubling time as useful for monitoring and treatment timing after biochemical recurrence (p. 1416).
**C. The degree of recovery of urinary continence after surgery.** Wrong, Recovery of continence does not supply the PSA kinetics specified for this recurrence assessment (p. 1416).
**D. The absence of local pain at a postoperative follow-up visit.** Wrong, Absence of local pain does not provide the PSA-doubling information used to assess biochemical recurrence and treatment timing (p. 1416).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1416.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: A 72-year-old man with localized prostate cancer is considering active surveillance rather than immediate treatment. He has T1c disease, PSA 4.8 ng/mL, Gleason score 6, and 3 of 12 positive biopsy cores. His hypertension is controlled and he is otherwise healthy. He worries about missing the opportunity for curative treatment. Which counseling statement accords with Hazzard?
o: Regular PSA testing and biopsies make progression before treatment a negligible concern
Surveillance uses low-intensity follow-up with an expectation of palliative rather than curative treatment
Local or metastatic progression remains a risk before treatment despite careful monitoring
Surveillance is intended for disease expected to progress to metastases despite curative treatment
explanation:
**Active surveillance** aims to delay treatment while preserving the prospect of successful definitive therapy. It can avoid overtreatment, but the source explicitly warns that even careful monitoring can miss the window for curative treatment (p. 1414).
"the strategy carries with it a risk of local or metastatic progression before active treatment is initiated." (p. 1414).
"even the most careful monitoring may miss the window for administering curative therapy." (p. 1414).

**A. Regular PSA testing and biopsies make progression before treatment a negligible concern.** Wrong, the source retains a risk of local or metastatic progression despite monitoring and specifically warns about the curative window (p. 1414).
**B. Surveillance uses low-intensity follow-up with an expectation of palliative rather than curative treatment.** Wrong, active surveillance differs from watchful waiting in monitoring intensity and the expectation of delayed, potentially curative therapy (p. 1414).
**C. Local or metastatic progression remains a risk before treatment despite careful monitoring.** Correct, this states the explicit risk that should be discussed in response to his concern (p. 1414).
**D. Surveillance is intended for disease expected to progress to metastases despite curative treatment.** Wrong, the source describes heterogeneous disease and the goal of delayed successful definitive therapy, not an expectation of metastatic progression despite that therapy (p. 1414).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1414.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: An 85-year-old man with heart failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease has a PSA of 12 ng/mL and an abnormal digital rectal examination. Biopsy reveals prostate adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 7. He has been hospitalized twice this year for heart-failure exacerbations, needs help with activities of daily living, and has an estimated life expectancy of 2–3 years. He has no urinary symptoms. His care plan is to defer cancer treatment until symptomatic disease develops. Which strategy does this describe?
o: Definitive treatment by radical prostatectomy
Definitive treatment by external beam radiation
Watchful waiting with treatment for symptomatic disease
Active surveillance with delayed potentially curative treatment
explanation:
**Watchful waiting** is defined by the intention to defer treatment until symptomatic disease develops. Hazzard states that it “involves deferring treatment until patients develop symptomatic disease” (p. 1414). Active surveillance differs in monitoring intensity and in the expectation of delayed, potentially curative treatment (p. 1414).

**A. Definitive treatment by radical prostatectomy.** Wrong, Radical prostatectomy is a definitive treatment strategy, rather than the stated plan to defer treatment until symptoms (p. 1414).
**B. Definitive treatment by external beam radiation.** Wrong, The plan describes observation until symptoms, rather than proceeding with definitive radiation treatment (p. 1414).
**C. Watchful waiting with treatment for symptomatic disease.** Correct, The plan matches the source definition of watchful waiting: treatment is deferred until symptomatic disease develops (p. 1414).
**D. Active surveillance with delayed potentially curative treatment.** Wrong, Active surveillance retains an expectation of delayed, potentially curative treatment and more intensive monitoring; that is not the stated symptom-triggered plan (p. 1414).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1414.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: A 77-year-old man has received androgen deprivation therapy for eight months. His son reports recent personality changes, irritability, and confusion fluctuating through the day. Oxybutynin was recently started for urinary urgency, and he takes diphenhydramine for sleep. He was previously cognitively well, and examination shows mild dehydration. Which interpretation of the oxybutynin–diphenhydramine combination matches Beers 2023?
o: Combined anticholinergic exposure reduces delirium risk while increasing fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure increases both delirium risk and fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure improves cognition while increasing fall risk
Combined anticholinergic exposure increases cognitive risk while reducing fall risk
explanation:
**Cumulative anticholinergic exposure** is relevant to this medication review. Oxybutynin and diphenhydramine are both listed as strongly anticholinergic; their combined use is associated with cognitive and fall-related harms (pp. 2070, 2074). "Use of more than one medication with anticholinergic properties increases the risk of cognitive decline, delirium, and falls or fractures." (p. 2070)

**A. Combined anticholinergic exposure reduces delirium risk while increasing fall risk.** Wrong, The table describes increased, not reduced, delirium risk with multiple anticholinergic drugs (p. 2070).
**B. Combined anticholinergic exposure increases both delirium risk and fall risk.** Correct, Both named drugs have strong anticholinergic properties, and the combination fits the risk statement for delirium and falls (pp. 2070, 2074).
**C. Combined anticholinergic exposure improves cognition while increasing fall risk.** Wrong, The cognitive concern is decline and delirium, rather than cognitive improvement from this combination (p. 2070).
**D. Combined anticholinergic exposure increases cognitive risk while reducing fall risk.** Wrong, Cognitive risk is correctly recognized, but the same interaction also increases rather than reduces fall risk (p. 2070).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2070, 2074.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2066, 2070, 2074, Tables 3, 5, 7

q: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer diagnosed six months ago has worsening fatigue, reduced appetite, and mild dyspnea over a month. Chemotherapy is controlling the disease, but her ECOG performance status has declined from 1 to 2. Her daughter is concerned about quality of life. Alongside assessment of the new symptoms, which approach to palliative care is supported by Hazzard?
o: Introduce palliative care alongside the ongoing oncology treatment
Postpone palliative care until chemotherapy has been discontinued
Postpone palliative care until progression is shown on imaging
Postpone palliative care until a terminal prognosis is certified
explanation:
**Palliative care can accompany active cancer treatment.** It addresses symptom burden and stress for the patient and family and does not require stopping curative or disease-directed care (p. 1045). "It is appropriate for any type of diagnosis, any stage of a serious illness, and importantly, can be provided together with curative treatment." (p. 1045).

**A. Introduce palliative care alongside the ongoing oncology treatment.** Correct, concurrent palliative and oncology care matches the source definition (p. 1045).
**B. Postpone palliative care until chemotherapy has been discontinued.** Wrong, the source permits concurrent treatment rather than requiring chemotherapy discontinuation (p. 1045).
**C. Postpone palliative care until progression is shown on imaging.** Wrong, the definition does not make radiographic progression a prerequisite; it applies at any stage of serious illness (p. 1045).
**D. Postpone palliative care until a terminal prognosis is certified.** Wrong, a terminal prognosis is not required for palliative care at any stage of serious illness (p. 1045).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1045.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An 81-year-old man has a 2 cm breast mass. Biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma that is estrogen-receptor positive, progesterone-receptor positive, and HER2 negative. He has mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 24/30), lives independently with home-aide support, and has well-controlled diabetes and hypertension. Geriatric assessment shows mild functional limitations and good social support. Which drug does Hazzard prefer for adjuvant endocrine therapy in men?
o: Anastrozole endocrine therapy
Tamoxifen endocrine therapy
Fulvestrant endocrine therapy
LHRH agonist therapy
explanation:
**Adjuvant endocrine therapy in men** has a specific preferred agent in Hazzard: “tamoxifen is the preferred adjuvant endocrine therapy in men” (p. 1406). The source discusses endocrine therapies for metastatic disease separately, so the treatment setting matters (p. 1406).

**A. Anastrozole endocrine therapy.** Wrong, The source preference for adjuvant endocrine treatment in men is tamoxifen; its separate discussion of aromatase inhibitors concerns metastatic disease (p. 1406).
**B. Tamoxifen endocrine therapy.** Correct, Tamoxifen is explicitly identified as the preferred adjuvant endocrine therapy in men, matching the setting asked about (p. 1406).
**C. Fulvestrant endocrine therapy.** Wrong, The source explicitly prefers tamoxifen for adjuvant endocrine treatment in men, rather than fulvestrant (p. 1406).
**D. LHRH agonist therapy.** Wrong, LHRH agonist androgen deprivation is discussed for metastatic hormone-receptor-positive disease, while tamoxifen is preferred for the adjuvant setting (p. 1406).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1406.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: A 78-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer, mild heart failure, and diabetes is being considered for systemic therapy. She is concerned about chemotherapy toxicity. Which assessment approach is supported by Hazzard before treatment selection?
o: Assess function and vulnerabilities with a comprehensive geriatric assessment
Assess physiologic reserve principally from the patient's chronological age
Use the ECOG performance score in place of a comprehensive geriatric assessment
Use the routine physical examination in place of an assessment of vulnerabilities
explanation:
**Comprehensive geriatric assessment** evaluates functional age and multiple domains of vulnerability. It can reveal problems missed by routine history, examination, and oncology performance-status tools, including in patients with good ECOG performance status (pp. 1387–1388).
"It can uncover problems that would not otherwise be identified by routine history and physical or by the traditional oncology performance status tools." (p. 1388).
"Aging is a heterogeneous process that is not captured by chronological age." (p. 1386).

**A. Assess function and vulnerabilities with a comprehensive geriatric assessment.** Correct, this directly evaluates the functional and vulnerability domains that help assess an older patient's risk of chemotherapy toxicity (p. 1388).
**B. Assess physiologic reserve principally from the patient's chronological age.** Wrong, chronological age does not capture the heterogeneous physiologic and functional effects of aging (p. 1386).
**C. Use the ECOG performance score in place of a comprehensive geriatric assessment.** Wrong, ECOG performance status is insufficient by itself; geriatric assessment adds information even with a good performance score (pp. 1387–1388).
**D. Use the routine physical examination in place of an assessment of vulnerabilities.** Wrong, routine history and examination can miss problems identified by the multidomain assessment (p. 1388).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1386, 1387, 1388.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 1387–1388

q: A 69-year-old woman who was cognitively at her usual baseline until this week develops confusion, disorientation, and agitation over several days. During examination her attention fluctuates and her level of consciousness is clouded. Which syndrome best fits and requires a search for an underlying medical cause?
o: Progressive dementia syndrome
Acute delirium syndrome
Major depressive disorder
Acute psychotic disorder
explanation:
**Delirium** is characterized by acute change, inattention, and fluctuating cognition or alertness. Hazzard identifies "Acute onset, varying levels of alertness, and inattention" as cardinal features (p. 880). The acute time course and altered consciousness in this patient fit delirium and warrant investigation of medical contributors (pp. 885–886).

**A. Progressive dementia syndrome.** Wrong, The table describes an insidious, progressive onset of dementia and preserved consciousness until end-stage disease, unlike this abrupt change from baseline (p. 886).
**B. Acute delirium syndrome.** Correct, The abrupt onset, fluctuating attention, and altered consciousness match the core delirium features (pp. 880, 886).
**C. Major depressive disorder.** Wrong, Depression can impair concentration, but the table describes normal consciousness; it does not fit the full acute fluctuating syndrome here (p. 886).
**D. Acute psychotic disorder.** Wrong, Acute psychosis may begin abruptly, but the table describes normal consciousness rather than the clouded level described here (p. 886).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 880, 885, 886.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.879–880

q: A 74-year-old woman with early-stage breast cancer is being considered for adjuvant chemotherapy. Geriatric assessment identifies limited walking ability and falls. Which tool is designed to estimate her risk of severe chemotherapy toxicity?
o: ECOG performance status based on clinician-rated daily activity
CARG-BC combining disease features and patient-reported predictors
G8 screening to identify the need for comprehensive geriatric assessment
ePrognosis estimating life expectancy in an older adult population
explanation:
**CARG-BC** combines disease and patient-reported predictors, including falls and limited walking ability, to estimate chemotherapy toxicity in early breast cancer (p. 1402). Hazzard says the score classifies patients by risk of "severe, debilitating, or deadly side effects to chemotherapy"; this differs from screening for assessment needs or estimating life expectancy (p. 1402).

**A. ECOG performance status based on clinician-rated daily activity.** Wrong, Clinician-rated performance status is a different assessment; the source reports that CARG-BC outperformed physician-rated performance status for the toxicity prediction described (p. 1402).
**B. CARG-BC combining disease features and patient-reported predictors.** Correct, This is the breast-cancer-specific toxicity model, and both falls and walking limitation are among its predictors (p. 1402).
**C. G8 screening to identify the need for comprehensive geriatric assessment.** Wrong, G8 is a screening step used to identify patients who may benefit from a comprehensive assessment, rather than the named breast-cancer toxicity model (pp. 1388, 1402).
**D. ePrognosis estimating life expectancy in an older adult population.** Wrong, The source describes ePrognosis as estimating life expectancy and as not cancer-specific, rather than predicting severe chemotherapy toxicity (p. 1402).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1402, 1388.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1388, 1402

q: An 85-year-old woman in the United States has metastatic breast cancer. Palliative chemotherapy initially helped, but after eight months she has increasing fatigue, two recent falls, and a decline in ECOG performance status from 2 to 3. She wishes to stop chemotherapy, prioritize comfort, and remain at home. Her physicians certify a prognosis of less than six months if the disease follows its expected course. Which plan best matches her stated goals?
o: Continue the current chemotherapy and add fall-focused physical therapy
Arrange hospice care focused on comfort and support at home
Change to another chemotherapy regimen with a lower treatment burden
Increase palliative visits while continuing the current chemotherapy
explanation:
**Hospice** provides comfort and support for patients nearing the end of life and their families. The stem supplies both the prognostic certification required for Medicare hospice and the patient's preference for comfort-focused care, rather than inferring eligibility from performance status alone (pp. 1045–1046). "Hospice care does not aim to shorten or prolong life, but rather provides comfort and support services" (p. 1045).

**A. Continue the current chemotherapy and add fall-focused physical therapy.** Wrong, this retains chemotherapy despite the explicitly stated preference to stop it and prioritize comfort (p. 1045).
**B. Arrange hospice care focused on comfort and support at home.** Correct, hospice's comfort and support focus matches the stated goals, with the required prognostic certification supplied (pp. 1045–1046).
**C. Change to another chemotherapy regimen with a lower treatment burden.** Wrong, switching regimens continues cancer-directed treatment that the patient has said she wishes to stop (p. 1045).
**D. Increase palliative visits while continuing the current chemotherapy.** Wrong, palliative involvement is compatible with many treatment plans, but this option still continues the chemotherapy she has declined (p. 1045).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1045, 1046.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: A 71-year-old woman with localized hormone receptor-positive breast cancer has recurrent falls and mild cognitive decline. Before selecting treatment, her clinicians want to estimate life expectancy and treatment tolerability. Which assessment is designed to uncover functional, medical, and social deficits that may be missed by a routine history and physical examination?
o: Fall-risk assessment using an event history and a clinical balance examination
Cognitive assessment using a screening test and an interview about memory changes
Comprehensive geriatric assessment covering function, comorbidity, cognition, and social support
Tumor assessment using receptor testing and imaging to establish disease extent
explanation:
**Comprehensive geriatric assessment** examines multiple domains that a routine history and physical examination may miss, including function, comorbidity, cognition, nutrition, social support, and medications. Hazzard combines global health status with tumor characteristics and patient preferences when considering breast cancer treatment and its tolerability (pp. 1401–1402). "may help to uncover age-related deficits that are not routinely obtained in a history and physical examination." (p. 1402).

**A. Fall-risk assessment using an event history and a clinical balance examination.** Wrong, fall assessment addresses an important presenting problem but does not cover the multiple medical, cognitive, nutritional, and social domains requested here (p. 1402).
**B. Cognitive assessment using a screening test and an interview about memory changes.** Wrong, cognition is one domain of the comprehensive assessment; a cognitive screen does not supply the broader functional, medical, and social assessment (p. 1402).
**C. Comprehensive geriatric assessment covering function, comorbidity, cognition, and social support.** Correct, the multidomain assessment is the approach described for uncovering otherwise missed deficits relevant to cancer treatment planning (p. 1402).
**D. Tumor assessment using receptor testing and imaging to establish disease extent.** Wrong, tumor characteristics inform cancer treatment, but do not replace global health assessment for life expectancy and tolerability (pp. 1401–1402).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1402, 1401.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1401–1402

q: A 67-year-old woman takes an aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer. Which effect described by Hazzard warrants fracture-risk assessment?
o: Decreased osteoporosis risk and decreased bone fracture risk
Increased osteoporosis risk and decreased bone fracture risk
Increased osteoporosis risk and increased bone fracture risk
Decreased osteoporosis risk and increased bone fracture risk
explanation:
**Aromatase inhibitors** increase the risks of osteoporosis and bone fractures (p. 1390). The source therefore states that "fracture risk should be assessed" and recommends advice about exercise and calcium/vitamin D supplementation (p. 1390).

**A. Decreased osteoporosis risk and decreased bone fracture risk.** Wrong, The source reports an increase in both risks, not a reduction in either (p. 1390).
**B. Increased osteoporosis risk and decreased bone fracture risk.** Wrong, Osteoporosis risk increases, but fracture risk also increases rather than decreases (p. 1390).
**C. Increased osteoporosis risk and increased bone fracture risk.** Correct, Both increased risks are stated as the reason to assess fracture risk (p. 1390).
**D. Decreased osteoporosis risk and increased bone fracture risk.** Wrong, Fracture risk increases, but the source also reports increased osteoporosis risk (p. 1390).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1390.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: A 76-year-old Hispanic woman with limited English presents with her son for a breast lump first noticed four months ago. Imaging and biopsy show a 3.5 cm invasive ductal carcinoma with axillary lymph node involvement. She has Medicare with limited supplemental coverage, lives in a rural area 90 miles from the cancer center, and lacks reliable transportation. Her son works two jobs and has limited availability. Which referral directly follows Hazzard's recommendation for patients at risk of problems with system navigation and social issues?
o: Refer for less intensive cancer therapy and follow-up arranged around transportation.
Refer for patient navigation, social work, and assistance with available resources.
Refer for delayed cancer treatment once the family supplies reliable transportation.
Refer for age-based regimen selection and adjustment of anticancer treatment intensity.
explanation:
**Patient navigation and social work** are recommended when breast cancer patients are at risk of system-navigation or social problems. Hazzard identifies access, transportation, social support, and cost as barriers, and supports geriatric assessment to optimize treatment decisions (p. 1406).
"Patients felt to be at risk for problems with system navigation and social issues should be referred for patient navigation, social work, and resource assistance whenever possible." (p. 1406).

**A. Refer for less intensive cancer therapy and follow-up arranged around transportation.** Wrong, lowering intensity is a treatment change, not the recommended referral for navigation and resource barriers; the source directs these patients to support services (p. 1406).
**B. Refer for patient navigation, social work, and assistance with available resources.** Correct, her transportation, support, and coverage difficulties fit the problems for which the source recommends navigation, social work, and resource assistance (p. 1406).
**C. Refer for delayed cancer treatment once the family supplies reliable transportation.** Wrong, waiting for the family to resolve the barriers postpones the referral that the source recommends to address those very problems (p. 1406).
**D. Refer for age-based regimen selection and adjustment of anticancer treatment intensity.** Wrong, chronological-age-based treatment selection does not provide the recommended barrier assistance; the source uses geriatric assessment, function, and life expectancy in optimizing treatment decisions (p. 1406).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1406.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: An 82-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has received palliative care alongside oncologic treatment for six months. Her disease has progressed despite second-line chemotherapy, and her oncologist estimates survival at two to three months. She has been hospitalized twice in the past month. Her family struggles with the limited prognosis, but she says she is tired of treatment and wants comfort at home. Which plan best aligns care with her expressed goals?
o: Continue the focus on tumor-directed care and explore third-line chemotherapy
Discuss home hospice with symptom management and support for the family
Continue the focus on tumor-directed care and explore clinical-trial enrollment
Increase hospital-based supportive visits as the main setting for ongoing care
explanation:
**Goal-concordant care** links treatment recommendations to what matters to the patient. Hazzard describes hospice as an option for symptom management and care at home; discussing it here applies those principles to her stated preference while supporting the family through the decision (pp. 1091–1092).
"providing options to the patient that are consistent with what has been found out is important to them." (p. 1091).
"In my experience, it can be one of the best programs for achieving the goals you mentioned for symptom management and care in the home." (p. 1092).

**A. Continue the focus on tumor-directed care and explore third-line chemotherapy.** Wrong, prioritizing further tumor-directed treatment does not address her expressed wish to focus on comfort at home; recommendations should reflect her goals (p. 1091).
**B. Discuss home hospice with symptom management and support for the family.** Correct, this offers the home-focused symptom care described and allows discussion with the patient and family (p. 1092).
**C. Continue the focus on tumor-directed care and explore clinical-trial enrollment.** Wrong, trial enrollment prioritizes another tumor-directed option rather than the goals she states; the source says options should be consistent with what is important to the patient (p. 1091).
**D. Increase hospital-based supportive visits as the main setting for ongoing care.** Wrong, hospital-centered visits do not directly implement the requested home-care focus; hospice is described as a program for symptom management at home (p. 1092).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1091, 1092.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An 82-year-old woman without bowel symptoms has previously undergone regular colorectal cancer screening. Her estimated life expectancy is about five years. Which approach follows the Hazzard authors' recommendation for routine screening?
o: Recommend discontinuing routine colorectal cancer screening.
Continue routine screening using colonoscopy.
Continue routine screening using fecal immunochemical testing.
Continue routine screening using flexible sigmoidoscopy.
explanation:
**Life expectancy** should be considered alongside the time needed for screening to benefit the patient (p. 163). The authors "recommend against screening for colorectal cancer if a person has an estimated life expectancy of less than 10 years" (p. 163). Their recommendation concerns screening itself, so changing the test does not address limited life expectancy.

**A. Recommend discontinuing routine colorectal cancer screening.** Correct, her estimated life expectancy falls below the authors' threshold for recommending against screening (p. 163).
**B. Continue routine screening using colonoscopy.** Wrong, colonoscopy still constitutes screening despite the life-expectancy consideration (p. 163).
**C. Continue routine screening using fecal immunochemical testing.** Wrong, changing to stool testing still continues screening, whereas the recommendation concerns colorectal screening generally (p. 163).
**D. Continue routine screening using flexible sigmoidoscopy.** Wrong, changing to sigmoidoscopy also continues screening despite the life-expectancy criterion (p. 163).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 163.
ref: Hazzard Ch 11 — PREVENTION AND SCREENING· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: After resection of colon cancer, eight lymph nodes were examined. How should this extent of nodal evaluation be interpreted according to Hazzard?
o: It meets the recommended minimum for an adequate lymph-node evaluation
It falls below the recommended minimum for an adequate lymph-node evaluation
It exceeds the recommended minimum for an adequate lymph-node evaluation
It meets a reduced recommended minimum for lymph-node evaluation in older adults
explanation:
**Adequate lymph-node evaluation** is described as examination of at least 12 lymph nodes. Inadequate evaluation correlates with inferior survival in the studies cited by Hazzard. Examining eight nodes falls below that stated minimum; this is an assessment of the extent of evaluation. (p. 1440)
"adequate lymph node evaluation (examination of at least 12 lymph nodes)" (p. 1440)
"Multiple studies have now demonstrated that inadequate lymph node evaluation correlates with inferior survival." (p. 1440)

**A. It meets the recommended minimum for an adequate lymph-node evaluation.** Wrong, eight nodes are fewer than the minimum of 12 used to define adequate evaluation in the source. (p. 1440)
**B. It falls below the recommended minimum for an adequate lymph-node evaluation.** Correct, the number examined is below the source’s minimum, so the extent of evaluation is inadequate by that definition. (p. 1440)
**C. It exceeds the recommended minimum for an adequate lymph-node evaluation.** Wrong, eight nodes are below, not above, the minimum of 12; the evaluation therefore cannot be described as exceeding that minimum. (p. 1440)
**D. It meets a reduced recommended minimum for lymph-node evaluation in older adults.** Wrong, the source applies the same definition of adequate evaluation when describing older adults as less likely to receive it; it does not describe a reduced recommended minimum for them. (p. 1440)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1440.
ref: Hazzard Ch 92 — GASTROINTESTINAL MALIGNANCIES · Harrison Ch 86 — Colorectal Cancer

q: An 84-year-old woman with frailty and localized colon cancer has been evaluated for open or laparoscopic-assisted colectomy. In the randomized studies summarized by Hazzard, how do postoperative pain and hospital stay with the laparoscopic approach compare with the open approach?
o: More postoperative pain and a shorter hospital stay
Less postoperative pain and a shorter hospital stay
Less postoperative pain and a longer hospital stay
More postoperative pain and a longer hospital stay
explanation:
**Laparoscopic-assisted colectomy** had similar outcomes to open colectomy in the cited randomized studies, with less pain and shorter hospitalization (p. 1440). Hazzard describes "slightly less postoperative pain and a 1-day shorter hospital stay." (p. 1440). These are study findings used for counseling, rather than a guaranteed result for this individual.

**A. More postoperative pain and a shorter hospital stay.** Wrong, shorter hospitalization matches the report, but greater postoperative pain does not: the studies reported slightly less pain (p. 1440).
**B. Less postoperative pain and a shorter hospital stay.** Correct, both directions match the study summary: less postoperative pain and a shorter stay (p. 1440).
**C. Less postoperative pain and a longer hospital stay.** Wrong, the pain comparison matches, but the studies reported a shorter rather than longer stay (p. 1440).
**D. More postoperative pain and a longer hospital stay.** Wrong, both comparisons conflict with the reported reduction in pain and length of stay (p. 1440).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1440.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1440

q: A 76-year-old man has undergone complete resection of stage III colon cancer (T3N1M0). He has coronary artery disease with a recent stent, hypertension, mild cognitive impairment, and an ECOG performance status of 1. His oncologist is considering adjuvant 5-fluorouracil-based treatment. Which statement describes the treatment evidence, without deciding his individual fitness for chemotherapy?
o: Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment loses its survival benefit in older subgroups
Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment is standard after resection of stage III disease
Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment is primarily established for node-negative stage II disease
Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment offers symptom relief without a postoperative survival benefit
explanation:
**Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine therapy** is an established treatment after complete resection of stage III colon cancer (p. 1440). Hazzard notes that "the previously observed survival benefit of fluoropyrimidine persisted in the older subgroup" (p. 1441). This is a statement about the evidence, not proof that this particular patient is fit for treatment.

**A. Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment loses its survival benefit in older subgroups.** Wrong, The reviewed older subgroup retained the fluoropyrimidine survival benefit (p. 1441).
**B. Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment is standard after resection of stage III disease.** Correct, The source identifies 5-FU-based adjuvant therapy as standard after resection of node-positive, stage III disease (p. 1440).
**C. Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment is primarily established for node-negative stage II disease.** Wrong, The source distinguishes the established stage III benefit from the less certain benefit in fully resected node-negative stage II disease (p. 1440).
**D. Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine treatment offers symptom relief without a postoperative survival benefit.** Wrong, The source describes superior survival with adjuvant 5-FU compared with observation, rather than symptom relief alone (pp. 1440-1441).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1440, 1441.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1440–1441

q: An 81-year-old woman has undergone complete resection of stage II, node-negative colon cancer after presenting with partial bowel obstruction. Pathology shows high-grade features and lymphovascular invasion. She has mild dementia and family support. Which statement about discussing adjuvant therapy is supported by Hazzard?
o: Consider adjuvant therapy because stage II has the established indication described for node-positive disease
Consider adjuvant therapy because presentation with obstruction is a high-risk feature for recurrence
Defer adjuvant therapy because obstruction identifies a stage II subgroup with lower recurrence risk
Consider adjuvant therapy because prospective benefit was demonstrated for fully resected stage II disease
explanation:
**High-risk features** matter within stage II colon cancer. Hazzard says a benefit of postoperative chemotherapy has not been prospectively demonstrated for fully resected stage II disease as a whole, but identifies "presentation with obstruction, perforation, or invasion into adjacent organs" as high-risk features in patients often considered for treatment (p. 1440). This supports a discussion based on the obstruction, without establishing a mandatory regimen or inferring treatment eligibility from the dementia label.

**A. Consider adjuvant therapy because stage II has the established indication described for node-positive disease.** Wrong, The source describes routine adjuvant therapy for regional node-positive stage III disease, not the same established indication for stage II as a whole (p. 1440).
**B. Consider adjuvant therapy because presentation with obstruction is a high-risk feature for recurrence.** Correct, Obstruction is explicitly listed as a high-risk presentation within stage II disease, supporting consideration of adjuvant therapy (p. 1440).
**C. Defer adjuvant therapy because obstruction identifies a stage II subgroup with lower recurrence risk.** Wrong, The source places obstruction among high-risk features for recurrence, rather than features that lower recurrence risk (p. 1440).
**D. Consider adjuvant therapy because prospective benefit was demonstrated for fully resected stage II disease.** Wrong, The source expressly states that a postoperative chemotherapy benefit has not been prospectively demonstrated in fully resected stage II disease as a group (p. 1440).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1440.
ref: Hazzard Ch 92 — GASTROINTESTINAL MALIGNANCIES · Harrison Ch 86 — Colorectal Cancer

q: The family of a 79-year-old man with rectal cancer asks about surgical outcomes in older adults. Which summary matches the French study described in Hazzard that compared surgical patients aged 80 or older with younger surgical patients?
o: Elective operative mortality was similar, and cancer-specific survival was lower in older patients.
Elective operative mortality was similar, and cancer-specific survival was comparable between the groups.
Elective operative mortality was higher in older patients, and cancer-specific survival was comparable.
Elective operative mortality was lower in older patients, and cancer-specific survival was higher.
explanation:
**Elective operative mortality and cancer-specific survival** need to be distinguished from overall survival in this study. Hazzard reports nearly identical operative mortality for elective surgery and comparable cancer-specific survival, although overall survival was greater in younger patients (p. 1440). "Among elective surgeries, the operative mortality was nearly identical (3%–4%)." (p. 1440).

**A. Elective operative mortality was similar, and cancer-specific survival was lower in older patients.** Wrong, the elective operative-mortality statement fits, but cancer-specific survival was comparable rather than lower in the older group (p. 1440).
**B. Elective operative mortality was similar, and cancer-specific survival was comparable between the groups.** Correct, both findings match the reported comparison: nearly identical elective operative mortality and comparable cancer-specific survival (p. 1440).
**C. Elective operative mortality was higher in older patients, and cancer-specific survival was comparable.** Wrong, the cancer-specific survival statement fits, but the elective-surgery subgroup had nearly identical operative mortality rather than higher mortality in older patients (p. 1440).
**D. Elective operative mortality was lower in older patients, and cancer-specific survival was higher.** Wrong, the study reported neither lower elective operative mortality nor higher cancer-specific survival in older patients; both outcomes were similar between groups (p. 1440).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1440.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1440

q: An 85-year-old woman with colon cancer requires surgery. She has heart failure and COPD. Her family wants everything possible done and prefers a familiar local community hospital. What does the Nationwide Inpatient Sample study described in Hazzard contribute to counseling about hospital volume?
o: Mortality in adults over 80 was similar in high-volume hospitals and smaller institutions
Mortality in adults over 80 was lower in high-volume hospitals than in smaller institutions
The mortality difference by hospital volume was less pronounced over age 80 than over age 65
Mortality in adults over 80 was higher in high-volume hospitals than in smaller institutions
explanation:
**Hospital surgical volume** was associated with perioperative mortality in the cited observational data. Among adults over 80, the reported mortality was 4.6% at high-volume centers and 7.3% at smaller institutions; the chapter therefore suggests considering high-volume hospitals for the oldest patients (p. 1440).
"This effect was even more pronounced for adults older than 80 years, where 4.6% of adults died at high-volume centers compared to 7.3% at smaller institutions" (p. 1440).
"Therefore, it may be preferable to send the very oldest adults with colon cancer to high-volume hospitals for their resections." (p. 1440).

**A. Mortality in adults over 80 was similar in high-volume hospitals and smaller institutions.** Wrong, the reported rates were lower at high-volume centers, rather than equivalent across settings (p. 1440).
**B. Mortality in adults over 80 was lower in high-volume hospitals than in smaller institutions.** Correct, this preserves the direction of the reported association and supports discussing a high-volume center; it is not an individual outcome prediction (p. 1440).
**C. The mortality difference by hospital volume was less pronounced over age 80 than over age 65.** Wrong, the source describes the mortality difference as more pronounced in adults over 80, rather than less pronounced (p. 1440).
**D. Mortality in adults over 80 was higher in high-volume hospitals than in smaller institutions.** Wrong, the reported direction favors high-volume centers: the smaller institutions had the higher mortality rate (p. 1440).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1440.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1440

q: When discussing prognosis after colon cancer surgery, Hazzard describes a surgical cohort in which cardiovascular disease was the next most frequent cause of death after colorectal cancer. What implication follows for counseling an older patient?
o: Reduce the importance assigned to comorbid disease when planning follow-up
Consider deaths from comorbid disease alongside deaths from colorectal cancer
Give another primary cancer greater prognostic weight than cardiovascular disease
Infer that cardiovascular death is more frequent than death from the original cancer
explanation:
**Competing causes of death** matter when interpreting survival after cancer surgery. In the reported cohort, Hazzard lists "cardiovascular disease (24.5%) and another primary cancer (7.4%)" after colorectal cancer among causes of death (p. 1440). Inference: counseling should therefore consider comorbid disease alongside the original cancer, without treating cohort proportions as a personal forecast.

**A. Reduce the importance assigned to comorbid disease when planning follow-up.** Wrong, This inference goes against the substantial contribution of cardiovascular disease described among deaths in the cohort (p. 1440).
**B. Consider deaths from comorbid disease alongside deaths from colorectal cancer.** Correct, This is the supported counseling inference: the cohort includes deaths from both colorectal cancer and comorbid cardiovascular disease (p. 1440).
**C. Give another primary cancer greater prognostic weight than cardiovascular disease.** Wrong, The reported ordering places cardiovascular disease ahead of another primary cancer, not below it (p. 1440).
**D. Infer that cardiovascular death is more frequent than death from the original cancer.** Wrong, The source places colorectal cancer ahead of cardiovascular disease in this cohort; it does not support that reversal (p. 1440).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1440.
ref: Hazzard Ch 92 — GASTROINTESTINAL MALIGNANCIES · Harrison Ch 86 — Colorectal Cancer

q: Why does detecting and removing colonic adenomatous polyps contribute to colorectal cancer prevention, according to Hazzard?
o: Removal treats invasive carcinoma already demonstrated by an adenoma
Removal precedes an adenoma's transformation into invasive malignancy
An adenoma protects the colon against additional tumors
Removal accelerates the adenoma's transformation into invasive malignancy
explanation:
**Adenomatous polyps are targets for prevention** because they can be removed before malignant transformation (p. 1439). Hazzard describes polyps that "are then removed before they transform into a malignancy over a 5- to 10-year period." (p. 1439). This is the preventive sequence being tested, rather than treatment of an already proven invasive cancer.

**A. Removal treats invasive carcinoma already demonstrated by an adenoma.** Wrong, the cited sequence distinguishes an adenoma from the malignancy into which it may transform; finding an adenoma does not itself demonstrate invasive carcinoma (p. 1439).
**B. Removal precedes an adenoma's transformation into invasive malignancy.** Correct, removal interrupts the sequence before malignant transformation, which is why the source links detection and removal to reduced cancer risk (p. 1439).
**C. An adenoma protects the colon against additional tumors.** Wrong, the source describes adenomas as lesions with potential for neoplastic transformation, not as protection against other tumors (p. 1439).
**D. Removal accelerates the adenoma's transformation into invasive malignancy.** Wrong, the preventive role is removal before transformation; accelerating transformation would not describe that mechanism (p. 1439).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1439.
ref: Hazzard Ch 92 — GASTROINTESTINAL MALIGNANCIES · Harrison Ch 86 — Colorectal Cancer

q: An 88-year-old man with colon adenocarcinoma, dementia, and functional decline is referred for discussion of cancer treatment. What does a comprehensive geriatric assessment contribute to treatment selection?
o: It derives functional age from the number of years lived
It identifies deficits beyond those found in routine oncology assessment
It infers absence of deficits from a good oncology performance score
It separates treatment selection from the effects of existing comorbidities
explanation:
**Comprehensive geriatric assessment** evaluates functional age through domains including function, comorbidity, nutrition, medication use, and cognition. It can uncover problems missed by routine history, examination, or oncology performance tools, and can identify older patients at increased risk of chemotherapy toxicity (p. 1388). "It can uncover problems that would not otherwise be identified by routine history and physical or by the traditional oncology performance status tools." (p. 1388).

**A. It derives functional age from the number of years lived.** Wrong, The source describes a multidomain assessment of functional age, rather than deriving it from chronological age (p. 1388).
**B. It identifies deficits beyond those found in routine oncology assessment.** Correct, The assessment can reveal clinically relevant deficits that routine assessment or oncology performance tools have missed (p. 1388).
**C. It infers absence of deficits from a good oncology performance score.** Wrong, The source includes patients with good ECOG performance status when describing the value of geriatric assessment; a good score does not establish absence of deficits (p. 1388).
**D. It separates treatment selection from the effects of existing comorbidities.** Wrong, Comorbidities that may interfere with cancer therapy are explicitly included, rather than separated from treatment assessment (p. 1388).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 92 — GASTROINTESTINAL MALIGNANCIES · Harrison Ch 86 — Colorectal Cancer

q: An 82-year-old man has a rapidly growing red, 1.5 cm lesion on his sun-exposed scalp that developed over six weeks. He has chronic lymphocytic leukemia and takes multiple medications. Biopsy confirms Merkel cell carcinoma. His family is concerned about functional decline and asks about treatment options. What should guide initial treatment planning according to Hazzard?
o: Prioritize chronological age when choosing the intended treatment intensity
Assess life expectancy, functional status, and patient preferences when planning treatment
Prioritize chronological age when choosing the intended observation strategy
Set treatment goals before discussing the patient's preferences and overall status
explanation:
**Individualized skin-cancer care** considers overall status and patient wishes after diagnosis (p. 1471). Hazzard states: “Once a lesion is biopsied and diagnosed, treatment recommendations should be tailored to the individual” (p. 1471). Life expectancy, function, treatment burden, and preferences inform that assessment (p. 1471).

**A. Prioritize chronological age when choosing the intended treatment intensity.** Wrong, Hazzard places overall status and patient wishes above chronological age when determining appropriate treatment (p. 1471).
**B. Assess life expectancy, functional status, and patient preferences when planning treatment.** Correct, These are the factors the source asks clinicians to consider when tailoring treatment to the individual (p. 1471).
**C. Prioritize chronological age when choosing the intended observation strategy.** Wrong, Chronological age should not take priority over overall status and patient wishes in choosing treatment or observation (p. 1471).
**D. Set treatment goals before discussing the patient's preferences and overall status.** Wrong, The source calls for shared decision-making involving the patient and family, so preferences and overall status belong in treatment planning (p. 1471).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1471.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1471

q: A 78-year-old woman with moderate dementia and a bleeding basal cell carcinoma on her nose becomes agitated during procedures. The team discusses Mohs surgery with her and her daughter. Which statement follows Hazzard's discussion and helps assess treatment burden?
o: Postoperative morbidity arises mainly from serial excisions rather than reconstruction
Functional status and cognitive limitations affect suitability for the procedure
Large studies show a higher postoperative complication rate in older adults
The cited comparative study found higher postoperative pain in older adults
explanation:
**Suitability for Mohs surgery includes functional and cognitive assessment**, because the procedure can be long and tedious (p. 1462). Hazzard advises considering "the patient’s functional status and any physical or cognitive limitations that would make them poor candidates for this form of surgery." (p. 1462). Inference: the reported procedural agitation belongs in that individualized discussion; it does not establish a treatment decision by itself.

**A. Postoperative morbidity arises mainly from serial excisions rather than reconstruction.** Wrong, the source states that extensive repair often contributes to morbidity, rather than the serial excisions (p. 1462).
**B. Functional status and cognitive limitations affect suitability for the procedure.** Correct, this directly matches the source’s assessment of suitability and is relevant to the cognitive and procedural difficulties in the stem (p. 1462).
**C. Large studies show a higher postoperative complication rate in older adults.** Wrong, the cited large studies found no difference in postsurgical complication incidence between older and younger adults (p. 1462).
**D. The cited comparative study found higher postoperative pain in older adults.** Wrong, the cited study reported greater mean postoperative pain among younger adults, not older adults (p. 1462).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1462.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1462

q: גבר בן 85, אפרו-אמריקאי, אובחן עם Merkel cell carcinoma שלב II לפני 3 חודשים. למרות שיש לו ביטוח Medicare, הוא טרם קיבל טיפול כירורגי דפיניטיבי. הרופא הראשוני שלו מוטרד מהעיכובים בטיפולו. בהתבסס על הממצאים הקיימים, איזו בעיית פערים משקף תרחיש זה בצורה הסבירה ביותר?
o: היעדר כיסוי במדיקייר לטיפול ניתוחי בקרצינומה של תאי מרקל מסביר את העיכוב, ולכן אין מדובר בפער בזמינות טיפול
מרחק גדול יותר של מטופלים שחורים מבית החולים הוא ההסבר לפער שנמצא בזמן עד לטיפול הניתוחי הדפיניטיבי
Healthcare disparities המשפיעות על עיתוי הטיפול ב-Black patients גם עם כיסוי Medicare
הזמן עד לטיפול בקרצינומה של תאי מרקל דומה בין הקבוצות, והעיכוב המתואר אינו משקף פער שנמצא במחקר
explanation: התשובה הנכונה היא healthcare disparities המשפיעות על עיתוי הטיפול ב-Black patients גם עם כיסוי Medicare. הפרק מצטט מחקר של למעלה מ-26,000 חולים מה-National Cancer Database שהראה כי הזמן לטיפול כירורגי דפיניטיבי ב-Merkel cell carcinoma שלב I-III היה ארוך משמעותית ב-Black patients (58.9 ימים) בהשוואה ל-non-Hispanic Whites (46.3 ימים). חשוב לציין שפערים אלה נמשכו הן עבור מבוטחי Medicare והן עבור מבוטחים פרטיים, אך לא בקרב מבוטחי Medicaid או חסרי ביטוח. המחקר מצא שכך קרה למרות ש-Black patients התגוררו בפועל קרוב יותר לבתי החולים מאשר non-Hispanic Whites, מה שמדגיש פערים מערכתיים שחורגים מבעיות גישה פשוטות. ממצא זה מדאיג במיוחד לנוכח האופי האגרסיבי של MCC והסיכון הגבוה לגרורות, שהופכים את הטיפול המוקדם לקריטי. האפשרות „היעדר כיסוי ביטוחי לטיפול בסרטן עור בחולים קשישים“ אינה נכונה כי הפרק מציין שמבוטחי Medicare אכן חווים פערים אלה, מה שמרמז שהכיסוי הביטוחי אינו הגורם העיקרי. האפשרות „מחסומים גיאוגרפיים – המטופל מתגורר רחוק ממרכזי הטיפול“ אינה נכונה כי המחקר המצוטט מצא ש-Black patients התגוררו קרוב יותר למרכזי הטיפול מאשר White patients, ובכל זאת חוו עיכובים. האפשרות „ציר זמן טיפולי תקין לחולים קשישים עם סרטן עור“ אינה נכונה כי 3 חודשים מהווים עיכוב משמעותי עבור גידול אגרסיבי כמו MCC, והפרק מדגיש את החשיבות הקריטית של זיהוי וטיפול מוקדמים. התרחיש משקף ישירות את ממצאי המחקר בנוגע ל-racial disparities מתמשכים בעיתוי הטיפול. Clinical Pearl: Healthcare disparities בטיפול בסרטן עור נמשכות גם עם כיסוי ביטוחי מספק – Black patients חווים עיכובים ארוכים משמעותית לטיפול דפיניטיבי בגידולים אגרסיביים כמו MCC, מה שמדגיש את הצורך בגישות מערכתיות להבטחת מתן טיפול שוויוני.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1470
retiredReason: US health-system policy (Medicare, Medicaid, PACE, US federal law or agency); not part of the Israeli exam.

q: A 76-year-old man with comorbidities is concerned about treatment of a well-demarcated, 5-mm nodular basal cell carcinoma on his back. Which explanation of treatment options and lesion location matches the examples in Hazzard?
o: Expect comparable cure rates with the same method on the back and nasal ala
Expect several effective options for the back lesion and individualize treatment
Expect reliable local cure with electrodesiccation and curettage for an ulcerated nasal lesion
Expect completion of radiation in one visit for an ulcerated nodular nasal lesion
explanation:
**Location and treatment burden** affect the choice of treatment for basal cell carcinoma. Hazzard contrasts a small, well-demarcated back lesion with lesions on the nasal ala and notes that radiation for its ulcerated nasal example "would require multiple visits" (p. 1470).

**A. Expect comparable cure rates with the same method on the back and nasal ala.** Wrong, The source explicitly says that the high cure rate described for the small back lesion does not apply in the same way at the high-risk nasal ala (p. 1470).
**B. Expect several effective options for the back lesion and individualize treatment.** Correct, The back-lesion example supports several effective treatments, while the source emphasizes an individualized choice and discussion of the procedure (p. 1470).
**C. Expect reliable local cure with electrodesiccation and curettage for an ulcerated nasal lesion.** Wrong, For the ulcerated lower-nose example, electrodesiccation and curettage has a cure rate below half, which does not support this assurance of reliable cure (p. 1470).
**D. Expect completion of radiation in one visit for an ulcerated nodular nasal lesion.** Wrong, The source specifies multiple radiation visits for the nasal example, so a one-visit assurance misrepresents its burden (p. 1470).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1470.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1470

q: A 73-year-old woman with an ulcerated 6-mm nodular basal cell carcinoma on her nose is considering Mohs surgery. Which description explains local tumor control with tissue preservation?
o: Electrodessication and curettage examine the entire margin microscopically during tissue removal
Mohs surgery selects margins by appearance and postpones their microscopic examination
Mohs examines complete margins in real time during staged excision
Electrodessication and curettage map residual margin cells to guide further targeted excision
explanation:
**Mohs micrographic surgery** uses staged excision with real-time microscopic evaluation of the entire surgical margin. Residual tumor is mapped to guide the next excision, allowing preservation of normal tissue while pursuing clear margins (p. 1462).
"serial tangential excisions with real-time microscopic evaluation of the entirety of the surgical margins to ensure that the tumor is excised completely." (p. 1462).
"If residual cancer cells are noted at a margin, the precise location is mapped and identified on the patient." (p. 1462).

**A. Electrodessication and curettage examine the entire margin microscopically during tissue removal.** Wrong, electrodessication and curettage remove gross tumor and destroy residual cells at the wound base and periphery; the complete microscopic margin method described belongs to Mohs surgery (pp. 1461–1462).
**B. Mohs surgery selects margins by appearance and postpones their microscopic examination.** Wrong, Mohs uses real-time microscopic examination to guide subsequent stages, not delayed examination after visually chosen margins (p. 1462).
**C. Mohs examines complete margins in real time during staged excision.** Correct, the staged, complete-margin examination is the mechanism the source links to tissue preservation and local control (p. 1462).
**D. Electrodessication and curettage map residual margin cells to guide further targeted excision.** Wrong, mapping residual cancer at a margin and excising the corresponding location is the Mohs technique, not the curettage-and-desiccation sequence (pp. 1461–1462).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1461, 1462.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.1461–1462

q: A person with limited life expectancy has a basal cell carcinoma in a low-risk area without other risk factors. Why might active surveillance with monitoring of growth and symptoms be considered?
o: The tumor tends to grow rapidly and respond to systemic treatment.
The tumor tends to spread early and require combined treatment.
The tumor tends to grow slowly and follow an indolent course.
The tumor tends to remain stable, permitting surveillance without continued tumor monitoring.
explanation:
**Low-risk basal cell carcinoma** is generally indolent and slow-growing. Hazzard describes active surveillance as an option for selected patients with limited life expectancy to avoid unnecessary treatment while monitoring growth or symptoms; it is not the standard of care (p. 1463).
"Since BCCs are generally indolent and slow-growing, active surveillance can help patients avoid unnecessary treatments while closely monitoring for tumor growth or development of symptoms." (p. 1463).

**A. The tumor tends to grow rapidly and respond to systemic treatment.** Wrong, rapid growth is inconsistent with the generally slow-growing behavior given as the rationale for surveillance (p. 1463).
**B. The tumor tends to spread early and require combined treatment.** Wrong, early spread requiring combined treatment does not match the indolent behavior underlying this selected low-risk surveillance approach (p. 1463).
**C. The tumor tends to grow slowly and follow an indolent course.** Correct, slow growth and an indolent course are the stated reasons to discuss surveillance in the circumstances given (p. 1463).
**D. The tumor tends to remain stable, permitting surveillance without continued tumor monitoring.** Wrong, the source describes surveillance with close monitoring for growth or symptoms; omitting that monitoring is not the approach it proposes (p. 1463).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1463.
ref: Hazzard Ch 93 — SKIN CANCER · Harrison Ch 81 — Cancer of the Skin

q: A 71-year-old woman with moderate dementia has a new pigmented lesion that has changed recently. Her dermatologist suspects melanoma, and diagnostic sampling is feasible. What is the next step described in the chapter?
o: Arrange repeat photography to monitor further change in the suspicious lesion
Apply cryotherapy as the initial local treatment of the suspicious lesion
Obtain a biopsy to establish the diagnosis of the suspicious lesion
Apply a topical medication as the initial treatment of the suspicious lesion
explanation:
**Diagnostic biopsy** is recommended for lesions concerning for high-risk skin cancer, including melanoma. The source states, "Biopsies should always be performed for lesions concerning for high-risk skin cancer" and includes melanoma among its examples (p. 1471). After diagnosis, treatment is individualized according to preferences, overall health, and the benefits and burdens of treatment (p. 1471).

**A. Arrange repeat photography to monitor further change in the suspicious lesion.** Wrong, Serial photographs do not provide the biopsy diagnosis recommended for a lesion suspicious for melanoma when sampling is feasible (p. 1471).
**B. Apply cryotherapy as the initial local treatment of the suspicious lesion.** Wrong, Starting local treatment with cryotherapy skips the recommended diagnostic biopsy before tailoring management (p. 1471).
**C. Obtain a biopsy to establish the diagnosis of the suspicious lesion.** Correct, This follows the specified diagnostic step for suspected melanoma; the subsequent treatment decision can then be individualized (p. 1471).
**D. Apply a topical medication as the initial treatment of the suspicious lesion.** Wrong, Starting a topical treatment also bypasses the recommended biopsy and diagnosis for a lesion concerning for melanoma (p. 1471).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1471.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1471

q: A 79-year-old man and his family are preparing for Mohs surgery. Which description of tumor removal should be included in the explanation?
o: Fixed-margin excision followed by delayed examination of sampled margins
Tissue destruction by freezing followed by clinical site assessment
Staged excision with real-time microscopy of the complete margins
Tissue destruction by cautery followed by clinical site assessment
explanation:
**Mohs micrographic surgery** removes tissue in stages while examining the entire surgical margin microscopically. Residual cancer is mapped so that the next layer can be removed from the corresponding site, preserving as much normal tissue as possible (p. 1462).
"serial tangential excisions with real-time microscopic evaluation of the entirety of the surgical margins to ensure that the tumor is excised completely." (p. 1462).
"If residual cancer cells are noted at a margin, the precise location is mapped and identified on the patient." (p. 1462).

**A. Fixed-margin excision followed by delayed examination of sampled margins.** Wrong, The procedure uses real-time examination of the entire margin and additional mapped stages, not delayed examination of sampled margins (p. 1462).
**B. Tissue destruction by freezing followed by clinical site assessment.** Wrong, Freezing with clinical reassessment does not describe serial excisions and microscopic margin examination (p. 1462).
**C. Staged excision with real-time microscopy of the complete margins.** Correct, This captures the staged removal and real-time evaluation of the entire surgical margin described in the source (p. 1462).
**D. Tissue destruction by cautery followed by clinical site assessment.** Wrong, Cautery with clinical reassessment does not supply the excised layers and microscopic margin mapping that define Mohs (p. 1462).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1462.
ref: Hazzard Ch 93 — SKIN CANCER · Harrison Ch 81 — Cancer of the Skin

q: An older woman has a bleeding basal cell carcinoma that requires wound care. Which feature of the tumor’s course explains why treatment should be considered?
o: A tendency toward early metastatic spread during the course of the disease
A tendency toward local tissue destruction with ulceration and bleeding
A tendency toward spontaneous disappearance as the untreated lesion progresses over time
A tendency to preserve surrounding tissue despite progressive enlargement of the tumor
explanation:
**Basal cell carcinoma** can cause substantial local morbidity despite its rare metastasis. Hazzard describes untreated growth producing local destruction, ulceration, bleeding, and other complications; the existing bleeding in the stem is consistent with that local disease burden (p. 1458). "If left untreated, relentless growth can lead to extensive local destruction, ulceration, drainage, bleeding, infection, and disfigurement." (p. 1458).

**A. A tendency toward early metastatic spread during the course of the disease.** Wrong, metastasis is described as rare, so frequent early metastatic spread is not the feature explaining this presentation (p. 1458).
**B. A tendency toward local tissue destruction with ulceration and bleeding.** Correct, local destruction, ulceration, and bleeding are explicitly described consequences of untreated growth, matching the concern raised in the stem (p. 1458).
**C. A tendency toward spontaneous disappearance as the untreated lesion progresses over time.** Wrong, the source describes persistent growth with local complications if untreated, rather than a tendency toward disappearance (p. 1458).
**D. A tendency to preserve surrounding tissue despite progressive enlargement of the tumor.** Wrong, growth can be locally destructive and can invade nearby structures, so preservation of local tissue is not the expected pattern described (p. 1458).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1458.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES · Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: A 77-year-old man has a red-purple scalp nodule that has grown rapidly over recent months. Merkel cell carcinoma is suspected. What is the rationale for early evaluation according to Hazzard?
o: Its slow progression supports observation until a further clinical change occurs
Its recurrence and metastatic risks support early identification and treatment
Its small size supports postponing evaluation of the regional lymph nodes
Its resemblance to an inflamed cyst supports postponing diagnostic tissue sampling
explanation:
**Merkel cell carcinoma** is an aggressive tumor with substantial recurrence and metastatic risk. Hazzard states, "Given its aggressive nature and risk for metastasis, it is critical to identify and treat MCC early" (p. 1470). An apparently small lesion or resemblance to an inflamed cyst does not remove the need for evaluation (p. 1470).

**A. Its slow progression supports observation until a further clinical change occurs.** Wrong, The source characterizes the tumor as aggressive, rather than slow-growing, and explicitly emphasizes early diagnosis and treatment (p. 1470).
**B. Its recurrence and metastatic risks support early identification and treatment.** Correct, This is the stated rationale: recurrence and metastatic potential make early identification and treatment important (p. 1470).
**C. Its small size supports postponing evaluation of the regional lymph nodes.** Wrong, The source describes occult regional nodal metastases even with the smallest clinical tumors; small size is not a sound basis for postponement (p. 1470).
**D. Its resemblance to an inflamed cyst supports postponing diagnostic tissue sampling.** Wrong, An inflamed cyst is a reported initial misdiagnosis, while rapid growth prompts biopsy and accurate diagnosis (p. 1470).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1470.
ref: Hazzard Ch 93 — SKIN CANCER · Harrison Ch 81 — Cancer of the Skin

q: A 78-year-old man with stage II NSCLC (T2N1M0) underwent successful lobectomy six weeks ago. His ECOG performance status is 1, creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL compared with a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL, and he has otherwise recovered well from surgery. The team is considering adjuvant chemotherapy. Which statement best reflects the evidence described by Hazzard?
o: Renal dysfunction favors cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence remains limited
Renal dysfunction complicates cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence remains limited
Renal dysfunction complicates cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence is extensive
Renal dysfunction favors cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence is extensive
explanation:
**Adjuvant chemotherapy selection** requires attention to treatment tolerance and the limits of the evidence. Hazzard notes that cisplatin regimens can be more difficult for older adults to tolerate, particularly with renal dysfunction, and states: “large, prospective trials evaluating carboplatin-based regimens remain sparse” (p. 1426). This supports recognizing the tolerance problem without claiming a well-established carboplatin substitute from these pages.

**A. Renal dysfunction favors cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence remains limited.** Wrong, The source identifies renal dysfunction as a setting of greater difficulty tolerating cisplatin, not a reason for improved tolerance (p. 1426).
**B. Renal dysfunction complicates cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence remains limited.** Correct, This accurately combines the stated cisplatin tolerance concern with the limited prospective evidence for carboplatin-based regimens (p. 1426).
**C. Renal dysfunction complicates cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence is extensive.** Wrong, The cisplatin concern is supported, but the source says large prospective carboplatin trials remain sparse, rather than extensive (p. 1426).
**D. Renal dysfunction favors cisplatin tolerance, while prospective carboplatin evidence is extensive.** Wrong, Both parts conflict with the source: renal dysfunction complicates tolerance and prospective carboplatin evidence is sparse (p. 1426).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1426.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: A 72-year-old woman has stage I NSCLC (T1bN0M0) and severe COPD (FEV1 30% predicted), coronary artery disease, and diabetes. She is not a surgical candidate. PET imaging shows a peripheral 2.5-cm nodule without metastatic disease. Which treatment delivers focused, ablative radiation to the primary lung tumor over a few fractions, as described in Hazzard?
o: Conventionally fractionated thoracic radiation therapy
Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT)
Symptom-directed palliation without local tumor treatment
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical lung resection
explanation:
**SBRT provides a local radiation approach** for medically inoperable early-stage NSCLC (p. 1425). Hazzard describes "focused and ablative radiation doses over a few fractions to the primary lung tumor with lower toxicity." (p. 1425). The cited comparison is with conventional radiotherapy, and the source reports prospective SBRT trials in medically inoperable patients (p. 1425).

**A. Conventionally fractionated thoracic radiation therapy.** Wrong, the source distinguishes conventional radiotherapy from the focused, ablative few-fraction SBRT technique asked about here (p. 1425).
**B. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT).** Correct, SBRT is the named technique that delivers focused ablative doses over a few fractions to the primary tumor (p. 1425).
**C. Symptom-directed palliation without local tumor treatment.** Wrong, symptom-directed palliation without local therapy does not deliver the tumor-directed radiation described in the question (p. 1425).
**D. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical lung resection.** Wrong, the stem excludes surgery, and chemotherapy followed by resection is not the radiation technique described by the source (p. 1425).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1425.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1425

q: In which population did the PACIFIC trial evaluate durvalumab, according to Hazzard?
o: Resected early-stage disease before the start of adjuvant systemic therapy
Metastatic disease progressing after completion of a course of chemotherapy
Unresectable stage III disease controlled after concurrent chemotherapy and radiation
Resected stage III disease before the start of postoperative radiation therapy
explanation:
**PACIFIC** evaluated durvalumab in patients with unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer whose disease was controlled after concurrent chemoradiation. The trial population is therefore defined by both disease stage and the treatment already completed, rather than by a postoperative treatment pathway. (p. 1426)
"In the PACIFIC trial, 713 patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC who had disease control after concurrent chemoradiation were randomized" (p. 1426)

**A. Resected early-stage disease before the start of adjuvant systemic therapy.** Wrong, the trial enrolled unresectable stage III disease after concurrent chemoradiation, not resected early-stage disease awaiting adjuvant therapy. (p. 1426)
**B. Metastatic disease progressing after completion of a course of chemotherapy.** Wrong, the trial population had controlled stage III disease, not metastatic disease progressing after chemotherapy. (p. 1426)
**C. Unresectable stage III disease controlled after concurrent chemotherapy and radiation.** Correct, this includes the unresectability, stage, disease control, and prior concurrent chemoradiation specified in the source. (p. 1426)
**D. Resected stage III disease before the start of postoperative radiation therapy.** Wrong, the trial enrolled unresectable disease after concurrent chemoradiation, not patients awaiting postoperative radiation. (p. 1426)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1426.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: According to Hazzard, in which setting are supporting data for adjuvant chemotherapy lacking?
o: After resection of stage II NSCLC in a patient who has recovered well
After resection of stage II NSCLC using a cisplatin-based doublet regimen
After curative-intent SBRT for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer
After resection when chemotherapy is delayed until postoperative recovery
explanation:
**Adjuvant chemotherapy evidence** depends on the preceding local treatment (p. 1426). The chapter describes benefit after surgery in selected stage II patients, including treatment delayed until recovery. It then states, "there are no data to support adjuvant chemotherapy after SBRT in early-stage NSCLC" (p. 1426).

**A. After resection of stage II NSCLC in a patient who has recovered well.** Wrong, a clinical benefit is described in selected stage II patients with proper surgical recovery, good performance status, and no significant comorbidities (p. 1426).
**B. After resection of stage II NSCLC using a cisplatin-based doublet regimen.** Wrong, cisplatin-based adjuvant doublets have improved cancer-related and overall survival after surgery (p. 1426).
**C. After curative-intent SBRT for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer.** Correct, the absence of supporting data is specifically stated for chemotherapy after SBRT in early-stage disease (p. 1426).
**D. After resection when chemotherapy is delayed until postoperative recovery.** Wrong, delayed adjuvant chemotherapy upon postoperative recovery is described as remaining efficacious (p. 1426).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1426.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1426

q: A 76-year-old man underwent complete resection of stage II NSCLC. A postoperative complication delayed adjuvant treatment, but he has now recovered and has good performance status. Which conclusion about chemotherapy timing is supported by Hazzard?
o: A delay after resection supports surveillance instead of chemotherapy
Adjuvant chemotherapy remains efficacious after delayed recovery
Preoperative chemotherapy is preferred because of proven outcome superiority
Evidence after resection also establishes adjuvant chemotherapy after SBRT
explanation:
**Delayed adjuvant chemotherapy** can remain efficacious once a patient recovers from lung cancer surgery. The source does not show better outcomes with preoperative rather than postoperative treatment and distinguishes resection evidence from the lack of supporting data after SBRT (p. 1426).
"delayed adjuvant chemotherapy administration upon recovery after surgery remains efficacious." (p. 1426).
"has not been shown to improve outcomes compared to postoperative administration." (p. 1426).

**A. A delay after resection supports surveillance instead of chemotherapy.** Wrong, Delay alone does not justify abandoning adjuvant treatment: the source reports continued efficacy after recovery (p. 1426).
