**A. The finding fits the usual synovial fluid pattern of osteoarthritis.** Wrong, The stated count is above the range commonly described for OA fluid and falls on the inflammatory or infectious side of the source distinction (p. 783).
**B. The finding supports attributing pain to cartilage wear without further evaluation.** Wrong, The elevated count suggests inflammatory or infectious arthritis, so the prior OA diagnosis does not adequately account for this fluid finding (p. 783).
**C. The finding calls for evaluation for inflammatory or infectious arthritis.** Correct, The count is above the source threshold for considering an inflammatory or infectious etiology; evaluating those possibilities is the clinical application of that distinction (p. 783).
**D. The finding confirms crystal arthritis despite the absence of observed crystals.** Wrong, The source associates visible gout or pseudogout crystals with crystal arthritis; no crystals were observed here, so this finding does not confirm that diagnosis (p. 783).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 783.
ref: Hazzard Ch 104 — INFECTION AND APPROPRIATE ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION

q: An 85-year-old resident with dementia has substantial agitation. Medical contributors have been assessed and nonpharmacologic interventions have been insufficient, so a psychotropic medication trial is planned. Which approach follows Hazzard?
o: Start at a high dose, increase slowly, and frequently reassess benefits and harms
Start at a low dose, increase rapidly, and frequently reassess benefits and harms
Start at a low dose, increase slowly, and reassess treatment benefits
Start at a low dose, increase slowly, and reassess benefits and harms
explanation:
**Psychotropic treatment** requires attention to adverse effects as well as symptom benefit. The chapter advises clinicians to "start low and go slow" and "frequently reassess the risk/benefit ratio of the medication" (p. 932), because these drugs are associated with adverse effects.

**A. Start at a high dose, increase slowly, and frequently reassess benefits and harms.** Wrong, a high starting dose conflicts with the recommendation to start low (p. 932).
**B. Start at a low dose, increase rapidly, and frequently reassess benefits and harms.** Wrong, rapid dose escalation conflicts with the recommendation to go slow (p. 932).
**C. Start at a low dose, increase slowly, and reassess treatment benefits.** Wrong, tracking benefit without assessing harm does not provide the required risk-benefit reassessment (p. 932).
**D. Start at a low dose, increase slowly, and reassess benefits and harms.** Correct, this combines cautious dosing with the repeated benefit-harm assessment recommended by the chapter (p. 932).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 932.
ref: Hazzard Ch 60 — BEHAVIORAL SYMPTOMS OF DEMENTIA AND PSYCHOACTIVE DRUG THERAPY
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: A woman with falls takes zolpidem. Her team considers switching to a short-half-life benzodiazepine on the assumption that a shorter duration prevents fall injuries. Which conclusion follows Hazzard?
o: A shorter half-life indicates a low risk of fall injuries
A shorter half-life justifies less frequent medication review
A shorter half-life does not establish a lower risk of fall injuries
A shorter half-life identifies a treatment that does not contribute to falls
explanation:
**Half-life does not establish clinical safety** in this comparison. Hazzard reports that fall-related injury risk with short-half-life benzodiazepines and Z-drugs may be similar to that with long-half-life benzodiazepines (p. 303).
"the risk of fall-related injuries in older adults prescribed short half-life benzodiazepines and so-called “Z-drugs” (eg, zolpidem) may actually be similar to that of long-half-life benzodiazepines." (p. 303).

**A. A shorter half-life indicates a low risk of fall injuries.** Wrong, the reported similarity in injury risk does not support classifying the short-half-life drug as low risk (p. 303).
**B. A shorter half-life justifies less frequent medication review.** Wrong, half-life does not resolve the fall-risk concern, so reduced review is not supported by this comparison (inference, p. 303).
**C. A shorter half-life does not establish a lower risk of fall injuries.** Correct, this preserves the uncertainty and possible similarity in risk described by the source (p. 303).
**D. A shorter half-life identifies a treatment that does not contribute to falls.** Wrong, a shorter half-life does not establish absence of contribution to fall injuries (p. 303).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 303.

q: An 83-year-old man with advanced heart and lung disease wants relief of breathlessness and distress. His daughter worries that adding palliative care means abandoning disease treatment. Which explanation matches the source definition?
o: Palliative care starts at the final stage after curative treatment ends
Palliative care makes prolonging life the primary goal of its plan
Palliative care relieves symptoms alongside disease treatment and patient goals
Palliative care makes normalization of disease measurements its central goal
explanation:
**Palliative care** focuses on relief of symptoms, pain, and stress and on care that matches the patient’s goals (p. 1045). It is not confined to the end of life: "It is appropriate for any type of diagnosis, any stage of a serious illness, and importantly, can be provided together with curative treatment." (p. 1045).

**A. Palliative care starts at the final stage after curative treatment ends.** Wrong, the source permits palliative care at any stage and alongside curative treatment (p. 1045).
**B. Palliative care makes prolonging life the primary goal of its plan.** Wrong, the definition emphasizes quality of life and symptom relief, with goals individualized rather than fixed on life prolongation (p. 1045).
**C. Palliative care relieves symptoms alongside disease treatment and patient goals.** Correct, this reflects concurrent symptom relief and goal-concordant disease care (p. 1045).
**D. Palliative care makes normalization of disease measurements its central goal.** Wrong, the source centers symptoms, quality of life, and patient goals rather than normalization of disease measurements (p. 1045).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1045.
chapterTitle: Palliative Care and Special Management Issues
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1045

q: A 76-year-old man undergoing rehabilitation after stroke has edema and a low serum albumin. Nutritional assessment is incomplete, and information about inflammation and protein loss is insufficient. What can be inferred from the albumin value?
o: It distinguishes nutritional deprivation from an ongoing inflammatory response
It should rise rapidly when adequate nutritional support is introduced
It indicates risk of undernutrition and adverse clinical outcomes
It allows nutritional support to be adjusted according to daily albumin changes
explanation:
**Low serum albumin** has low specificity for protein-energy undernutrition because inflammation and other diseases also affect it. The value signals nutritional and outcome risk, while its slow response to refeeding makes it unsuitable for judging the adequacy of nutritional support (p. 423).
"a low albumin indicates only that the patient is at risk for being undernourished, and for increased morbidity and mortality." (p. 423).
"Serum albumin does not increase rapidly with refeeding and should not be utilized as an indicator of the adequacy of nutritional support." (p. 423).

**A. It distinguishes nutritional deprivation from an ongoing inflammatory response.** Wrong, Hazzard states that the effects of inflammation cannot currently be distinguished from nutritional deprivation using albumin (p. 423).
**B. It should rise rapidly when adequate nutritional support is introduced.** Wrong, albumin does not rise rapidly with refeeding, so this expected response is unsupported (p. 423).
**C. It indicates risk of undernutrition and adverse clinical outcomes.** Correct, it matches the source's limited interpretation of low albumin without diagnosing the cause of the low value (p. 423).
**D. It allows nutritional support to be adjusted according to daily albumin changes.** Wrong, albumin should not be used as an indicator of adequate nutritional support; daily adjustment based on it would apply the value beyond that limitation (p. 423).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 423.

q: An 80-year-old woman with moderate vascular dementia in a memory-care unit has refused bathing for two weeks and smells of urine. She becomes aggressive when approached with bathing equipment, but there is no immediate danger. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis and takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and acetaminophen 650 mg twice daily. Her daughter says she used to be meticulous about cleanliness. Alongside assessing causes of distress, which approach follows first-line behavioral care?
o: Start risperidone before attempting to adjust the bathing routine
Use a sedative before attempting to adjust the bathing routine
Try bathing at a calmer time using a reassuring approach
Increase bedtime medication before attempting to adjust the bathing routine
explanation:
**Nonpharmacologic care** is first-line for neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia unless immediate safety requires another approach. A calm, individualized interaction is consistent with that principle; choosing a calmer bathing time is an application to this trigger (pp. 925–926). "Nonpharmacologic interventions are first-line in the management of NPS in dementia patients to avoid the risks and side effects associated with medications." (p. 925).

**A. Start risperidone before attempting to adjust the bathing routine.** Wrong, behavioral approaches precede psychotropics outside specified urgent circumstances; no trial of such approaches is described (p. 925).
**B. Use a sedative before attempting to adjust the bathing routine.** Wrong, using sedation before adapting care bypasses the recommended first-line approach and adds medication risks (p. 925).
**C. Try bathing at a calmer time using a reassuring approach.** Correct, adapting the interaction and using a reassuring manner applies the nonpharmacologic guidance to bathing-related distress (pp. 925–926; inference about timing).
**D. Increase bedtime medication before attempting to adjust the bathing routine.** Wrong, escalating sleep medication does not implement the first-line behavioral adjustment to the bathing trigger (p. 925).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 925, 926.
ref: Hazzard Ch 59 — DEMENTIA INCLUDING ALZHEIMER DISEASE

q: A patient develops respiratory depression after an opioid dose increase. Alongside respiratory support, which medication does Hazzard identify for reversal of potentially fatal opioid overdose?
o: Methadone
Naloxone
Buprenorphine
Naltrexone
explanation:
**Naloxone** is used for overdose reversal rather than ongoing treatment of opioid use disorder. Hazzard states: "Naloxone does not treat OUD, but it can reverse potentially fatal opioid overdoses" (p. 326). The same page distinguishes opioid agonist treatment and naltrexone maintenance from acute overdose reversal.

**A. Methadone.** Wrong, Methadone is a full opioid agonist used to prevent withdrawal and reduce cravings; that role does not reverse opioid toxicity (p. 326).
**B. Naloxone.** Correct, The source explicitly identifies naloxone as able to reverse potentially fatal opioid overdose (p. 326).
**C. Buprenorphine.** Wrong, Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist used in opioid use disorder; the acute reversal agent specified by the source is naloxone (p. 326).
**D. Naltrexone.** Wrong, Although naltrexone is an antagonist, the source requires patients not to be taking opioids when it is initiated because it can precipitate withdrawal; it is not the acute overdose-reversal treatment described (p. 326).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 326.

q: An 82-year-old woman develops a first episode of Clostridium difficile infection after antibiotic treatment. The illness is mild to moderate, she is stable, and she can take oral medication. Which treatment approach is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Use intravenous vancomycin to treat the colonic infection
Prefer oral metronidazole for its effectiveness in older patients
Use oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin for the infection
Continue the precipitating antibiotic to support infection treatment
explanation:
**Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin** is the initial approach described for mild to moderate disease (p. 1305). Older patients given metronidazole have a high risk of failure and recurrence, and "Intravenous vancomycin does not penetrate the colonic lumen" (p. 1305). The source also begins treatment by withdrawing the precipitating antibiotic if possible (p. 1305).

**A. Use intravenous vancomycin to treat the colonic infection.** Wrong, The intravenous route does not deliver effective treatment to the colonic lumen in this infection (p. 1305).
**B. Prefer oral metronidazole for its effectiveness in older patients.** Wrong, The source favors oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin over metronidazole because of failure and recurrence concerns in older patients (p. 1305).
**C. Use oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin for the infection.** Correct, Both oral agents are listed for initial treatment of mild to moderate disease, matching this presentation (p. 1305).
**D. Continue the precipitating antibiotic to support infection treatment.** Wrong, The source advises withdrawal of the precipitating antibiotic if possible, rather than continuing it as treatment support (p. 1305).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1305.
ref: Hazzard Ch 104 — INFECTION AND APPROPRIATE ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION

q: A man with established dementia becomes more somnolent and dependent on assistance. Which information about the time course particularly supports superimposed delirium?
o: Gradual memory decline over months to years
Longstanding language difficulty progressing over months
Abrupt worsening of attention and alertness from baseline
Stable executive difficulty with little change over the year
explanation:
**Change from baseline** and its time course help distinguish delirium from chronic impairment (p. 886). Hazzard describes "acute onset, inattention, altered level of consciousness, and global cognitive impairment" as key features of delirium (p. 886).

**A. Gradual memory decline over months to years.** Wrong, a months-to-years trajectory describes chronic impairment rather than the abrupt change characteristic of delirium (p. 886).
**B. Longstanding language difficulty progressing over months.** Wrong, slowly progressive longstanding difficulty does not supply the acute change central to this distinction (p. 886).
**C. Abrupt worsening of attention and alertness from baseline.** Correct, abrupt deterioration in attention and alertness matches the source’s delirium features and can occur on top of dementia (p. 886).
**D. Stable executive difficulty with little change over the year.** Wrong, stable impairment does not account for a new acute alteration in mental status (p. 886).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 886.

q: An 81-year-old nursing-home resident with moderate dementia is found on the floor and cannot explain what happened. She has osteoporosis, hypertension, and anxiety and takes weekly alendronate, lisinopril 5 mg, and sertraline 50 mg. Her right leg is shortened and externally rotated, and imaging confirms a hip fracture. Hemoglobin is 10.2 and creatinine 1.3. Her son asks how dementia affects the choice of surgery. Which explanation follows Hazzard?
o: Bed rest supports walking recovery; moderate dementia favors avoiding surgical repair
Conservative care improves alignment; nursing-home residence favors choosing nonsurgical treatment
Surgery supports alignment and walking; assess prior function and goals
Dementia establishes operative risk; further assessment of comorbidities adds little
explanation:
**Hip-fracture surgery requires an individualized assessment.** Hazzard describes better alignment and likelihood of ambulation with surgery, while identifying selected situations in which nonsurgical care may be appropriate (p. 797). "The clearest benefit of surgery over the nonsurgical approach is that surgery results in better anatomic alignment and better likelihood of ambulation." (p. 797).

**A. Bed rest supports walking recovery; moderate dementia favors avoiding surgical repair.** Wrong, the source attributes the walking advantage to surgery, and does not make moderate dementia alone a reason to select bed rest (p. 797).
**B. Conservative care improves alignment; nursing-home residence favors choosing nonsurgical treatment.** Wrong, better alignment is a surgical benefit in the source; residence alone does not supply the individualized evaluation it requires (p. 797).
**C. Surgery supports alignment and walking; assess prior function and goals.** Correct, the source combines potential surgical benefits with assessment of prefracture function, cognition, comorbidities, and the patient’s goals (p. 797).
**D. Dementia establishes operative risk; further assessment of comorbidities adds little.** Wrong, the source requires a broader assessment rather than drawing a surgical conclusion from the dementia label alone (p. 797).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 797.

q: An older man with depression, social withdrawal, and weight loss says there is no point in going on. Before adjusting medication, which assessment does Hazzard recommend for every depressed older patient?
o: Assessment of auditory memory and new learning
Assessment of suicidal thoughts, intent, and plans
Assessment of walking speed and handgrip strength
Assessment of exercise tolerance and respiratory function
explanation:
**Suicide risk assessment** is required in depressed older patients. It includes thoughts, intent, plans, and access to lethal means (p. 1008). "All depressed older patients should be assessed for suicide risk." (p. 1008).

**A. Assessment of auditory memory and new learning.** Wrong, memory testing does not assess the suicidal thoughts, intent, plans, and access to means specified by the recommendation (p. 1008).
**B. Assessment of suicidal thoughts, intent, and plans.** Correct, this addresses the stated risk domain; assessment should also include access to lethal means (p. 1008).
**C. Assessment of walking speed and handgrip strength.** Wrong, physical performance assessment does not substitute for the recommended suicide-risk inquiry (p. 1008).
**D. Assessment of exercise tolerance and respiratory function.** Wrong, cardiorespiratory assessment does not address the suicide-risk questions required by the cited recommendation (p. 1008).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1008.

q: An 84-year-old woman with osteoarthritis becomes drowsy while taking oxycodone. The team is reducing it and considering nonopioid treatment. Oral NSAIDs are unsuitable; she has no liver disease and no described neuropathic pain. If treatment continues for a prolonged period, which acetaminophen plan is consistent with the osteoarthritis chapter of Hazzard?
o: Use 1 g every six hours and monitor liver toxicity during prolonged use
Use 1 g three times daily and defer liver monitoring during prolonged use
Use 1 g three times daily with benefit assessment and liver monitoring
Use 1 g every six hours and assess benefit while deferring liver monitoring
explanation:
**Acetaminophen requires both a dose limit and benefit assessment.** Hazzard describes small or absent average benefit, a possible role when NSAIDs are unsuitable, and a maximum daily dose of 3 g in this chapter (p. 787). "Regular monitoring for hepatotoxicity is recommended in those with prolonged use" (p. 787). Inference from the dosing arithmetic: 1 g three times daily totals 3 g, whereas 1 g every six hours totals 4 g.

**A. Use 1 g every six hours and monitor liver toxicity during prolonged use.** Wrong, this totals 4 g daily, above the chapter’s stated maximum; monitoring does not correct the excessive total (p. 787).
**B. Use 1 g three times daily and defer liver monitoring during prolonged use.** Wrong, the total is within the stated maximum, but deferring monitoring during prolonged use conflicts with the source recommendation (p. 787).
**C. Use 1 g three times daily with benefit assessment and liver monitoring.** Correct, this totals 3 g daily and includes monitoring during prolonged use while checking whether the drug is helpful (p. 787).
**D. Use 1 g every six hours and assess benefit while deferring liver monitoring.** Wrong, this exceeds the stated maximum and omits the monitoring recommended for prolonged use (p. 787).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 787.

q: An 84-year-old widower with vascular dementia (MoCA 19/30), hypertension, and stage 3a CKD (eGFR 52 mL/min) lives alone. His wife died six months ago and his daughter visits weekly. He has stopped bathing, wears the same clothes for days, has unpaid bills, and has only spoiled food in the refrigerator. Apart from poor hygiene, examination is unremarkable; BP is 142/88. He takes amlodipine 10 mg and donepezil 10 mg daily. Home-based primary care is being considered. Which description matches that model in Hazzard?
o: Primary care delivered in a hospital ward by an interdisciplinary team
Primary care delivered at home with interdisciplinary coordination and follow-up
Primary care delivered through occasional home visits without coordinated follow-up
Primary care delivered in an office with telephone contact replacing home visits
explanation:
**Home-based primary care** delivers primary care in the homes of older adults with severe and disabling chronic illness (p. 202). The described program combines an interdisciplinary team with periodic follow-up and on-call telephone coverage: "Periodic follow-up by members of the team is complemented by on-call telephone coverage." (p. 202). This explains the model being considered without assuming that a particular drug change or hospital admission has already been ruled out.

**A. Primary care delivered in a hospital ward by an interdisciplinary team.** Wrong, an inpatient ward is not the location of the home-based model described on this page (p. 202).
**B. Primary care delivered at home with interdisciplinary coordination and follow-up.** Correct, home delivery, interdisciplinary coordination, and continued follow-up are the defining elements described (p. 202).
**C. Primary care delivered through occasional home visits without coordinated follow-up.** Wrong, the model includes periodic team follow-up and care coordination, rather than disconnected home visits (p. 202).
**D. Primary care delivered in an office with telephone contact replacing home visits.** Wrong, telephone coverage complements home care; it does not replace primary care in the home (p. 202).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 202.
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
chapterTitle: COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE

q: A 79-year-old woman is being assessed for home palliative care after three admissions in four months for heart-failure exacerbations. She has ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF 25%), stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m²), and mild cognitive impairment. She takes furosemide 80 mg twice daily, carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 5 mg daily, and spironolactone 12.5 mg daily. She lives with her daughter, who works full time. The patient says she wants “no more hospitals,” but her daughter insists on calling emergency services whenever she becomes breathless. What should be done next to address their differing care expectations?
o: Set a DNR order and stop heart-failure drugs before clarifying goals
Arrange a family meeting to clarify goals and treatment preferences
Arrange hospice enrollment before discussing the patient’s preferences
Increase the diuretic dose as the response to the disagreement
explanation:
**Goals-of-care communication** connects a treatment plan with what matters to the patient. Hazzard recommends inviting family members to key conversations so that “they too can understand the patient’s preferences” (p. 1093). Caregiver participation supplements direct communication with the patient; it should not replace it, including when cognitive impairment is present (p. 1093).

**A. Set a DNR order and stop heart-failure drugs before clarifying goals.** Wrong, a treatment-limitation order and medication withdrawal do not clarify the patient’s goals or the daughter’s understanding before a plan is made (pp. 1090–1093).
**B. Arrange a family meeting to clarify goals and treatment preferences.** Correct, a shared discussion makes room for the patient’s preferences and helps the daughter understand them before translating them into a care plan (pp. 1090, 1093).
**C. Arrange hospice enrollment before discussing the patient’s preferences.** Wrong, hospice is a major care decision; the source notes that patients and families may need discussion before making such changes (p. 1091).
**D. Increase the diuretic dose as the response to the disagreement.** Wrong, a diuretic change does not resolve the stated communication problem or determine how the patient’s preferences should guide the care plan (pp. 1091, 1093).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1093, 1090, 1091.

q: A transition to a different care setting is being planned for a person with dementia. Which feature should be preserved to reduce difficulty adapting to change?
o: Frequent changes in surroundings to encourage flexibility.
Frequent changes in caregivers to encourage flexibility.
Consistency in the care team and the environment.
Reduced contact with familiar caregivers and surroundings.
explanation:
People with dementia have difficulty adapting to stressors and change (p. 259). **Consistency** matters because they "generally benefit from consistency in caregiver teams and environment" (p. 259). Major environmental changes may increase behavioral symptoms, making transitions particularly burdensome (p. 259).

**A. Frequent changes in surroundings to encourage flexibility.** Wrong, environmental changes are associated with difficulty adapting and increased behavioral symptoms (p. 259).
**B. Frequent changes in caregivers to encourage flexibility.** Wrong, frequent caregiver changes work against the consistency described as beneficial (p. 259).
**C. Consistency in the care team and the environment.** Correct, both environmental and caregiver consistency follow the approach described in the source (p. 259).
**D. Reduced contact with familiar caregivers and surroundings.** Wrong, reducing familiar contact removes the consistency in care teams and surroundings described as beneficial (p. 259).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 259.
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
chapterTitle: COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE

q: A 76-year-old woman with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment has recurrent hypoglycemia while taking metformin, glipizide, and insulin according to glucose readings. The acute episode has been treated. Her eGFR is stable at 38 mL/min/1.73 m2, without acute illness or impaired perfusion. What should be the focus of medication adjustment to prevent recurrence?
o: Stop metformin while maintaining glipizide and insulin doses
Reduce glipizide and insulin according to glucose readings
Increase glipizide while maintaining the insulin regimen
Increase insulin doses while maintaining the glipizide dose
explanation:
**Insulin and sulfonylureas** identify patients at risk for hypoglycemia, whereas metformin rarely causes it when used alone. The source recommends regimens designed to minimize hypoglycemia and dose reduction when treatment is excessive; applied here, the change should focus on the hypoglycemia-associated drugs (pp. 315, 1574, 1576).
"outpatient diabetes regimens be designed specifically to minimize hypoglycemia." (p. 1574).
"individuals at risk for hypoglycemia (ie, being treated with insulin or a sulfonylurea drug)." (p. 1574).

**A. Stop metformin while maintaining glipizide and insulin doses.** Wrong, This leaves the insulin and sulfonylurea exposure unchanged. Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia alone, and the supplied renal function is above the source's contraindication threshold, although renal monitoring remains appropriate (pp. 1574, 1576).
**B. Reduce glipizide and insulin according to glucose readings.** Correct, Reducing the hypoglycemia-associated agents applies the source's dose-reduction principle; glucose readings guide assessment of the response (pp. 315, 1574).
**C. Increase glipizide while maintaining the insulin regimen.** Wrong, Increasing sulfonylurea exposure intensifies a regimen already producing hypoglycemia, contrary to the stated prevention goal (pp. 315, 1574).
**D. Increase insulin doses while maintaining the glipizide dose.** Wrong, Increasing insulin similarly intensifies treatment despite recurrent hypoglycemia rather than minimizing it (pp. 315, 1574).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1574, 1576, 315.

q: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes oxybutynin for overactive bladder. Which pair of effects fits its antimuscarinic action and warrants medication review?
o: Increased salivation and more frequent bowel movements.
Increased salivation and less frequent bowel movements.
Dry mouth and less frequent bowel movements.
Dry mouth and more frequent bowel movements.
explanation:
**Antimuscarinic adverse effects** extend beyond the bladder (p. 713). Hazzard describes “bothersome systemic anticholinergic side effects such as dry mouth and constipation” (p. 713). The combination of oral dryness and reduced bowel frequency therefore matches the source-described adverse-effect pattern.

**A. Increased salivation and more frequent bowel movements.** Wrong, The source describes dry mouth and constipation, so both increased salivation and increased bowel frequency oppose the stated pattern (p. 713).
**B. Increased salivation and less frequent bowel movements.** Wrong, Reduced bowel frequency fits constipation, but increased salivation does not fit the source's dry-mouth effect (p. 713).
**C. Dry mouth and less frequent bowel movements.** Correct, Both dry mouth and reduced bowel frequency match the anticholinergic effects listed in the source (p. 713).
**D. Dry mouth and more frequent bowel movements.** Wrong, Dry mouth fits, but more frequent bowel movements do not match the constipation described with these drugs (p. 713).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 713.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: A 77-year-old woman with COPD is returning home after rehabilitation. She transfers and walks short distances on level ground independently but cannot climb stairs safely. Her bedroom and bathroom are upstairs; no daytime caregiver or stair lift is available. A bedroom, toilet, and accessible washing area can be arranged downstairs. Which plan matches her current abilities?
o: Place the bedroom upstairs and the toilet downstairs
Place both the bedroom and the toilet downstairs
Place the bedroom downstairs and the toilet upstairs
Keep the bedroom upstairs with evening help on stairs
explanation:
**Home discharge planning** must match mobility, daily activities, and available support. Hazzard describes arranging ground-floor living when a patient can transfer and walk short distances safely but cannot independently manage the stairs; applying that principle here favors accessible facilities on one floor (p. 798; clinical application).
"the patient would need to be able to negotiate a full flight of stairs independently and safely;" (p. 798).
"the patient would need to rearrange the home to live on the ground floor and be able to transfer and ambulate short distances on a level surface independently and safely;" (p. 798).

**A. Place the bedroom upstairs and the toilet downstairs.** Wrong, This still requires stair use between essential activities, which is incompatible with the stated inability and lack of daytime help (p. 798; application).
**B. Place both the bedroom and the toilet downstairs.** Correct, Ground-floor living uses the preserved transfer and level-walking abilities without requiring unsupported stair use (p. 798; application).
**C. Place the bedroom downstairs and the toilet upstairs.** Wrong, An upstairs toilet still requires the stair ability that the patient lacks (p. 798; application).
**D. Keep the bedroom upstairs with evening help on stairs.** Wrong, Evening help does not provide access to essential facilities when assistance is unavailable during the day (p. 798; application).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 798.
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
chapterTitle: COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE

q: An older patient with renal impairment who is receiving morphine develops myoclonus and increased sensitivity to pain. Which mechanism does Hazzard describe as a concern?
o: Increased metabolite clearance with reduced neurologic effects
Accumulation of a morphine metabolite with neurotoxicity
Accelerated morphine breakdown with a lower metabolite concentration
Increased metabolite excretion with improved cognitive functioning
explanation:
**Morphine metabolite accumulation** is a concern in renal insufficiency. The source associates accumulation of morphine-3-glucuronide with neurotoxicity, including hyperalgesia, allodynia, and myoclonus (p. 1074). "Morphine-3-glucoronide builds up in renal insufficiency, common in older adults and is responsible for symptoms of neurotoxicity (eg, hyperalgesia, allodynia, myoclonus)." (p. 1074).

**A. Increased metabolite clearance with reduced neurologic effects.** Wrong, the described renal-insufficiency problem is metabolite buildup rather than increased clearance (p. 1074).
**B. Accumulation of a morphine metabolite with neurotoxicity.** Correct, metabolite buildup and the listed neurotoxic symptoms fit the concern raised by this presentation (p. 1074).
**C. Accelerated morphine breakdown with a lower metabolite concentration.** Wrong, the text describes accumulation, not a reduction in metabolite concentration due to accelerated breakdown (p. 1074).
**D. Increased metabolite excretion with improved cognitive functioning.** Wrong, increased excretion and improved cognition do not describe the accumulation and neurotoxicity reported here (p. 1074).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1074.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: A 92-year-old woman with frailty has unintentional weight loss of 15 lb, exhaustion, grip strength of 14 kg, slow walking, and low activity. She lives alone, uses a walker, and has mild cognitive impairment. After hospitalization for a urinary tract infection she declines facility-based rehabilitation; her daughter visits daily but works full-time. Her creatinine clearance is 42 mL/min. Which home exercise component targets the loss of muscle strength described in Hazzard?
o: Aerobic walking sessions as the strength-restoration programme
Progressive resistance exercises guided initially by a physical therapist
Stretching sessions as the strength-restoration programme
General advice to stay active as the strength-restoration programme
explanation:
**Resistance exercise** improves skeletal muscle function and mass, including in patients with sarcopenia (p. 737). Expert guidance helps teach correct technique and avoid injury. "Including resistance exercise is key to improve muscle function." (p. 737).

**A. Aerobic walking sessions as the strength-restoration programme.** Wrong, the source distinguishes ordinary cardiovascular exercise from the resistance component required to improve muscle function in sarcopenia (p. 737).
**B. Progressive resistance exercises guided initially by a physical therapist.** Correct, resistance exercise targets strength, with initial advice and supervision from an exercise or physical therapist (p. 737).
**C. Stretching sessions as the strength-restoration programme.** Wrong, stretching can accompany a multifaceted programme, but it does not replace the resistance component identified as key (p. 737).
**D. General advice to stay active as the strength-restoration programme.** Wrong, the source says general activity advice should not replace a formal exercise programme (p. 737).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 737.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes takes insulin glargine. Recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia is documented, and HbA1c is below his individualized target. After treating the acute episodes, what direction of treatment adjustment is appropriate?
o: Reduce treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response
Increase treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response
Maintain treatment intensity and target a lower HbA1c
Add an insulin secretagogue and monitor the glucose response
explanation:
**Overly tight glycemic control** increases hypoglycemia in older adults. Applying the source's dose-reduction principle to recurrent hypoglycemia with HbA1c below the individualized target supports reducing treatment intensity; glucose monitoring assesses the response and detects further hypoglycemia (pp. 315, 1574).
"Tight glycemic control has been consistently shown to produce higher rates of hypoglycemia in older adults." (p. 315).
"In some cases, there will be a need to deprescribe drug therapy by reducing the dose or stopping the medication entirely." (p. 315).

**A. Reduce treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response.** Correct, This addresses the excessive treatment intensity indicated by the supplied hypoglycemia and below-target HbA1c (pp. 315, 1574).
**B. Increase treatment intensity and monitor the glucose response.** Wrong, Increasing intensity would pursue still tighter control despite the hypoglycemia associated with that approach (p. 315).
**C. Maintain treatment intensity and target a lower HbA1c.** Wrong, A lower HbA1c target fails to address the adverse effect already occurring with below-target control (p. 315).
**D. Add an insulin secretagogue and monitor the glucose response.** Wrong, Adding glucose-lowering treatment intensifies the regimen rather than applying the dose-reduction approach to the documented adverse effect (p. 315).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 315, 1574.

q: למטופלת עם דמנציה וקשיי בליעה נשקלת דרך הזנה. מהו העיקרון המומלץ בהחלטה על צורת מתן המזון והנוזלים?
o: בחירת דרך הזנה לפי אבחנת הדמנציה ודחיית הערכת הבליעה
החלטה רפואית אישית ובחינת אפשרות להאכלה דרך הפה
בחירת זונדה כפתרון המועדף להזנה ממושכת בקביעות
החלטה על צינור הזנה לפי נוחות הצוות בהגשת הארוחות
explanation:
בהמלצות הישראליות, **דרך ההזנה** נבחרת באופן אישי לפי מצבו וצרכיו של החולה. האכלה דרך הפה היא הדרך המועדפת ונבחנת בכל שלב, ובבעיות בליעה יש לקבל הערכה מתאימה (עמ׳ 5).
"בהתאם למצבו של החולה עם קיהיון, למקום שהותו, לצרכיו, ולהיבטים הרפואיים הקשורים בצורת מתן המזון והנוזלים" (עמ׳ 5).
"הדרך המועדפת למתן המזון והנוזלים היא דרך הפה." (עמ׳ 5).

**א. בחירת דרך הזנה לפי אבחנת הדמנציה ודחיית הערכת הבליעה.** שגויה, ההחלטה אמורה להתבסס על מצב החולה וצרכיו, ובבעיות בליעה נדרשת הערכה מתאימה, ולא על האבחנה לבדה (עמ׳ 5).
**ב. החלטה רפואית אישית ובחינת אפשרות להאכלה דרך הפה.** נכונה, הדבר משלב את ההחלטה האישית עם העדפת ההאכלה דרך הפה ובחינתה בכל שלב (עמ׳ 5).
**ג. בחירת זונדה כפתרון המועדף להזנה ממושכת בקביעות.** שגויה, המסמך מציין זונדה כפתרון זמני עד להחלטה אחרת, ולכן אין להציג אותה כפתרון מועדף קבוע (עמ׳ 4).
**ד. החלטה על צינור הזנה לפי נוחות הצוות בהגשת הארוחות.** שגויה, ההחלטה היא רפואית ומותאמת למצב ולצרכים של החולה, ולא נקבעת לפי נוחות הגשת הארוחות (עמ׳ 5).

מקור: המלצות למתן מזון ונוזלים לחולה עם קיהיון, עמ׳ 4, 5.
ref: Hazzard Ch 72 — ETHICAL ISSUES· Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss

q: בביקור בית אצל גבר בן 86 נמצאו היעדר מזון ותנאי היגיינה ירודים, והוא מתקשה לדאוג לבריאותו. הוא הובא למוסד רפואי, ובבדיקה הראשונית עלה חשד להזנחה. מי מהצוות צריך להיות מוזמן מיד לצד הרופא לפי הנוהל?
o: נציג מחלקת הגבייה לצורך בדיקת הזכאות למימון
יועץ משפטי לצורך פתיחת הליך מינוי אפוטרופוס
עובד סוציאלי לבירור נסיבות והערכת סיכון
מנהל תפעול לצורך תכנון השמה במוסד חלופי
explanation:
**בירור חשד להזנחה** כולל הערכה רפואית וסוציאלית. העובד הסוציאלי משוחח עם המטופל והמלווים, מתעד ומעריך סיכון להמשך ההתעמרות. המינוי המשפטי או ההשמה אינם מחליפים את שלב הבירור הזה (עמ׳ 6).
"בכל מקרה בו קיים חשד להתעמרות יוזמן מיד רופא לבדיקת הנפגע." (עמ׳ 6).
"בכל מקרה שלגביו קיים חשד להתעמרות יוזמן מיד עובד סוציאלי." (עמ׳ 6).

**א. נציג מחלקת הגבייה לצורך בדיקת הזכאות למימון.** שגויה, בדיקת מימון אינה התפקיד הנדרש בשלב בירור החשד (עמ׳ 6).
**ב. יועץ משפטי לצורך פתיחת הליך מינוי אפוטרופוס.** שגויה, הליך משפטי אינו תחליף להזמנת העובד הסוציאלי המיידית (עמ׳ 6).
**ג. עובד סוציאלי לבירור נסיבות והערכת סיכון.** נכונה, זהו איש המקצוע שהנוהל מורה להזמין מיד ולשלב בבירור (עמ׳ 6).
**ד. מנהל תפעול לצורך תכנון השמה במוסד חלופי.** שגויה, תכנון השמה אינו מחליף בירור נסיבות וסיכון בידי עובד סוציאלי (עמ׳ 6).

מקור: משרד הבריאות, נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, עמ׳ 6.

sourceChecked.source: משרד הבריאות, נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות

q: A woman hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure has a reduced response to an oral diuretic. Which mechanism explains a possible advantage of intravenous administration according to Hazzard?
o: Increased drug absorption through an edematous bowel wall
Increased drug clearance caused by an edematous bowel wall
Reduced drug absorption through an edematous bowel wall
Reduced drug clearance caused by an edematous bowel wall
explanation:
**Bowel wall edema** can decrease oral diuretic absorption in acute heart failure. Intravenous administration avoids this absorption step and may therefore produce more effective diuresis (p. 1182; application of the stated mechanism). The source attributes this in part to "bowel wall edema, which may decrease the drug’s absorption." (p. 1182).

**A. Increased drug absorption through an edematous bowel wall.** Wrong, increased absorption would not explain the stated advantage; the source identifies decreased absorption through edematous bowel (p. 1182).
**B. Increased drug clearance caused by an edematous bowel wall.** Wrong, clearance is not the bowel-related mechanism described; the source identifies impaired absorption (p. 1182).
**C. Reduced drug absorption through an edematous bowel wall.** Correct, decreased absorption is the mechanism explicitly given for a possible intravenous advantage during an acute episode (p. 1182).
**D. Reduced drug clearance caused by an edematous bowel wall.** Wrong, decreased clearance is not the explanation given for bypassing oral administration; the described problem is absorption (p. 1182).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1182.

q: A person with dementia leaves home, becomes lost, and cannot summon help. Which direct safety intervention is described in Hazzard?
o: A plan to change the timing of cognitive medication
Round-the-clock supervision and an emergency plan
A plan to increase daytime sleep and reduce activity
More independent trips in the neighborhood for practice
explanation:
**Wandering with impaired emergency response** requires a direct safety plan. Hazzard lists continuous supervision and an emergency plan, alongside identification and safe-return measures (p. 926).
"Provide 24-hour supervision for the patient" (p. 926).
"Develop an emergency plan. Inform neighbors, fire department, and police of the patient’s condition" (p. 926).

**A. A plan to change the timing of cognitive medication.** Wrong, Changing medication timing does not provide the supervision or emergency response specified for this hazard (p. 926).
**B. Round-the-clock supervision and an emergency plan.** Correct, The supervision and emergency plan directly implement the measures listed for wandering and inability to respond to emergencies (p. 926).
**C. A plan to increase daytime sleep and reduce activity.** Wrong, The table advises limiting daytime napping and providing structured activity; increased sleep and reduced activity do not implement its safety measures (p. 926).
**D. More independent trips in the neighborhood for practice.** Wrong, Independent outings without supervision conflict with the stated need for continuous supervision in this situation (p. 926).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 926.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and recently diagnosed mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 22/30) receives home-based primary care. Her daughter found her unconscious twice in the past month, both times early in the morning before breakfast. She takes glimepiride 4 mg twice daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily. Her latest HbA1c is 6.8%, creatinine clearance is 58 mL/min, and prebreakfast fingerstick glucose readings range from 68 to 95 mg/dL. Which approach to the sulfonylurea agrees with Hazzard when hypoglycemia is a concern?
o: Stop glimepiride and follow glucose to reassess treatment needs.
Continue glimepiride at a reduced dose to retain sulfonylurea treatment.
Replace glimepiride with glipizide to retain treatment from the same class.
Replace glimepiride with glyburide to retain treatment from the same class.
explanation:
**Sulfonylureas** increase insulin secretion, and hypoglycemia is their main adverse effect. Hazzard advises avoiding this class when there is concern about hypoglycemia, even though individual agents differ in risk; the low readings and episodes in this vignette make that concern relevant without proving the cause of the unconsciousness (p. 1579).
"Their primary mechanism of action is to enhance insulin secretion by the β-cells of the endocrine pancreas." (p. 1579).

**A. Stop glimepiride and follow glucose to reassess treatment needs.** Correct, discontinuation follows the source advice to avoid sulfonylureas when hypoglycemia is a concern; glucose follow-up allows reassessment after removing the drug (p. 1579; clinical application).
**B. Continue glimepiride at a reduced dose to retain sulfonylurea treatment.** Wrong, a reduced dose still retains a sulfonylurea, whereas the source advises avoiding the class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**C. Replace glimepiride with glipizide to retain treatment from the same class.** Wrong, glipizide may be safer than other agents, but the same paragraph advises avoiding the whole class when hypoglycemia is a concern (p. 1579).
**D. Replace glimepiride with glyburide to retain treatment from the same class.** Wrong, glyburide is not recommended in older patients because its long half-life is associated with greater hypoglycemia risk (p. 1579).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1579.

q: An 89-year-old man with advanced Parkinson disease develops rigidity and fever after running out of carbidopa-levodopa and stopping it abruptly. Which medication change is the recognized trigger of a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome described by Hazzard?
o: Gradually adding an extra levodopa dose during the day
Moving a regular levodopa dose to a nearby time
Abruptly stopping the regular levodopa doses during the day
Dividing regular levodopa doses into smaller doses that day
explanation:
**Abrupt levodopa withdrawal** is the trigger identified in this passage. When temporary withdrawal is needed for severe psychosis, Hazzard advises stepwise withdrawal to avoid "the neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome that could occur with sudden withdrawal of levodopa" (p. 946). The medication interruption in the stem matches that warning.

**A. Gradually adding an extra levodopa dose during the day.** Wrong, the described trigger is withdrawal of established levodopa, whereas this option adds treatment. It does not describe the interruption in the stem (p. 946).
**B. Moving a regular levodopa dose to a nearby time.** Wrong, moving a dose to a nearby time describes continued dosing rather than the sudden cessation named in the source and stem (p. 946).
**C. Abruptly stopping the regular levodopa doses during the day.** Correct, the source explicitly links sudden levodopa withdrawal to the malignant-like syndrome; running out and abruptly stopping treatment is that change (p. 946).
**D. Dividing regular levodopa doses into smaller doses that day.** Wrong, splitting doses while continuing the medication does not describe sudden withdrawal. The cited warning concerns stopping levodopa, not the continued dosing described here (p. 946).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 946.
ref: Hazzard Ch 61 — PARKINSON DISEASE AND RELATED DISORDERS · Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: A 78-year-old man with mild dementia is undergoing rehabilitation after hip fracture surgery. He develops an abrupt change in attention, reduced food intake, and blood pressure lower than usual. What is the appropriate diagnostic approach?
o: Treat the change as progression of dementia and adjust supportive care
Begin pharmacologic sedation and use the response to determine the diagnosis
Confirm delirium and assess acute contributors by history and examination
Change a single medication and use improvement to conclude the investigation
explanation:
**New delirium** can be the presenting sign of serious acute illness. Assessment should establish the change from baseline and systematically seek contributors, because several causes may coexist and treating one factor may not resolve the syndrome (pp. 881, 885).
"delirium is often the only sign of life-threatening illness, such as sepsis, pneumonia, or myocardial infarction in older persons." (p. 885).
"A thorough history and physical examination constitute the foundation of the medical evaluation of suspected delirium." (p. 885).

**A. Treat the change as progression of dementia and adjust supportive care.** Wrong, an abrupt change from baseline requires delirium assessment rather than an assumption of dementia progression (p. 885).
**B. Begin pharmacologic sedation and use the response to determine the diagnosis.** Wrong, the diagnosis rests on cognitive assessment, observation, and history rather than response to sedation (p. 885).
**C. Confirm delirium and assess acute contributors by history and examination.** Correct, this follows the source's sequence of establishing delirium and evaluating potential acute causes (p. 885).
**D. Change a single medication and use improvement to conclude the investigation.** Wrong, removal of one factor often fails because delirium is commonly multifactorial; it does not replace a full assessment (p. 881).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 885, 881.

q: An 84-year-old woman with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 6), COPD requiring home oxygen, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22) lives alone, uses a walker, and receives help from her daughter with shopping and medication. She takes furosemide 40 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, and albuterol as needed. Potassium is 5.8, creatinine 2.8 (stable), and bicarbonate 18. She feels well apart from mild fatigue. Which change addresses Hazzard's contraindication to continuing mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist treatment?
o: Stop spironolactone given hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction.
Continue spironolactone while adding oral sodium bicarbonate.
Continue spironolactone while reducing the dose of furosemide.
Continue spironolactone while adding a potassium-binding agent.
explanation:
**Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists** are contraindicated in significant renal dysfunction or preexisting hyperkalemia (p. 1181). The source states, "These agents are contraindicated in patients with significant renal dysfunction (creatinine ≥ 2.5 mg/dL) or preexisting hyperkalemia" (p. 1181). The question asks which change removes that contraindicated exposure, rather than ranking a complete hyperkalemia treatment plan.

**A. Stop spironolactone given hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction.** Correct, this removes the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist exposure in the setting of the stated contraindications (p. 1181).
**B. Continue spironolactone while adding oral sodium bicarbonate.** Wrong, adding bicarbonate while continuing the drug does not implement the source's contraindication to that exposure (p. 1181).
**C. Continue spironolactone while reducing the dose of furosemide.** Wrong, reducing another diuretic leaves the contraindicated mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist exposure in place (p. 1181).
**D. Continue spironolactone while adding a potassium-binding agent.** Wrong, adding another potassium treatment leaves the contraindicated exposure in place; it is not the withdrawal asked for (p. 1181).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1181.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 79-year-old man returns home after hospitalization and takes multiple medications. His wife plans to fill a weekly pill organizer. Which medication-reconciliation step helps identify errors during the transition home?
o: Compare the home medication list with discharge orders and resolve discrepancies
Compare the inpatient medication orders with admission orders and resolve discrepancies
Compare the recorded drug-allergy list with discharge orders and resolve discrepancies
Compare the current laboratory results with discharge orders and resolve discrepancies
explanation:
**Medication reconciliation** compares the current medication list with newly ordered medications. It is intended to identify and resolve omissions, additions, duplications, and dosing or frequency errors during transitions of care (p. 257). "Compare the medications on the two lists." (Table 18-6, p. 257).

**A. Compare the home medication list with discharge orders and resolve discrepancies.** Correct, this compares the home regimen with the regimen prescribed for the transition and addresses discrepancies (p. 257).
**B. Compare the inpatient medication orders with admission orders and resolve discrepancies.** Wrong, this concerns the admission regimen and does not compare the home regimen with discharge orders relevant to this transition (p. 257).
**C. Compare the recorded drug-allergy list with discharge orders and resolve discrepancies.** Wrong, an allergy history is useful, but it does not supply the current medication list needed to identify omissions or duplications (p. 257).
**D. Compare the current laboratory results with discharge orders and resolve discrepancies.** Wrong, laboratory results do not supply the current medication list needed for this reconciliation (p. 257).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 257.
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
chapterTitle: COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE

q: An 81-year-old woman in assisted living is assessed because her care needs have increased. She has moderate Alzheimer disease, osteoporosis with a recent vertebral fracture, and urinary incontinence. Her caregiver reports new dependence in bathing and dressing, previously performed independently, and two falls this month. Her medicines are donepezil 10 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, and acetaminophen as needed. Which response to oxybutynin matches Beers 2023?
o: Continue oxybutynin because its adverse effects are confined to the urinary tract
Review oxybutynin for discontinuation because of adverse cognitive effects
Increase oxybutynin because stronger anticholinergic activity protects cognitive function
Switch bladder antimuscarinics because the cognitive warning does not extend across the class
explanation:
**Bladder antimuscarinics** have potential anticholinergic effects, and oxybutynin has the best evidence for adverse cognitive effects in this group. Beers recommends avoiding anticholinergics in dementia or cognitive impairment because of adverse CNS effects (pp. 2066, 2074).
"Oxybutynin has the best evidence for adverse cognitive effects." (p. 2074).
"However, caution is warranted for all bladder antimuscarinics given their potential anticholinergic effects." (p. 2074).

**A. Continue oxybutynin because its adverse effects are confined to the urinary tract.** Wrong, adverse cognitive effects show that the relevant harms extend beyond the urinary tract (p. 2074).
**B. Review oxybutynin for discontinuation because of adverse cognitive effects.** Correct, it applies the cognitive-impairment criterion to oxybutynin without promising reversal of all functional decline (pp. 2066, 2074).
**C. Increase oxybutynin because stronger anticholinergic activity protects cognitive function.** Wrong, anticholinergic activity is the cognitive concern in this criterion, not a protective effect (pp. 2066, 2074).
**D. Switch bladder antimuscarinics because the cognitive warning does not extend across the class.** Wrong, Beers urges caution for all bladder antimuscarinics; changing within the class does not justify dismissing the warning (p. 2074).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2066, 2074.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 77-year-old man with heart failure and multimorbidity has stabilized after hospitalization but continues to have symptoms and treatment burden. A palliative care consultation is being considered. Which description of its role matches Hazzard?
o: Improve quality of life and relieve symptoms alongside disease treatment
Replace disease treatment after determining that the illness is terminal
Defer symptom treatment until a decision is made to stop curative care
Shorten the remaining lifespan as the central purpose of supportive care
explanation:
**Palliative care** aims to improve quality of life and relieve the symptoms, pain and stress of serious illness. It is appropriate at any stage and can accompany curative treatment; it therefore need not wait for a terminal-stage decision (p. 1045).
"Palliative care aims to improve the quality of life for both the patient with serious illness and the family." (p. 1045).
"It is appropriate for any type of diagnosis, any stage of a serious illness, and importantly, can be provided together with curative treatment." (p. 1045).

**A. Improve quality of life and relieve symptoms alongside disease treatment.** Correct, this combines the stated aims of symptom relief and quality of life with the ability to continue disease-directed treatment (p. 1045).
**B. Replace disease treatment after determining that the illness is terminal.** Wrong, the source allows palliative care at any stage together with curative treatment, rather than defining it as replacement after a terminal diagnosis (p. 1045).
**C. Defer symptom treatment until a decision is made to stop curative care.** Wrong, symptom relief is a core purpose and is compatible with continued curative treatment (p. 1045).
**D. Shorten the remaining lifespan as the central purpose of supportive care.** Wrong, the described purpose is quality of life and relief of suffering; even hospice is stated not to aim at shortening or prolonging life (p. 1045).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1045.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: חולה הנוטה למות שהיא בעלת כשרות מסרבת להארכת חייה, ומוצע לה טיפול שגרתי בזיהום נלווה. מהי הגישה לפי סעיף 15 לחוק?
o: להסיק שסירוב להארכת חיים מחייב מניעת כל טיפול
לכבד רצון ולעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע לקבל טיפול
להתחיל טיפול בזיהום בהתעלם מהסירוב שהביעה
להעביר לבני המשפחה את ההחלטה במקום החולה
explanation:
החוק מבחין בין **כיבוד רצון החולה** לבין החובה לעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע לקבל טיפולים נלווים ומקלים. אין לתרגם הגבלת טיפול להארכת חיים למניעה גורפת של טיפול, וגם אין בכך היתר להתעלם מסירוב של חולה בעלת כשרות (עמ׳ 10, סעיף 15).
"חולה הנוטה למות שהוא בעל כשרות, אשר אינו רוצה שחייו יוארכו, יש לכבד את רצונו ולהימנע מטיפול רפואי בו." (עמ׳ 10).
"על המטפלים בחולה הנוטה למות כאמור בסעיף קטן (א) לעשות מאמץ סביר כדי לשכנעו לקבל חמצן," (עמ׳ 10).

**א. להסיק שסירוב להארכת חיים מחייב מניעת כל טיפול.** שגויה, הסעיף מחייב מאמץ לשכנע לקבל טיפול נלווה ומקל, ולכן אינו מורה על מניעה גורפת (עמ׳ 10).
**ב. לכבד רצון ולעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע לקבל טיפול.** נכונה, שני חלקי התשובה משקפים את החובות המשלימות בסעיף (עמ׳ 10).
**ג. להתחיל טיפול בזיהום בהתעלם מהסירוב שהביעה.** שגויה, הוראת השכנוע אינה מבטלת את החובה לכבד את רצונה (עמ׳ 10).
**ד. להעביר לבני המשפחה את ההחלטה במקום החולה.** שגויה, במקרה של חולה בעלת כשרות ההוראה היא לכבד את רצון החולה עצמה (עמ׳ 10).

מקור: חוק החולה הנוטה למות, תשס_ו-2005.pdf, עמ׳ 10.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: A 73-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment takes diphenhydramine nightly for sleep and reports feeling foggy the next day. Which approach to the drug is supported by Hazzard?
o: Increase the dose to overcome tolerance to its sedating effect
Avoid the drug as a primary treatment for insomnia
Continue the drug to improve cognition on the following day
Give the drug earlier in the evening to prevent next-day effects
explanation:
**Diphenhydramine** has a long half-life that may cause next-day sedation, and its adverse effects include delirium and decreased cognition (p. 661). "For these reasons, diphenhydramine should not be used as a primary treatment for insomnia in older patients." (p. 661). Tolerance to sedation does not remove these reasons to avoid it as primary insomnia treatment (p. 661; inference).

**A. Increase the dose to overcome tolerance to its sedating effect.** Wrong, rapid tolerance is described, but increasing the dose does not address the source's reasons for avoiding the drug as primary insomnia treatment (p. 661; application).
**B. Avoid the drug as a primary treatment for insomnia.** Correct, this follows the recommendation in a patient reporting a recognized next-day adverse effect (p. 661).
**C. Continue the drug to improve cognition on the following day.** Wrong, decreased cognition is an adverse effect described in the source, not a reason to continue treatment for cognitive benefit (p. 661).
**D. Give the drug earlier in the evening to prevent next-day effects.** Wrong, the long half-life may produce next-day sedation; an earlier dose does not establish that these effects will be prevented (p. 661; inference).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 661.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: An initial parenteral antibiotic dose is being selected for an older adult with a complicated urinary tract infection. Which statement about antibiotic selection agrees with Hazzard?
o: Oral beta-lactams are generally more effective than fluoroquinolones for complicated UTI
Aminoglycosides are generally avoided because available parenteral alternatives are less toxic
Nitrofurantoin is suitable for complicated UTI because its renal penetration is adequate
Fosfomycin is suitable for complicated UTI because its renal penetration is adequate
explanation:
**Aminoglycoside toxicity** is the reason Hazzard generally favors available parenteral alternatives for the initial dose. It states that aminoglycosides "are usually avoided because they are more toxic than other available parenteral antibiotics" (p. 1711). The same passage separately addresses reduced efficacy of oral beta-lactams and inadequate renal penetration of nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin in complicated UTI (p. 1711).

**A. Oral beta-lactams are generally more effective than fluoroquinolones for complicated UTI.** Wrong, oral beta-lactams are described as generally less effective than fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX for complicated UTI (p. 1711).
**B. Aminoglycosides are generally avoided because available parenteral alternatives are less toxic.** Correct, the source explicitly gives greater toxicity than available parenteral alternatives as the reason for usually avoiding aminoglycosides (p. 1711).
**C. Nitrofurantoin is suitable for complicated UTI because its renal penetration is adequate.** Wrong, the source advises against nitrofurantoin for complicated UTI because renal penetration is inadequate (p. 1711).
**D. Fosfomycin is suitable for complicated UTI because its renal penetration is adequate.** Wrong, the source gives inadequate renal penetration as the reason not to use fosfomycin for complicated UTI (p. 1711).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1711.
ref: Hazzard Ch 106 — URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS· Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: An 82-year-old woman starts gabapentin for neuropathic pain and develops somnolence, dizziness, and unsteadiness. Evaluation shows no orthostatic fall in blood pressure. Which recognized pair of effects fits these new symptoms?
o: Increased alertness and improved orientation
Central nervous system depression and improved orientation
Central nervous system depression and disorientation
Increased alertness and disorientation
explanation:
**Gabapentinoids** are used for neuropathic pain but have central nervous system adverse effects (p. 1064). The source lists "central nervous system depression, fatigue, dizziness, and disorientation"; the new symptoms fit that adverse-effect profile without proving drug causation (p. 1064).

**A. Increased alertness and improved orientation.** Wrong, increased alertness and improved orientation are inconsistent with the listed depression and disorientation (p. 1064).
**B. Central nervous system depression and improved orientation.** Wrong, central nervous system depression fits, but improved orientation does not match the listed disorientation (p. 1064).
**C. Central nervous system depression and disorientation.** Correct, both effects are included in the adverse-effect profile of gabapentin and related anticonvulsants (p. 1064).
**D. Increased alertness and disorientation.** Wrong, disorientation fits, but increased alertness conflicts with the listed central nervous system depression (p. 1064).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1064.

q: A 76-year-old man with HFpEF receives a diuretic for congestion. After excessive diuresis he develops fatigue, low blood pressure, and worsening prerenal azotemia. Which mechanism explains this risk?
o: Increased ventricular diastolic volume with increased congestion
Reduced ventricular diastolic volume with reduced cardiac output
Increased ventricular contractility with increased stroke volume
Prolonged ventricular filling time with increased cardiac output
explanation:
**Volume sensitivity in HFpEF** makes careful diuretic titration important (p. 1186). Hazzard describes "a reduction in left ventricular diastolic volume, with a resultant decline in stroke volume and cardiac output" after excessive diuresis, with fatigue, hypotension, and prerenal azotemia (p. 1186).

**A. Increased ventricular diastolic volume with increased congestion.** Wrong, the described consequence is reduced diastolic volume, not increased volume and congestion (p. 1186).
**B. Reduced ventricular diastolic volume with reduced cardiac output.** Correct, the reduction in filling volume and output matches the source’s mechanism and listed manifestations (p. 1186).
**C. Increased ventricular contractility with increased stroke volume.** Wrong, the source describes declining stroke volume, not an increase from enhanced contractility (p. 1186).
**D. Prolonged ventricular filling time with increased cardiac output.** Wrong, the cited mechanism is volume depletion with reduced output, not prolonged filling and greater output (p. 1186).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1186.

q: An 83-year-old woman develops hyponatremia after diuretic treatment. Evaluation confirms hypovolemic hyponatremia with volume depletion, no congestion, and no life-threatening neurological symptoms. Which treatment principle matches her volume status?
o: Restrict water and increase a loop diuretic to treat congestion.
Replace volume with isotonic saline and monitor serum sodium.
Give hypertonic saline to treat established SIADH.
Observe for spontaneous correction based on dilute urine.
explanation:
**Volume status** guides the treatment of hyponatremia because the associated fluid abnormality must also be treated (p. 587). For volume-depleted patients, the text states: “Hypovolemic individuals will respond to 0.9% saline with correction of the hyponatremia” (p. 587). Frequent sodium monitoring is required to avoid excessive correction.

**A. Restrict water and increase a loop diuretic to treat congestion.** Wrong, Water restriction with high-dose loop diuretics is described for hypervolemic patients, whereas this patient has volume depletion without congestion (p. 587).
**B. Replace volume with isotonic saline and monitor serum sodium.** Correct, Isotonic saline addresses the documented hypovolemia; monitoring checks that sodium correction is adequate without being excessive (p. 587).
**C. Give hypertonic saline to treat established SIADH.** Wrong, The stem establishes hypovolemia rather than SIADH; the source differentiates these states and specifies isotonic saline for hypovolemic patients (p. 587).
**D. Observe for spontaneous correction based on dilute urine.** Wrong, Spontaneous correction is described when dilute urine is already being excreted; the stem instead establishes a volume deficit requiring treatment (p. 587).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: A 77-year-old man is undergoing rehabilitation after a prolonged admission. He still needs help with transfers and daily activities. Which approach matches discharge planning within Hazzard’s rehabilitation framework?
o: Choose the discharge destination from muscle strength and walking ability
Choose the discharge destination from family availability and time at home
Choose the discharge destination from function, living environment, and support
Choose the discharge destination from the admission diagnosis and illness severity
explanation:
**Rehabilitation planning** integrates functional abilities with the environment and participation in everyday life. The ICF example addresses where a person will live and how to remain active in the community alongside strength and walking ability. (p. 819)
"addressing where she will live after discharge and how to keep her active in her community." (p. 819)
"Understanding the relationships between the different components and addressing them is the key to a successful rehabilitation." (p. 819)

**A. Choose the discharge destination from muscle strength and walking ability.** Wrong, strength and walking matter, but this leaves out living circumstances and participation that the framework also requires. (p. 819)
**B. Choose the discharge destination from family availability and time at home.** Wrong, family availability is an environmental consideration, but it does not encompass functional needs and the physical living environment. (p. 819)
**C. Choose the discharge destination from function, living environment, and support.** Correct, this incorporates function and the physical and social environment instead of using a single dimension of the framework. (p. 819)
**D. Choose the discharge destination from the admission diagnosis and illness severity.** Wrong, the framework extends beyond disease to how the person lives with disability, so diagnosis and severity do not complete discharge planning. (p. 819)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 819.
ref: Hazzard Ch 55 — REHABILITATION· Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss

q: An 86-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson disease, depression, and recurrent urinary tract infections attends follow-up. She lives in assisted living, uses a wheelchair, and has mild dysphagia. Her daughter reports worsening tremor and two falls this month. Medicines are carbidopa-levodopa 25/250 mg four times daily, pramipexole 1 mg three times daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and nitrofurantoin 100 mg daily for prophylaxis. Her creatinine clearance is 28 mL/min. Which statement about nitrofurantoin follows Beers 2023?
o: Continue nitrofurantoin because long-term suppression reduces the pulmonary and hepatic toxicity risks
Avoid nitrofurantoin because kidney function and long-term use meet avoidance criteria
Continue nitrofurantoin because the avoidance criteria are independent of the level of kidney function
Continue nitrofurantoin because the toxicity concerns primarily concern short courses rather than prolonged use
explanation:
**Nitrofurantoin** is recommended for avoidance when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min or when used for long-term suppression. Beers cites pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy, particularly with long-term use (p. 2057).
"Avoid in individuals with CrCl <30 mL/ min or for long-term suppression." (p. 2057).
"Potential for pulmonary toxicity, hepatoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy, especially with long-term use; safer alternatives available." (p. 2057).

**A. Continue nitrofurantoin because long-term suppression reduces the pulmonary and hepatic toxicity risks.** Wrong, long-term use is associated with particular toxicity concern and is itself a reason for avoidance (p. 2057).
**B. Avoid nitrofurantoin because kidney function and long-term use meet avoidance criteria.** Correct, her reported clearance is below the cited threshold and the prescription is for long-term suppression, meeting both conditions (p. 2057).
**C. Continue nitrofurantoin because the avoidance criteria are independent of the level of kidney function.** Wrong, creatinine clearance is explicitly included in the avoidance criterion (p. 2057).
**D. Continue nitrofurantoin because the toxicity concerns primarily concern short courses rather than prolonged use.** Wrong, Beers emphasizes toxicity especially with long-term use, not primarily with short courses (p. 2057).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2057.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: A man with Alzheimer disease taking donepezil reports poor sleep. Which pair of adverse effects is listed for donepezil in Hazzard and should be considered during medication review?
o: Insomnia and bradycardia
Insomnia and tachycardia
Excessive sleep and bradycardia
Excessive sleep and tachycardia
explanation:
**Medication review** should include the adverse effects listed for donepezil. The table includes insomnia and bradycardia or heart block; this supports considering the medication during assessment without establishing that it explains every behavioral symptom (p. 912).
"Bradycardia or heart block, syncope, nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, vomiting, muscle cramps, fatigue, anorexia" (p. 912).

**A. Insomnia and bradycardia.** Correct, Both insomnia and bradycardia are listed adverse effects, matching the sleep concern and a recognized cardiac effect (p. 912).
**B. Insomnia and tachycardia.** Wrong, Insomnia is listed, but the cardiac effect in the table is bradycardia or heart block rather than tachycardia (p. 912).
**C. Excessive sleep and bradycardia.** Wrong, Bradycardia is listed, but the sleep adverse effect in the table is insomnia rather than excessive sleep (p. 912).
**D. Excessive sleep and tachycardia.** Wrong, Neither the proposed sleep effect nor the proposed heart-rate direction matches the listed pair (p. 912).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 912.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: An 81-year-old woman with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction takes spironolactone. Repeated testing shows hyperkalemia and significant renal dysfunction, with creatinine 2.7 mg/dL. Which decision about mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists is supported by Hazzard?
o: Continue spironolactone at the current dose to preserve its heart-failure benefit
Stop spironolactone for the contraindication and monitor potassium and renal function
Substitute eplerenone to preserve treatment with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
Increase spironolactone to strengthen the diuretic effect of her treatment
explanation:
**Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists** are potassium-sparing, and their contraindications apply to spironolactone and eplerenone (p. 1181). "These agents are contraindicated in patients with significant renal dysfunction (creatinine ≥ 2.5 mg/dL) or preexisting hyperkalemia." The case meets these source-defined contraindications (p. 1181).

**A. Continue spironolactone at the current dose to preserve its heart-failure benefit.** Wrong, the patient meets the listed contraindications, so continuing for benefit conflicts with the source’s restriction (p. 1181).
**B. Stop spironolactone for the contraindication and monitor potassium and renal function.** Correct, stopping applies the contraindication; potassium and renal function are the safety variables the source directs clinicians to monitor (p. 1181).
**C. Substitute eplerenone to preserve treatment with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.** Wrong, eplerenone shares the class contraindications and does not avoid this potassium-sparing risk (p. 1181).
**D. Increase spironolactone to strengthen the diuretic effect of her treatment.** Wrong, increasing a potassium-sparing drug does not address the stated contraindication (p. 1181).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1181.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1181

q: גבר בן 84 עם mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 22/30), יתר לחץ דם, ו-CKD stage 3a (eGFR 45) משתחרר לאחר ניתוח לתיקון hip fracture. הוא גר לבד בבית דו-קומתי. לפני האשפוז היה עצמאי ב-ADLs אך נזקק לעזרה בניהול כספים ותרופות. לאחר הניתוח הוא זקוק לסיוע בהתרחצות ולבישה. בתו עובדת full-time ויכולה לבקר פעמיים בשבוע. Medicare Part A מכסה 20 יום ב-skilled nursing facility. איזו disposition בשחרור מאזנת בצורה הטובה ביותר בין צרכיו הפונקציונליים למשאבים הזמינים?
o: שחרור ישיר הביתה עם physical therapy פעמיים בשבוע
העברה ל-skilled nursing facility למשך 20 יום, ולאחר מכן הערכה מחדש
אשפוז קבוע בבית אבות בשל cognitive impairment
שחרור הביתה עם שירותי aide פרטי 24 שעות
explanation:
התשובה הנכונה היא העברה ל-skilled nursing facility (SNF) לצורך שיקום. למטופל זה יש גם cognitive impairment וגם deficits פונקציונליים חדשים המצריכים שיקום אינטנסיבי שלא ניתן לספק בבטחה בבית עם תמיכה משפחתית מוגבלת. Medicare מכסה עד 20 יום במלואם, מה שמאפשר זמן לשיפור פונקציונלי ותכנון טיפול.

אופציה A (שחרור הביתה עם PT) היא המלכודת — רבים מהרופאים משחררים מטופלים הביתה באופן רפלקסיבי, אך למטופל זה יש תלות חדשה ב-ADLs, cognitive impairment המשפיע על compliance לתרופות, והוא גר לבד בבית דו-קומתי (סיכון fall). זהו שחרור לא בטוח.

אופציה C (אשפוז קבוע) מוקדמת מדי — רבים מהקשישים מחלימים ומשיבים תפקוד משמעותי לאחר hip fracture עם שיקום מתאים. cognitive impairment לבדו אינו מחייב institutionalization.

אופציה D (aide פרטי 24 שעות) אינה ריאלית כלכלית עבור רוב המשפחות ואינה מכוסה על ידי Medicare. עלות aide פרטי היא $15–25 לשעה ($360–600 ליום).

Clinical Pearl: החלטות post-acute care חייבות לקחת בחשבון את התפקוד הפרה-מורבידי, הdeficits הנוכחיים, מצב קוגניטיבי, בטיחות הבית ותמיכה סוציאלית. שיקום ב-SNF לאחר hip fracture מפחית שיעורי readmission ב-40% בהשוואה לשחרור ישיר הביתה.
ref: Hazzard Ch 17 — COMMUNITY-BASED LONG-TERM SERVICES AND SUPPORT, AND HOME-BASED MEDICAL CARE
