o: Replacing functional assessment with a summary of the history and examination
Identifying functional and cognitive deficits to help guide treatment planning
Choosing treatment by age while reducing the assessment of comorbid disease
Replacing medication review with an assessment of the stage of the tumor
explanation:
**Comprehensive geriatric assessment** includes function, comorbidity, cognition, psychological state, support, nutrition and medication review (p. 1402). It "may help to uncover age-related deficits that are not routinely obtained in a history and physical examination" (p. 1402). These findings can guide interventions that improve the ability to undergo cancer treatment (p. 1402).

**A. Replacing functional assessment with a summary of the history and examination.** Wrong, the assessment adds information not routinely obtained in the history and examination; replacing functional assessment with that summary loses one of its stated domains (p. 1402).
**B. Identifying functional and cognitive deficits to help guide treatment planning.** Correct, function and cognition are assessed to uncover deficits, and the findings can guide interventions supporting the ability to undergo treatment (p. 1402).
**C. Choosing treatment by age while reducing the assessment of comorbid disease.** Wrong, the assessment explicitly includes comorbid conditions as well as function and cognition; reducing comorbidity assessment misses part of the information it is intended to provide (p. 1402).
**D. Replacing medication review with an assessment of the stage of the tumor.** Wrong, medication review is an explicit assessment component; tumor staging does not supply that review (p. 1402).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1402.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with advanced dementia and breast cancer metastatic to bone presents with two days of shouting, agitation, food refusal, and pulling at her clothes. She is nonverbal at baseline and grimaces during abdominal palpation. Temperature is 37.1 degrees C, heart rate 88, and blood pressure 142/78. She receives memantine 10 mg twice daily and acetaminophen 650 mg three times daily. Which approach best addresses the acute behavioral change?
o: Escalate analgesia and defer investigation of the abdominal findings
Start an antipsychotic and defer assessment of medical triggers
Evaluate medical contributors with examination and targeted testing
Increase scheduled acetaminophen and defer assessment of medical triggers
explanation:
**Acute behavioral change** requires evaluation for potentially treatable contributors, with symptom management and safety addressed in parallel. Hazzard emphasizes history, examination, and clinically directed testing, including attention to an acute abdominal process (p. 885).
"Identifying the potentially multifactorial contributors to the delirium is of paramount importance." (p. 885).

**A. Escalate analgesia and defer investigation of the abdominal findings.** Wrong, Pain warrants attention, but symptom treatment with deferred investigation would miss the recommended evaluation of potentially serious contributors (p. 885).
**B. Start an antipsychotic and defer assessment of medical triggers.** Wrong, Suppressing agitation does not replace assessment of the acute change and localizing abdominal finding (p. 885; application).
**C. Evaluate medical contributors with examination and targeted testing.** Correct, This follows the source's assessment strategy without presuming a specific abdominal diagnosis or a fixed test bundle (p. 885).
**D. Increase scheduled acetaminophen and defer assessment of medical triggers.** Wrong, Adjusting analgesia without evaluating the new symptoms and abdominal finding would leave possible medical contributors unassessed (p. 885).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 885.
ref: Hazzard Ch 58 — DELIRIUM· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: A patient with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia receives conservative-management advice. Which approach accords with Hazzard?
o: Maintain hydration and avoid thiazides
Restrict fluid intake and avoid thiazides
Maintain adequate fluid intake and add a thiazide
Restrict fluid intake and add a thiazide
explanation:
Conservative management aims to maintain **euvolemia** through adequate fluid and solute intake. Thiazides and immobilization should be avoided because they could exacerbate hypercalcemia (p. 1538).
"maintenance of euvolemia with adequate fluid and solute intake, avoidance of thiazides and immobilization that could exacerbate hypercalcemia" (p. 1538).

**A. Maintain hydration and avoid thiazides.** Correct, Both components match the source: maintain euvolemia and avoid a drug class that could worsen hypercalcemia (p. 1538).
**B. Restrict fluid intake and avoid thiazides.** Wrong, Avoiding thiazides is appropriate, but routine fluid restriction conflicts with adequate intake to maintain euvolemia (p. 1538).
**C. Maintain adequate fluid intake and add a thiazide.** Wrong, Adequate intake is appropriate, but adding a thiazide introduces a factor the source advises avoiding (p. 1538).
**D. Restrict fluid intake and add a thiazide.** Wrong, Both components conflict with maintaining euvolemia and avoiding thiazides that could exacerbate hypercalcemia (p. 1538).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1538.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 57 — Hypercalcemia and Hypocalcemia

q: An 85-year-old woman with severe cancer pain and renal impairment needs an opioid regimen adjusted. Which pharmacokinetic principle should guide dose selection and monitoring?
o: Reduced renal clearance limits accumulation and favors a high starting dose
Altered drug distribution shortens elimination and reduces monitoring needs
Reduced drug clearance increases accumulation and calls for cautious dosing
Reduced lean body mass lowers sensitivity and favors rapid dose escalation
explanation:
**Reduced clearance increases the risk of opioid accumulation.** Hazzard describes a narrow balance between safe dosing and respiratory depression or overdose in older adults with reduced clearance (p. 1060). It also links age-related distribution changes to a longer elimination time. The source notes that "older adults may be more susceptible to the accumulation of opioids" (p. 1060).

**A. Reduced renal clearance limits accumulation and favors a high starting dose.** Wrong, reduced clearance increases susceptibility to accumulation rather than limiting it (p. 1060).
**B. Altered drug distribution shortens elimination and reduces monitoring needs.** Wrong, the source describes a longer elimination time with these distribution changes (p. 1060).
**C. Reduced drug clearance increases accumulation and calls for cautious dosing.** Correct, cautious dosing addresses the accumulation and adverse-effect risks described by the source (p. 1060).
**D. Reduced lean body mass lowers sensitivity and favors rapid dose escalation.** Wrong, the source describes increased adverse-effect risk and lower starting doses rather than rapid escalation based on lower sensitivity (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1060.
ref: Hazzard Ch 68 — PAIN MANAGEMENT· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: אישה בת 73 עם סרטן שד בשלב מוקדם מסרבת לניתוח ואומרת: 'חייתי חיים טובים.' היא עצמאית בכל ה-ADLs, הולכת 2 מיילים ביום, ומתנדבת בכנסייה. התרופה היחידה שלה היא lisinopril 5mg. MMSE 30/30. בתה טוענת שהיא בדיכאון ודורשת הערכה פסיכיאטרית. איזה גישה היא המתאימה ביותר?
o: לכבד את החלטתה ולדון בטיפולים חלופיים
לקבל ייעוץ פסיכיאטרי להערכת כשירות
להתחיל escitalopram 5mg ביום ולהעריך מחדש בעוד 4 שבועות
לפנות לוועדת האתיקה
explanation:
**סירוב לטיפול** דורש שיחה על המידע וההעדפות, ולא ביטול אוטומטי של רצון המטופלת. יש להסביר את ההשלכות ואת החלופות ולוודא **הבנה ובחירה מרצון**; ציון קוגניטיבי לבדו אינו מחליף תהליך זה. ההעדפה לשיחה ישירה המכבדת את עמדתה, לפני ייחוס הסירוב לדיכאון או העברת ההכרעה לאחרים, היא הסקה מחובת ההסכמה מדעת (סעיף 13; עמ׳ PDF 8).
"לא יינתן טיפול רפואי למטופל אלא אם כן נתן לכך המטופל הסכמה מדעת לפי הוראות פרק זה." (חוק זכויות החולה, סעיפים 13 ו־14א, עמ׳ PDF 8 עד 9).

**א. לכבד את החלטתה ולדון בטיפולים חלופיים.** נכונה, זו פתיחת התהליך המתאימה: לברר את עמדתה, לוודא שהבינה את התועלת והסיכונים ולדון גם בחלופות או בהיעדר טיפול. כיבוד העמדה אינו ויתור על הסבר ועל בירור הבנה (סעיף 13; עמ׳ PDF 8).
**ב. לקבל ייעוץ פסיכיאטרי להערכת כשירות.** שגויה, אין בשאלה ממצא שמחייב להעביר אוטומטית את הערכת ההבנה לפסיכיאטר. יש להתחיל בתהליך הסכמה ישיר ומותאם; אם יתגלה קושי ניתן להרחיב בירור. זו הסקה מחובת מסירת המידע ובדיקת ההבנה (סעיפים 13 ו־14א; עמ׳ PDF 8 עד 9).
**ג. להתחיל escitalopram 5mg ביום ולהעריך מחדש בעוד 4 שבועות.** שגויה, הדרישה המשפחתית אינה קובעת אבחנת דיכאון ואינה מהווה הסכמה לטיפול תרופתי. יש לברר עם המטופלת את עמדתה ולקבל החלטה לאחר מידע מתאים, ולא להתנות את הדיון מראש בנטילת תרופה; זו הסקה מעקרון ההסכמה (סעיף 13; עמ׳ PDF 8).
**ד. לפנות לוועדת האתיקה.** שגויה, הפנייה לוועדה בשלב זה מדלגת על בירור רצון המטופלת והבנתה. אין בתיאור מחלוקת שכבר בוררה ומחייבת מסלול כזה; זו הסקה מן הקדימות לתהליך הסכמה ישיר (סעיף 13; עמ׳ PDF 8).

מקור: חוק זכויות החולה, סעיפים 13 ו־14א, עמ׳ PDF 8 עד 9.
ref: Hazzard Ch 72 — ETHICAL ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: An older adult taking an opioid has undergone clearance of a fecal impaction. Under Hazzard’s stepwise approach, what ongoing treatment helps prevent recurrence?
o: Stop the laxative regimen after clearance and wait for another obstruction
Continue a regular laxative regimen tailored to constipation and recurrence risk
Replace ongoing laxative treatment with a plan for elective bowel resection
Replace ongoing laxative treatment with a plan for deliberate fluid restriction
explanation:
**Post-disimpaction treatment** addresses recurrence risk rather than ending with clearance of the impaction. Hazzard directs: "When impaction resolves, give laxative regimen for chronic constipation in high-risk patients for long-term treatment to avoid recurrence" (Table 87-11, p. 1378).

**A. Stop the laxative regimen after clearance and wait for another obstruction.** Wrong, waiting for another obstruction omits the long-term laxative regimen specifically recommended to prevent recurrence (p. 1378).
**B. Continue a regular laxative regimen tailored to constipation and recurrence risk.** Correct, a regular regimen for high-risk chronic constipation is the stated continuation after the impaction resolves (p. 1378).
**C. Replace ongoing laxative treatment with a plan for elective bowel resection.** Wrong, surgery is reserved for a small proportion with medically refractory constipation; it does not replace the specified routine post-disimpaction regimen (p. 1378).
**D. Replace ongoing laxative treatment with a plan for deliberate fluid restriction.** Wrong, fluid restriction is not the recommended continuation; replacing laxatives with it omits the long-term regimen specified to avoid recurrence (p. 1378).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1378.
ref: Hazzard Ch 87 — CONSTIPATION· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: A woman with breast cancer and bone metastases asks why denosumab or a bisphosphonate has been proposed. What role does Hazzard describe for this treatment?
o: Inhibit osteoclasts and reduce the risk of skeletal-related events
Stimulate osteoblasts to accelerate the formation of new bone tissue
Block estrogen receptors to suppress the growth of the tumor
Block the HER2 receptor to inhibit division of tumor cells
explanation:
**Osteoclast inhibition** is the action Hazzard attributes to bisphosphonates or denosumab in women with bone metastases. The stated benefit is a reduction in **skeletal-related events**, linking the proposed treatment to the bone involvement in this stem (p. 1404).
"Osteoclast inhibition with bisphosphonates or denosumab significantly reduces the risk of skeletal-related events in women with bone metastases." (p. 1404).

**A. Inhibit osteoclasts and reduce the risk of skeletal-related events.** Correct, This states both the action and the clinical benefit reported for women with bone metastases (p. 1404).
**B. Stimulate osteoblasts to accelerate the formation of new bone tissue.** Wrong, The source attributes the benefit to osteoclast inhibition, rather than osteoblast stimulation to accelerate new bone formation (p. 1404).
**C. Block estrogen receptors to suppress the growth of the tumor.** Wrong, The proposed agents are described here as osteoclast inhibitors that reduce skeletal events, rather than as estrogen-receptor blockers (p. 1404).
**D. Block the HER2 receptor to inhibit division of tumor cells.** Wrong, The source assigns these agents an osteoclast-inhibiting role; HER2 receptor blockade does not describe the treatment proposed in the stem (p. 1404).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1404.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: An older patient has suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression. Naloxone is being considered during emergency treatment. What is its purpose?
o: Reverse the effects of the opioid overdose
Preserve opioid effects to prevent withdrawal symptoms
Reduce opioid craving as long-term maintenance treatment
Provide long-acting opioid substitution for pain treatment
explanation:
**Naloxone** can reverse potentially fatal opioid overdose. Hazzard distinguishes this emergency reversal role from treatment of opioid use disorder itself. (p. 326)
"Naloxone does not treat OUD, but it can reverse potentially fatal opioid overdoses" (p. 326)

**A. Reverse the effects of the opioid overdose.** Correct, this is the overdose-reversal role explicitly described in the source. (p. 326)
**B. Preserve opioid effects to prevent withdrawal symptoms.** Wrong, preserving the opioid effect conflicts with the stated purpose of reversing the overdose. (p. 326)
**C. Reduce opioid craving as long-term maintenance treatment.** Wrong, the source explicitly distinguishes naloxone from treatment of opioid use disorder, so maintenance craving treatment is not its role here. (p. 326)
**D. Provide long-acting opioid substitution for pain treatment.** Wrong, the source identifies reversal of opioid overdose, rather than substitution with a long-acting opioid, as its purpose. (p. 326)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 326.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: A 75-year-old woman completed adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer three months ago. She has increasing difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs and fell last week. Her BMI is 19, grip strength 14 kg, and gait speed 0.6 m/s. She takes anastrozole 1 mg daily and calcium/vitamin D. Which rehabilitation principle follows Hazzard's discussion of maintaining and restoring muscle mass and strength?
o: Combine progressive resistance training with adequate protein and energy intake
Increase energy intake while restricting activity to prevent further muscle atrophy
Provide an adequate diet while using bed rest to preserve existing muscle strength
Increase nutritional intake while postponing exercise until muscle repletion is complete
explanation:
**Nutrition and physical activity** both contribute to muscle maintenance and recovery. The source recommends addressing nutrient intake and exercise together and describes loss of muscle mass and function during inactivity even when the diet is adequate (p. 407).
"Efforts at repletion should focus on both increasing nutrient intake and exercise." (p. 407).
"Overfeeding does not prevent muscle atrophy associated with inactivity and may exacerbate the functional consequences since the excess nutrients are converted to fat." (p. 407).

**A. Combine progressive resistance training with adequate protein and energy intake.** Correct, this combines the two components the source identifies; evidence for the resistance-training/high-protein combination cited on this page comes from healthy older men, not this specific cancer scenario (p. 407).
**B. Increase energy intake while restricting activity to prevent further muscle atrophy.** Wrong, overfeeding does not prevent inactivity-related atrophy and can increase fat rather than restore function (p. 407).
**C. Provide an adequate diet while using bed rest to preserve existing muscle strength.** Wrong, adequate nutrition does not prevent muscle and functional loss during bed rest (p. 407).
**D. Increase nutritional intake while postponing exercise until muscle repletion is complete.** Wrong, the source recommends both nutrient repletion and exercise, rather than nutrition as a preparatory substitute for activity (p. 407).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 407.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: A 79-year-old man taking a diuretic presents after reduced intake. He has weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, and hyponatremia. Evaluation establishes hypovolemia without pulmonary congestion or edema. Which treatment addresses this mechanism?
o: Give isotonic sodium chloride with frequent sodium monitoring
Restrict water and increase loop diuresis with frequent sodium monitoring
Give a hypotonic solution to replace water with frequent sodium monitoring
Await spontaneous dilute urine excretion without correcting hypovolemia
explanation:
**Volume status** guides hyponatremia treatment. The source describes correction with isotonic saline in hypovolemic patients and requires frequent sodium monitoring to avoid excessive correction (p. 587).
"Hypovolemic individuals will respond to 0.9% saline with correction of the hyponatremia." (p. 587).
"Hypervolemic individuals such as those with heart failure will respond to a combination of high-dose loop diuretic and water restriction." (p. 587).

**A. Give isotonic sodium chloride with frequent sodium monitoring.** Correct, isotonic saline addresses the established hypovolemia, with monitoring to control the correction (p. 587).
**B. Restrict water and increase loop diuresis with frequent sodium monitoring.** Wrong, water restriction with loop diuresis is the approach described for hypervolemic patients, whereas this patient is hypovolemic (p. 587).
**C. Give a hypotonic solution to replace water with frequent sodium monitoring.** Wrong, the source specifies isotonic saline for this volume-depleted state, not hypotonic water replacement (p. 587).
**D. Await spontaneous dilute urine excretion without correcting hypovolemia.** Wrong, the self-correction pathway described applies to people already excreting dilute urine; it does not address the established volume deficit here (p. 587).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An 81-year-old woman treated for ER-positive/PR-positive breast cancer 5 years ago has new back pain and weight loss. MRI shows multiple vertebral metastases, and biopsy confirms recurrent breast cancer. She has mild cognitive impairment, lives in assisted living, and has a creatinine clearance of 42 mL/min. She declines further chemotherapy but is willing to discuss endocrine treatment. Her metastases are not rapidly progressive or life-threatening. Which approach accords with Hazzard?
o: Offer endocrine treatment with radiation assessment for painful bone lesions
Recommend cytotoxic chemotherapy as the initial systemic treatment for her recurrence
Treat her refusal of chemotherapy as a reason to forgo systemic palliation
Defer radiation consultation because the recurrent lesions involve bone
explanation:
**Endocrine treatment and local palliation** remain options when chemotherapy is declined. For disease that is not rapidly progressive or life-threatening, Hazzard states, "all women with hormone receptor–positive, metastatic breast cancer should have an initial trial of endocrine therapy"; symptomatic bone lesions also warrant consideration of palliative radiation (p. 1403).

**A. Offer endocrine treatment with radiation assessment for painful bone lesions.** Correct, Her receptor-positive disease and absence of rapid or life-threatening progression fit endocrine treatment; the painful bone lesions also fit consideration of local radiation (p. 1403).
**B. Recommend cytotoxic chemotherapy as the initial systemic treatment for her recurrence.** Wrong, The source places initial endocrine therapy in this setting; chemotherapy is described for endocrine-refractory, triple-negative, or rapidly progressive or life-threatening disease (p. 1403).
**C. Treat her refusal of chemotherapy as a reason to forgo systemic palliation.** Wrong, Declining chemotherapy does not remove the source-supported endocrine approach for the disease described; she is willing to consider that alternative (p. 1403).
**D. Defer radiation consultation because the recurrent lesions involve bone.** Wrong, Symptomatic bone lesions are explicitly among the sites for which palliative radiation should be considered (p. 1403).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1403.
ref: Hazzard Ch 89 — BREAST DISEASE · Harrison Ch 84 — Breast Cancer

q: An 82-year-old man with localized low-risk prostate cancer asks about active surveillance and the possibility of later curative treatment. He has moderate COPD, diabetes with neuropathy, polypharmacy including gabapentin and oxybutynin, recurrent falls with declining daily function, and reduced renal function. Which description of active surveillance agrees with Hazzard?
o: Scheduled PSA and examinations, with repeat biopsy and treatment when progression is detected
Symptom-based observation, with treatment deferred until symptomatic disease becomes apparent
Scheduled examinations, with repeat biopsy omitted when the initial biopsy shows low-risk disease
Scheduled PSA testing, with curative options considered preserved despite any disease progression
explanation:
**Active surveillance** combines monitoring with the expectation of delayed but potentially curative treatment. Hazzard distinguishes it from watchful waiting by "the intensity of monitoring and the expectation of delayed but successful definitive, potentially curative therapy" (p. 1414). It still carries a risk of progression and of missing the opportunity for curative treatment; selection should be discussed with the urologist (p. 1414).

**A. Scheduled PSA and examinations, with repeat biopsy and treatment when progression is detected.** Correct, The source describes regular PSA and examination monitoring, repeat biopsies when warranted, and intervention when evidence indicates progression (p. 1414).
**B. Symptom-based observation, with treatment deferred until symptomatic disease becomes apparent.** Wrong, Deferring treatment until symptomatic disease describes watchful waiting, which the source distinguishes from active surveillance (p. 1414).
**C. Scheduled examinations, with repeat biopsy omitted when the initial biopsy shows low-risk disease.** Wrong, The active-surveillance protocol includes repeat biopsy as warranted by PSA and examination findings; an initially low-risk biopsy does not remove that component (p. 1414).
**D. Scheduled PSA testing, with curative options considered preserved despite any disease progression.** Wrong, The source warns that progression can occur and that even careful monitoring may miss the window for curative therapy (p. 1414).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1414.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: After radical prostatectomy, a patient's PSA does not fall to an undetectable level. Which evaluation does Hazzard recommend?
o: Defer salvage assessment pending the development of new bone pain
Evaluate salvage radiotherapy with or without androgen deprivation
Defer salvage assessment pending the development of urinary symptoms
Defer salvage assessment pending a new abnormality on rectal examination
explanation:
**Persistently detectable postoperative PSA** warrants assessment for salvage treatment (p. 1415). Hazzard states that such patients "should be evaluated for adjuvant salvage therapy, including EBRT with or without ADT, or ADT alone" (p. 1415).

**A. Defer salvage assessment pending the development of new bone pain.** Wrong, The PSA finding itself calls for salvage evaluation; the recommendation does not require waiting for bone pain (p. 1415).
**B. Evaluate salvage radiotherapy with or without androgen deprivation.** Correct, External-beam radiotherapy with or without androgen deprivation is among the listed salvage options for this PSA finding (p. 1415).
**C. Defer salvage assessment pending the development of urinary symptoms.** Wrong, The source recommends evaluation because PSA has not become undetectable, without requiring urinary symptoms first (p. 1415).
**D. Defer salvage assessment pending a new abnormality on rectal examination.** Wrong, The recommendation is triggered by persistent PSA, without requiring a new rectal examination abnormality (p. 1415).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1415.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: An older man with an enlarged prostate and lower urinary tract symptoms asks about finasteride because he wants rapid relief. Which description of its action and onset agrees with Hazzard?
o: It relaxes muscle immediately, making symptom relief within hours the expected response
It increases dihydrotestosterone production, producing a rapid improvement in urinary symptoms
It improves bladder contraction, providing relief before a change in prostate size
It decreases prostate size gradually, with a slow onset of symptom improvement
explanation:
**Finasteride** blocks conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone and decreases prostate size. Its slow onset makes it unsuitable for rapid symptom relief: "They have a slow onset of action, and improvement in LUTS may take 6 to 10 months" (p. 566).

**A. It relaxes muscle immediately, making symptom relief within hours the expected response.** Wrong, the source describes gradual prostate-size reduction and a slow onset, not immediate muscle relaxation with relief within hours (p. 566).
**B. It increases dihydrotestosterone production, producing a rapid improvement in urinary symptoms.** Wrong, finasteride blocks the conversion to dihydrotestosterone; increasing its production is not the described mechanism (p. 566).
**C. It improves bladder contraction, providing relief before a change in prostate size.** Wrong, the described mechanism reduces prostate size, and the source states that these drugs do not help men seeking rapid improvement (p. 566).
**D. It decreases prostate size gradually, with a slow onset of symptom improvement.** Correct, this matches the reduction in prostate size and delayed improvement in lower urinary tract symptoms (p. 566).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 566.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES · Harrison Ch 13 — Palliative and End-of-Life Care

q: According to Hazzard, which statement describes the use of prostate brachytherapy in relation to disease risk and prostate size?
o: Brachytherapy is generally indicated as treatment for patients who have high-risk prostate cancer.
Brachytherapy is generally used as monotherapy for patients who have a large prostate.
Brachytherapy is generally combined with external beam radiation for patients with intermediate-risk disease.
Brachytherapy is generally unsuitable as monotherapy for low-risk disease with a small prostate.
explanation:
**Prostate brachytherapy** is selected according to disease risk and prostate size. Hazzard describes monotherapy for low-risk disease with a small prostate, combination with external beam radiation for intermediate-risk disease, and poor candidacy in high-risk disease (p. 1415). "For intermediate-risk patients, brachytherapy is frequently combined with EBRT (40–50 Gy)." (p. 1415).

**A. Brachytherapy is generally indicated as treatment for patients who have high-risk prostate cancer.** Wrong, high-risk patients are described as generally poor candidates for this modality. Presenting them as the usual treatment population conflicts with that risk-based selection (p. 1415).
**B. Brachytherapy is generally used as monotherapy for patients who have a large prostate.** Wrong, the monotherapy indication specifies a small prostate, not a large one. Prostate size is part of the source’s selection criteria for brachytherapy monotherapy (p. 1415).
**C. Brachytherapy is generally combined with external beam radiation for patients with intermediate-risk disease.** Correct, the source explicitly describes frequent combination with external beam radiation in intermediate-risk disease. This is the risk group and treatment combination named in the option (p. 1415).
**D. Brachytherapy is generally unsuitable as monotherapy for low-risk disease with a small prostate.** Wrong, low-risk disease with a small prostate is the source’s stated monotherapy indication. Describing that combination as unsuitable excludes the group specifically identified for treatment (p. 1415).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1415.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: A 77-year-old man is undergoing active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer. A repeat biopsy now shows primary Gleason pattern 4. Which management change does this finding support?
o: Continue active surveillance according to the original low-risk classification
Focus management on BPH symptoms and follow subsequent symptom changes
Evaluate tumor-directed treatment because the biopsy indicates disease progression
Defer further tumor evaluation until symptoms of metastatic disease appear
explanation:
A new **primary Gleason pattern 4** on repeat biopsy is a marker of progression during active surveillance. Hazzard includes this finding among changes that suggest progression and states that "intervention with appropriately selected therapy should be initiated" (p. 1414). The finding calls for reassessing tumor management rather than continuing on the basis of the original classification.

**A. Continue active surveillance according to the original low-risk classification.** Wrong, The updated biopsy changes the information on which surveillance was based; primary pattern 4 is explicitly listed as evidence of progression (p. 1414).
**B. Focus management on BPH symptoms and follow subsequent symptom changes.** Wrong, Symptom-focused BPH care does not address the biopsy evidence of cancer progression for which the source advises appropriately selected intervention (p. 1414).
**C. Evaluate tumor-directed treatment because the biopsy indicates disease progression.** Correct, The new histology meets a stated progression trigger and therefore supports evaluation for tumor-directed intervention (p. 1414).
**D. Defer further tumor evaluation until symptoms of metastatic disease appear.** Wrong, Active surveillance uses findings such as biopsy progression to trigger intervention, rather than waiting for metastatic symptoms (p. 1414).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1414.
ref: Hazzard Ch 38 — BENIGN PROSTATE DISORDERS · Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: An older adult with castration-resistant prostate cancer is being considered for enzalutamide. Which history calls for the specific neurologic caution described in Hazzard?
o: A known history of tension-type headache
A known history of a seizure disorder
A known history of gradually declining hearing
A known history of mechanical back pain
explanation:
**Enzalutamide** is an androgen receptor antagonist. The source reports seizures with these agents and specifically advises caution in patients with a known seizure disorder; the relevant history is therefore a pre-existing seizure disorder. (p. 1417)
"these drugs should be used with caution in patients with a known seizure disorder." (p. 1417)
"Enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide are androgen receptor antagonists" (p. 1417)

**A. A known history of tension-type headache.** Wrong, headache is listed among common adverse effects, but the specific history prompting the caution asked about is a known seizure disorder. (p. 1417)
**B. A known history of a seizure disorder.** Correct, this matches the history explicitly named in the warning, which follows the source’s report of seizures with these agents. (p. 1417)
**C. A known history of gradually declining hearing.** Wrong, gradual hearing decline does not meet the source’s stated criterion of a known seizure disorder for this specific warning. (p. 1417)
**D. A known history of mechanical back pain.** Wrong, mechanical back pain does not meet the source’s stated criterion of a known seizure disorder for this specific warning. (p. 1417)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1417.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 98 — Paraneoplastic Syndromes: Endocrinologic/Hematologic

q: A 76-year-old man with osteoporosis following androgen-deprivation therapy is considering denosumab. What is its mechanism of action?
o: Binding RANKL and increasing osteoclast activity
Binding the androgen receptor and increasing osteoclast activity
Binding RANKL and inhibiting osteoclast activation
Binding the androgen receptor and inhibiting osteoclast activation
explanation:
**Denosumab** is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds RANKL. This inhibits osteoclast activation and activity, the mechanism asked about here (p. 776).
"Denosumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to RANKL and inhibits osteoclast activation and activity." (p. 776).

**A. Binding RANKL and increasing osteoclast activity.** Wrong, RANKL binding inhibits rather than increases osteoclast activation and activity (p. 776).
**B. Binding the androgen receptor and increasing osteoclast activity.** Wrong, The source identifies RANKL as the target and inhibition as the effect, rather than androgen-receptor binding and stimulation (p. 776).
**C. Binding RANKL and inhibiting osteoclast activation.** Correct, The target and inhibitory effect both match the source description (p. 776).
**D. Binding the androgen receptor and inhibiting osteoclast activation.** Wrong, The inhibitory effect is paired with the wrong target: denosumab binds RANKL, not the androgen receptor (p. 776).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 776.
ref: Hazzard Ch 51 — OSTEOPOROSIS· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: An 84-year-old man with a urinary catheter is hospitalized with complicated UTI and sepsis. Culture identifies a ceftriaxone-susceptible organism, he has no allergy to the drug, and his condition still requires hospitalization. Which option is appropriate during this severe phase?
o: Oral nitrofurantoin with monitoring of clinical response
Oral fosfomycin with monitoring of clinical response
IV ceftriaxone with monitoring of clinical response
An oral beta-lactam with monitoring of clinical response
explanation:
**Complicated UTI with severe illness** supports parenteral treatment while antimicrobial choice is guided by susceptibility. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin have inadequate renal penetration for complicated UTI, and oral beta-lactams should be avoided when other treatment options are available (p. 1711).
"Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin should not be used for complicated UTI because of inadequate renal penetration." (p. 1711).
"Oral beta-lactam agents are usually less effective than FQ and TMP-SMX for treatment of complicated UTI including acute pyelonephritis" (p. 1711).

**A. Oral nitrofurantoin with monitoring of clinical response.** Wrong, The source specifically rejects nitrofurantoin for complicated UTI because renal penetration is inadequate (p. 1711).
**B. Oral fosfomycin with monitoring of clinical response.** Wrong, Fosfomycin is rejected for the same inadequate renal penetration in complicated UTI (p. 1711).
**C. IV ceftriaxone with monitoring of clinical response.** Correct, Ceftriaxone is a listed parenteral agent; its use here applies the severe-illness approach to the documented susceptibility (p. 1711).
**D. An oral beta-lactam with monitoring of clinical response.** Wrong, An oral beta-lactam is not the favored choice when another active option is available and the patient remains severely ill (p. 1711).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1711.
ref: Hazzard Ch 106 — URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: A 79-year-old man with locally advanced prostate cancer has received leuprolide for 18 months. He reports progressive fatigue, poor appetite, and loss of interest in woodworking. His PHQ-9 score is 14; his wife died 8 months ago. Testosterone is below 20 ng/dL and creatinine clearance is 44 mL/min. If depression is confirmed after excluding other causes, which drug belongs to the first-line group described in Hazzard's cancer chapter?
o: Sertraline as initial antidepressant treatment
Nortriptyline as initial antidepressant treatment
Bupropion as initial antidepressant treatment
Venlafaxine as initial antidepressant treatment
explanation:
The cancer chapter recommends excluding other causes before diagnosing depression and identifies **selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors** as first-line drugs. It lists bupropion and venlafaxine as second-line drugs and nortriptyline as third-line; this is a question about that stated hierarchy, not a patient-specific proof of superiority (p. 1392).
"Before making the diagnosis in older adults, it is important to exclude other causes." (p. 1392).
"For depression treatment, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors like citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and sertraline are first-line choice of drugs in older adults," (p. 1392).

**A. Sertraline as initial antidepressant treatment.** Correct, Sertraline is expressly included in the first-line SSRI group (p. 1392).
**B. Nortriptyline as initial antidepressant treatment.** Wrong, Nortriptyline is described as a third-line drug, so it does not meet the requested first-line category (p. 1392).
**C. Bupropion as initial antidepressant treatment.** Wrong, Bupropion is placed in the second-line group rather than the first-line group (p. 1392).
**D. Venlafaxine as initial antidepressant treatment.** Wrong, Venlafaxine is placed in the second-line group rather than the first-line group (p. 1392).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1392.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1392, Anxiety and depression

q: An 83-year-old man with castration-resistant prostate cancer and extensive bone metastases has severe back pain despite morphine 30 mg every 4 hours. Pain prevents independent transfers; he previously walked with a walker. MRI shows multilevel vertebral metastases without cord compression. Creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. His severe pain is localized to one spinal area. Which basis for palliative radiation referral accords with Hazzard?
o: Base radiation referral on demonstration of spinal cord compression
Base radiation referral on first achieving adequate relief with narcotics
Base radiation referral on severe focal bone pain despite narcotics
Base radiation referral on absence of disease in other vertebral levels
explanation:
**Palliative radiation** addresses painful bone metastases and does not require cord compression. Hazzard states, "Palliative radiation therapy can provide significant pain relief for symptomatic bone metastases" and recommends referral for one or two areas of severe pain inadequately controlled with narcotics (p. 1419).

**A. Base radiation referral on demonstration of spinal cord compression.** Wrong, The referral indication is severe focal bone pain inadequately controlled with narcotics; cord compression is not a prerequisite in that indication (p. 1419).
**B. Base radiation referral on first achieving adequate relief with narcotics.** Wrong, Inadequate narcotic pain control is itself a reason for referral, rather than a reason to keep postponing it (p. 1419).
**C. Base radiation referral on severe focal bone pain despite narcotics.** Correct, Severe pain localized to one area despite morphine matches the described referral setting (p. 1419).
**D. Base radiation referral on absence of disease in other vertebral levels.** Wrong, The source bases this referral on the painful areas and inadequate analgesia; the stem specifies one severe pain area despite multilevel metastases (p. 1419).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1419.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: A 77-year-old man is starting androgen-deprivation therapy for prostate cancer. He asks how treatment affects bone health. Which approach is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Consider deferring bone-density testing because treatment strengthens bone during therapy
Consider bone-density testing because treatment increases the risk of bone loss
Consider pain-guided follow-up because treatment lowers the expected fracture risk
Consider bone assessment after treatment because bone protection persists during therapy
explanation:
**Androgen-deprivation therapy** increases the risk of bone loss, and fracture rates are higher in treated patients. Hazzard therefore identifies bone-mineral-density testing as a way to evaluate overall bone health during testosterone-suppressing therapy. (p. 1417)
"Patients with decreased testosterone caused by orchiectomy or ADT also have a significantly increased risk of bone loss." (p. 1417)
"Fracture rates are also higher in patients on ADT." (p. 1417)

**A. Consider deferring bone-density testing because treatment strengthens bone during therapy.** Wrong, the source describes increased bone loss, not bone strengthening, so the stated reason for deferring testing is incorrect. (p. 1417)
**B. Consider bone-density testing because treatment increases the risk of bone loss.** Correct, testing evaluates bone health in the setting of the increased bone-loss risk described with testosterone suppression. (p. 1417)
**C. Consider pain-guided follow-up because treatment lowers the expected fracture risk.** Wrong, the source reports higher fracture rates during androgen-deprivation therapy, so an expected reduction in fractures does not justify this follow-up approach. (p. 1417)
**D. Consider bone assessment after treatment because bone protection persists during therapy.** Wrong, bone mineral density declines during therapy; the proposed protection during treatment contradicts that description. (p. 1417)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1417.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: A patient receiving antiresorptive treatment underwent a tooth extraction. An area of exposed, necrotic jaw bone has now failed to heal for ten weeks. Which complication matches this finding?
o: An atypical insufficiency fracture of the femur during antiresorptive treatment
Reduced bone density measured during the course of antiresorptive treatment
Osteonecrosis of the jaw associated with antiresorptive treatment
Joint pain without bone damage following the use of antiresorptive treatment
explanation:
**Osteonecrosis of the jaw** is associated with antiresorptive treatment, and invasive dental procedures may increase its risk (p. 777). Hazzard defines it as "the presence of exposed and necrotic bone in the maxillofacial region that does not heal within 8 weeks." (p. 777). The ten-week lesion described in the stem fits that definition.

**A. An atypical insufficiency fracture of the femur during antiresorptive treatment.** Wrong, atypical femoral fractures are located in the subtrochanteric region or femoral shaft, not the maxillofacial site described here (p. 777).
**B. Reduced bone density measured during the course of antiresorptive treatment.** Wrong, a density measurement does not characterize the exposed, necrotic, nonhealing lesion; the source defines this clinical finding as osteonecrosis of the jaw (p. 777).
**C. Osteonecrosis of the jaw associated with antiresorptive treatment.** Correct, the anatomical site, exposed necrotic bone, and failure to heal beyond eight weeks match the definition (p. 777).
**D. Joint pain without bone damage following the use of antiresorptive treatment.** Wrong, the stem documents necrotic bone; a description without bone damage misses the defining lesion (p. 777).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 777.
ref: Hazzard Ch 51 — OSTEOPOROSIS · Harrison Ch 180 — Actinomycosis

q: Watchful waiting is discussed with a man who has prostate cancer. Which principle defines this approach in Hazzard?
o: Intensive monitoring with an expectation of later potentially curative treatment
Initial prostatectomy followed by monitoring for recurrence of the disease
Initial radiation treatment followed by monitoring of the treatment response
Deferral of treatment until the patient develops symptomatic disease
explanation:
**Watchful waiting** defers treatment until symptomatic disease develops. **Active surveillance** differs in the intensity of monitoring and the expectation of delayed definitive, potentially curative therapy; the two terms therefore describe different management strategies (p. 1414).
"The concept of observation or watchful waiting involves deferring treatment until patients develop symptomatic disease." (p. 1414).
"Active surveillance or expectant management differs from watchful waiting in the intensity of monitoring and the expectation of delayed but successful definitive, potentially curative therapy." (p. 1414).

**A. Intensive monitoring with an expectation of later potentially curative treatment.** Wrong, The expectation of delayed potentially curative treatment and the monitoring intensity characterize active surveillance, rather than the stated watchful-waiting principle (p. 1414).
**B. Initial prostatectomy followed by monitoring for recurrence of the disease.** Wrong, Initial prostatectomy provides treatment before the onset of symptoms; it does not represent deferring treatment until symptomatic disease develops (p. 1414).
**C. Initial radiation treatment followed by monitoring of the treatment response.** Wrong, Initial radiation likewise starts treatment rather than deferring it until symptomatic disease, so subsequent monitoring does not make it watchful waiting (p. 1414).
**D. Deferral of treatment until the patient develops symptomatic disease.** Correct, This is the definition given by the source: treatment is deferred until the patient develops symptomatic disease (p. 1414).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1414.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: An older man with high-risk prostate cancer is asymptomatic and has a limited life expectancy. He and his team are considering watchful waiting. What distinguishes this approach from active surveillance intended to permit delayed curative treatment?
o: Frequent examinations and biopsies to initiate curative treatment when progression appears.
Initiation of local treatment at diagnosis with the aim of curing the cancer.
Initiation of hormonal treatment at diagnosis with the aim of curing the cancer.
Deferral of treatment during observation until symptomatic disease develops.
explanation:
**Watchful waiting** defers treatment until symptomatic disease develops (p. 1414). **Active surveillance** differs in its monitoring intensity and expectation of delayed, potentially curative treatment; Hazzard allows consideration of watchful waiting in asymptomatic men with high-risk disease and limited life expectancy (p. 1414).
"The concept of observation or watchful waiting involves deferring treatment until patients develop symptomatic disease." (p. 1414).

**A. Frequent examinations and biopsies to initiate curative treatment when progression appears.** Wrong, Intensive monitoring intended to trigger delayed curative treatment describes active surveillance rather than waiting for symptomatic disease (p. 1414).
**B. Initiation of local treatment at diagnosis with the aim of curing the cancer.** Wrong, Starting local treatment at diagnosis does not defer treatment until symptomatic disease, which is the defining feature of watchful waiting (p. 1414).
**C. Initiation of hormonal treatment at diagnosis with the aim of curing the cancer.** Wrong, Starting hormonal treatment at diagnosis is not watchful waiting. In addition, the source states that primary androgen deprivation is not curative (pp. 1414-1415).
**D. Deferral of treatment during observation until symptomatic disease develops.** Correct, Deferring treatment until symptoms develop is the explicit definition of watchful waiting (p. 1414).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1414, 1415.
ref: Hazzard Ch 90 — PROSTATE CANCER · Harrison Ch 92 — Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate

q: A man with lower urinary tract symptoms has not improved with empiric treatment. He has low urinary flow and residual urine, but bladder outlet obstruction and impaired detrusor contractility remain possible. Which test is the standard for diagnosing obstruction?
o: Cystoscopic inspection of the bladder outlet
Cystometric pressure measurement during bladder filling
Residual-volume measurement after spontaneous voiding
Pressure-flow measurement during bladder emptying
explanation:
**Pressure-flow testing** measures bladder pressure and flow simultaneously during voiding. Low flow alone is not specific for obstruction because impaired detrusor contractility can also cause it; high pressure with low flow indicates obstruction (p. 562).
"The standard for diagnosing BOO is pressure-flow study, which simultaneously measures flow rate versus bladder pressure during voiding." (p. 562).
"A high bladder pressure combined with a low flow rate is indicative of BOO." (p. 562).

**A. Cystoscopic inspection of the bladder outlet.** Wrong, the source specifically says cystoscopy should not be used to diagnose bladder outlet obstruction (p. 562).
**B. Cystometric pressure measurement during bladder filling.** Wrong, filling cystometry assesses detrusor function during filling rather than the pressure-flow relationship during voiding (p. 562).
**C. Residual-volume measurement after spontaneous voiding.** Wrong, residual volume is not significantly associated with bladder outlet obstruction and does not resolve this distinction (p. 562).
**D. Pressure-flow measurement during bladder emptying.** Correct, simultaneous pressure and flow measurement is the diagnostic standard and distinguishes the high-pressure, low-flow pattern (p. 562).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 562.
ref: Hazzard Ch 47 — INCONTINENCE· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: According to the PACIFIC trial description in Hazzard, what was concluded about durvalumab after disease control with chemoradiation in unresectable stage III lung cancer?
o: A survival benefit supported adoption as standard care
A survival disadvantage supported preference for the control treatment
A survival benefit was confined to patients undergoing resection
A tolerability disadvantage prevented adoption as standard care
explanation:
**Durvalumab** was studied after disease control with concurrent chemoradiation in unresectable stage III NSCLC. Hazzard attributes adoption as standard care to acceptable tolerability and a survival benefit in this trial population (p. 1426). "Given acceptable tolerability and the survival benefit, durvalumab has become the new SOC." (p. 1426).

**A. A survival benefit supported adoption as standard care.** Correct, The source explicitly links the survival benefit and acceptable tolerability to adoption as standard care (p. 1426).
**B. A survival disadvantage supported preference for the control treatment.** Wrong, The source reports a survival benefit with durvalumab, rather than a survival disadvantage favoring the control treatment (p. 1426).
**C. A survival benefit was confined to patients undergoing resection.** Wrong, The trial population had unresectable disease after chemoradiation; the reported conclusion was not confined to patients after resection (p. 1426).
**D. A tolerability disadvantage prevented adoption as standard care.** Wrong, Tolerability was considered acceptable and contributed to adoption, rather than preventing it (p. 1426).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1426.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: A 78-year-old woman who has never smoked has stage IV lung adenocarcinoma, brain metastases, and an EGFR L858R mutation. She takes amlodipine, metformin, and simvastatin, has reduced renal function, and lives independently but has stopped driving because of mild cognitive impairment. Which initial treatment is supported by the FLAURA results described in Hazzard, including improved overall survival and efficacy in CNS metastases?
o: Gefitinib
Osimertinib
Erlotinib
Carboplatin with pemetrexed
explanation:
**EGFR-targeted therapy** is guided by the tumor mutation. Hazzard identifies osimertinib as an initial treatment for EGFR-mutant NSCLC, citing FLAURA's "superior outcomes, improved overall survival, and efficacy in patients with central nervous system (CNS) metastases" (p. 1427).

**A. Gefitinib.** Wrong, Gefitinib is identified as a first-generation EGFR inhibitor; the improved survival and CNS-efficacy findings cited from FLAURA are attributed to osimertinib, not gefitinib (p. 1427).
**B. Osimertinib.** Correct, The source specifically connects initial osimertinib treatment with these FLAURA results in EGFR-mutant NSCLC; L858R is one of the stated sensitizing mutations (p. 1427).
**C. Erlotinib.** Wrong, Erlotinib is another first-generation EGFR inhibitor. It is not the agent to which the cited FLAURA survival and CNS-efficacy findings are attributed (p. 1427).
**D. Carboplatin with pemetrexed.** Wrong, For an identified actionable mutation, the source describes better disease control, quality of life, and progression-free survival with mutation-targeted treatment than standard chemotherapy; the cited FLAURA result concerns osimertinib (p. 1427).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1427.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: An 84-year-old man with early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer is medically inoperable because of severe lung disease. The team proposes stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT). Which description captures its technical advantage over conventional radiation in Hazzard?
o: Radiation to a broad volume in small doses over a prolonged treatment course
Focused, ablative radiation doses to the lung tumor over a few fractions
Low-dose radiation to the whole body to control microscopic sites of disease
Radiation to a broad thoracic field in small doses over several weeks
explanation:
**SBRT** delivers focused, ablative radiation doses to the primary lung tumor over a few fractions. Hazzard describes lower toxicity than conventional radiotherapy and reports local tumor control in medically inoperable candidates, explaining why it is discussed for patients unable to undergo surgery (p. 1425).
"allows the delivery of focused and ablative radiation doses over a few fractions to the primary lung tumor with lower toxicity." (p. 1425).
"Prospective trials of SBRT in medically inoperable candidates showed local control rates exceeding 92% with limited toxicity," (p. 1425).

**A. Radiation to a broad volume in small doses over a prolonged treatment course.** Wrong, A broad treatment volume and prolonged small-dose course do not describe the focused, ablative, few-fraction technique identified as SBRT (p. 1425).
**B. Focused, ablative radiation doses to the lung tumor over a few fractions.** Correct, This matches the source description of how SBRT delivers local treatment to the primary lung tumor in medically inoperable patients (p. 1425).
**C. Low-dose radiation to the whole body to control microscopic sites of disease.** Wrong, The source identifies the primary lung tumor as the target; whole-body low-dose radiation does not describe this local technique (p. 1425).
**D. Radiation to a broad thoracic field in small doses over several weeks.** Wrong, The source describes a few focused, ablative fractions, rather than small doses to a broad thoracic field over weeks (p. 1425).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1425.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: An older woman recovers slowly after resection of stage II NSCLC. What does the delayed recovery mean for consideration of adjuvant chemotherapy, according to Hazzard?
o: Favor surveillance because delayed postoperative chemotherapy has lost its efficacy
Assess chemotherapy suitability after recovery, considering performance status and comorbidities
Select chemotherapy on the basis of recovery, setting performance status aside
Start chemotherapy before recovery to compensate for the postoperative delay
explanation:
**Delayed adjuvant chemotherapy** remains a consideration after recovery from surgery. Hazzard reports that "delayed adjuvant chemotherapy administration upon recovery after surgery remains efficacious." (p. 1426). The selection described for older adults with stage II disease includes proper surgical recovery, good performance status, and no significant comorbidities (p. 1426).

**A. Favor surveillance because delayed postoperative chemotherapy has lost its efficacy.** Wrong, the source reports efficacy after delayed postoperative administration upon recovery, so the delay does not establish loss of efficacy (p. 1426).
**B. Assess chemotherapy suitability after recovery, considering performance status and comorbidities.** Correct, this uses the recovery, performance-status, and comorbidity criteria described when selecting older adults for treatment (p. 1426).
**C. Select chemotherapy on the basis of recovery, setting performance status aside.** Wrong, good performance status is part of the source’s selection criteria and should not be set aside merely because recovery has occurred (p. 1426).
**D. Start chemotherapy before recovery to compensate for the postoperative delay.** Wrong, the benefit of delayed treatment is described upon recovery, and proper recovery is part of patient selection; the passage does not support starting before that recovery (p. 1426).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1426.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: A patient with cancer and diagnosed adrenal insufficiency is clinically stable and is not under acute physiologic stress. The patient receives regular hydrocortisone replacement. Which timing principle does Hazzard emphasize?
o: Schedule the doses in the afternoon and evening
Schedule the doses in the evening and at bedtime
Schedule the doses in the morning and at lunchtime
Schedule the doses at night and close to bedtime
explanation:
**Hydrocortisone replacement** should avoid late-afternoon or evening doses because a late dose may cause insomnia. The table gives a divided regimen using morning and lunchtime administration, which supports the proposed timing for stable replacement therapy (p. 1531). "Avoid hydrocortisone in the late afternoon or evening" (p. 1531).

**A. Schedule the doses in the afternoon and evening.** Wrong, Evening administration conflicts with the instruction to avoid late dosing because of insomnia (p. 1531).
**B. Schedule the doses in the evening and at bedtime.** Wrong, Both evening and bedtime dosing place treatment in the late period the source advises avoiding (p. 1531).
**C. Schedule the doses in the morning and at lunchtime.** Correct, The divided regimen in the table places doses in the morning and at lunchtime, avoiding the late doses associated with insomnia (p. 1531).
**D. Schedule the doses at night and close to bedtime.** Wrong, Moving the regimen to the night or bedtime conflicts with avoiding late hydrocortisone administration (p. 1531).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1531.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 80 — Oncologic Emergencies

q: A medication review before cancer treatment identifies oxybutynin use. Which statement reflects Beers 2023 regarding its cognitive effects among bladder antimuscarinics?
o: The evidence favors oxybutynin because it protects cognition within this drug class
Evidence for adverse cognitive effects is best established for oxybutynin
The evidence supports considering the other bladder antimuscarinics free of anticholinergic effects
The evidence supports omitting assessment of anticholinergic effects during oxybutynin treatment
explanation:
**Oxybutynin** has the best evidence of adverse cognitive effects within this drug group. Comparative data lack consistent quality, and caution extends to the other bladder antimuscarinics because of their potential anticholinergic effects (p. 2074): "Oxybutynin has the best evidence for adverse cognitive effects."

**A. The evidence favors oxybutynin because it protects cognition within this drug class.** Wrong, the evidence concerns adverse cognitive effects, not cognitive protection (p. 2074).
**B. Evidence for adverse cognitive effects is best established for oxybutynin.** Correct, this directly reflects the statement about the evidence for oxybutynin’s adverse cognitive effects (p. 2074).
**C. The evidence supports considering the other bladder antimuscarinics free of anticholinergic effects.** Wrong, the footnote calls for caution with all bladder antimuscarinics because of potential anticholinergic effects (p. 2074).
**D. The evidence supports omitting assessment of anticholinergic effects during oxybutynin treatment.** Wrong, the stated potential for anticholinergic effects warrants caution rather than dispensing with assessment (p. 2074).

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2074.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: In which population was durvalumab studied in the PACIFIC trial as described in Hazzard?
o: Resectable stage III NSCLC after complete surgical resection
Stage IV NSCLC after disease control with chemotherapy
Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent chemoradiation
Unresectable stage III NSCLC after sequential chemotherapy and radiation
explanation:
**PACIFIC** studied unresectable stage III NSCLC with disease control after concurrent chemoradiation. These features define the population from which the trial evidence described on this page was obtained; applying them to identify the study population is an inference from the reported enrollment description (p. 1426). "patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC who had disease control after concurrent chemoradiation were randomized" (p. 1426).

**A. Resectable stage III NSCLC after complete surgical resection.** Wrong, The described population had unresectable disease after chemoradiation, rather than resectable disease after complete surgery (p. 1426).
**B. Stage IV NSCLC after disease control with chemotherapy.** Wrong, The reported population had stage III disease after concurrent chemoradiation, not stage IV disease after chemotherapy (p. 1426).
**C. Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent chemoradiation.** Correct, This includes the reported stage, unresectability, and concurrent treatment; the source also specifies disease control before randomization (p. 1426).
**D. Unresectable stage III NSCLC after sequential chemotherapy and radiation.** Wrong, The trial description specifies concurrent chemoradiation, not sequential delivery of the two treatments (p. 1426).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1426.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: A 76-year-old woman taking sertraline and hydrochlorothiazide presents with new confusion and a seizure. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, and urine is concentrated; she is clinically euvolemic. Alongside evaluation and treatment of contributing causes, which sodium-directed treatment should be started according to Hazzard?
o: Stop suspected drugs and restrict fluid, with frequent sodium monitoring.
Infuse isotonic saline, with frequent sodium monitoring.
Infuse hypertonic saline, with frequent sodium monitoring.
Give a loop diuretic and restrict fluid, with frequent sodium monitoring.
explanation:
**Severe symptomatic hyponatremia** is an emergency: “Severe symptomatic hyponatremia is a medical emergency warranting immediate treatment, no matter what the underlying cause is” (p. 587). The seizure makes immediate sodium-directed treatment relevant here; the source describes hypertonic saline for SIADH with concentrated urine and requires frequent monitoring to avoid excessive correction (p. 587). Applying that treatment pattern to the euvolemic, concentrated-urine presentation supports hypertonic saline while causes are investigated.

**A. Stop suspected drugs and restrict fluid, with frequent sodium monitoring.** Wrong, Stopping contributing medications is relevant, but this plan omits the immediate sodium-raising treatment required by the severe symptomatic presentation (p. 587).
**B. Infuse isotonic saline, with frequent sodium monitoring.** Wrong, The source describes isotonic saline for hypovolemic patients; this patient is euvolemic with concentrated urine and severe symptoms (p. 587).
**C. Infuse hypertonic saline, with frequent sodium monitoring.** Correct, Hypertonic saline matches the source's treatment pattern for severe hyponatremia with impaired water excretion; frequent monitoring is necessary to avoid excessive correction (p. 587; application).
**D. Give a loop diuretic and restrict fluid, with frequent sodium monitoring.** Wrong, Loop diuretics with water restriction are described for hypervolemic patients; this patient is euvolemic and requires immediate treatment of severe symptoms (p. 587).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: An 80-year-old patient receiving pembrolizumab develops severe colitis attributed to immune-related toxicity. Which treatment principle does Hazzard describe for severe immune-related adverse events?
o: Provide antidiarrheal medication with outpatient follow-up until symptoms improve.
Provide high-dose corticosteroids and treatment in a hospital setting.
Provide nutritional support with continued follow-up in an outpatient setting.
Provide fluid replacement with continued follow-up in an outpatient setting.
explanation:
**Immune checkpoint inhibitors** increase T-cell activity and can cause immune-related adverse events, including colitis (p. 1391). A subset of these events is severe and requires **high-dose corticosteroids and hospitalization** (p. 1391).
"While some irAEs can be mild, a subset can be severe requiring high-dose steroids and hospitalizations." (p. 1391).

**A. Provide antidiarrheal medication with outpatient follow-up until symptoms improve.** Wrong, The source describes high-dose steroids and hospitalization for severe immune-related toxicity; outpatient symptom treatment does not provide that response to the severe colitis specified here (p. 1391).
**B. Provide high-dose corticosteroids and treatment in a hospital setting.** Correct, High-dose steroids and hospitalization are the treatment principle explicitly stated for the severe subset of immune-related adverse events (p. 1391).
**C. Provide nutritional support with continued follow-up in an outpatient setting.** Wrong, Outpatient nutritional support does not provide the high-dose steroids and hospital care described for severe immune-related toxicity (p. 1391).
**D. Provide fluid replacement with continued follow-up in an outpatient setting.** Wrong, Outpatient fluid replacement does not provide the high-dose steroids and hospital care described for the severe immune-related event in the stem (p. 1391).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1391.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 80 — Oncologic Emergencies

q: A 78-year-old man with limited-stage small-cell lung cancer completed concurrent chemoradiation 3 months ago. He had an excellent response, with dose reductions for neutropenia. He remains independent, but his daughter reports new forgetfulness. Creatinine clearance is 40 mL/min and the latest brain MRI is normal. During discussion of prophylactic cranial irradiation, which potential treatment effect warrants attention according to Hazzard?
o: Earlier brain metastases, with increased risk following prophylactic cranial irradiation.
Late neurocognitive effects, with particular concern about preexisting cognitive impairment.
Improved cognitive function, with lower risk after whole-brain radiation therapy.
Fewer treatment-related adverse events, with lower risk among older recipients.
explanation:
**Prophylactic cranial irradiation** has potential benefit in responding limited-stage small-cell lung cancer, but whole-brain radiation also carries a risk of late neurocognitive effects (p. 1432). Hazzard identifies preexisting mild cognitive impairment as a concern in older adults (p. 1432); inference applied to this stem: the reported forgetfulness makes cognition relevant without establishing that diagnosis. "Any form of WBRT may confer risk of later-term neurocognitive effects" (p. 1432).

**A. Earlier brain metastases, with increased risk following prophylactic cranial irradiation.** Wrong, the studies summarized in limited-stage disease describe lowering the risk of brain metastases. The increased risk proposed here contradicts that reported benefit of prophylactic cranial irradiation (p. 1432).
**B. Late neurocognitive effects, with particular concern about preexisting cognitive impairment.** Correct, late neurocognitive effects are a stated risk of whole-brain radiation, with particular concern in older patients with baseline mild cognitive impairment. Inference applied to the stem: the daughter’s report makes cognition relevant but does not prove a radiation-induced deficit (p. 1432).
**C. Improved cognitive function, with lower risk after whole-brain radiation therapy.** Wrong, Hazzard describes risk of late neurocognitive effects after whole-brain radiation. It does not describe that treatment as improving cognition or lowering the risk of cognitive injury (p. 1432).
**D. Fewer treatment-related adverse events, with lower risk among older recipients.** Wrong, older adults with limited-stage disease are described as being at increased risk of treatment-related adverse events, even though they may still derive a survival advantage (p. 1432).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1432.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: Before treatment for lung cancer, grip strength is found to be below the reference values for sex and population. How should this finding be interpreted in the evaluation of sarcopenia?
o: It supports attributing weakness to sarcopenia before considering other causes
It supports postponing intervention until muscle mass measurement is complete
It supports suspicion of sarcopenia and assessment and treatment of weakness
It supports postponing intervention until impaired gait speed is also present
explanation:
**Low grip strength** raises suspicion of sarcopenia, but other causes of weakness should be considered. Hazzard states that low grip strength predicts adverse outcomes regardless of cause and merits intervention even when further diagnostic tests are unavailable (p. 735). "sarcopenia should be suspected, as it is the most frequent reason of muscle weakness." (p. 735).

**A. It supports attributing weakness to sarcopenia before considering other causes.** Wrong, The source calls for consideration of other causes, including hand osteoarthritis and neurological disorders; the grip result does not determine the cause by itself (p. 735).
**B. It supports postponing intervention until muscle mass measurement is complete.** Wrong, The source supports intervention even when additional diagnostic tests are unavailable, so muscle mass measurement is not a prerequisite for starting it (p. 735).
**C. It supports suspicion of sarcopenia and assessment and treatment of weakness.** Correct, The finding supports suspicion of sarcopenia while also warranting consideration of other causes and intervention for the weakness (p. 735).
**D. It supports postponing intervention until impaired gait speed is also present.** Wrong, The stated basis for intervention is low grip strength itself; requiring a further gait deficit would delay the intervention supported by this finding (p. 735).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 735.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: An 83-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer is undergoing systemic treatment planning. An ALK molecular alteration has been identified. What is the significance of molecular testing for treatment selection according to Hazzard?
o: It supports inferring the molecular alteration from age to select treatment
It supports choosing standard chemotherapy because a treatment target was identified
It supports selecting therapy directed at the alteration identified in the tumor
It supports inferring the molecular alteration from smoking history to select treatment
explanation:
**Tumor molecular testing** guides treatment selection in advanced non-small cell lung cancer. Hazzard states: "Initial molecular testing of the tumor sample to determine therapy in NSCLC is endorsed by multiple organizations and considered a SOC" (p. 1427). When an alteration such as ALK is identified, targeting it is associated with better disease control, quality of life and progression-free survival than standard chemotherapy in the source’s discussion (p. 1427).

**A. It supports inferring the molecular alteration from age to select treatment.** Wrong, the association between age and molecular alteration is not strongly established; testing identifies the alteration in the tumor rather than inferring it from age (p. 1427).
**B. It supports choosing standard chemotherapy because a treatment target was identified.** Wrong, the source describes benefits from targeting an identified alteration compared with standard chemotherapy; identifying a target is not the stated reason to choose standard chemotherapy (p. 1427).
**C. It supports selecting therapy directed at the alteration identified in the tumor.** Correct, the ALK result provides the molecular target for the treatment-selection approach described in the source (p. 1427).
**D. It supports inferring the molecular alteration from smoking history to select treatment.** Wrong, molecular alterations can occur in patients with a smoking history, so smoking history is not a substitute for identifying the tumor’s alteration (p. 1427).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1427.
ref: Hazzard Ch 91 — LUNG CANCER · Harrison Ch 83 — Neoplasms of the Lung

q: אישה בת 79 עם NSCLC שלב IV (PD-L1 5%, ללא מוטציות) שמתקדמת לאחר קו ראשון של carboplatin/pemetrexed/pembrolizumab. היא זקוקה לסיוע של הליכון לאחר שפיתחה peripheral neuropathy. Performance status הוא ECOG 2. היא שואלת על אפשרויות קו שני. בתה רוצה 'שייעשה הכל' אך המטופלת נראית מהססת. איזה גישה מתייחסת בצורה הטובה ביותר ל-goals of care?
o: להמליץ על docetaxel כטיפול סטנדרטי של קו שני
להציע best supportive care בהתחשב בסטטוס התפקודי שלה
להציע docetaxel עם ramucirumab לתגובה טובה יותר
לבחון מה המשמעות של 'שייעשה הכל' עבור כל אחד מהם
explanation:
**הסכמה מדעת** דורשת שהמטופלת תבין את מטרת הטיפול, את התועלת, את הסיכון ואת החלופות, ותוכל לבחור מרצונה. רצון הבת לעשות הכול אינו מבהיר עדיין מה המטופלת עצמה מבקשת להשיג. לכן בירור **מטרות הטיפול** והמשמעות שכל אחת מייחסת לבקשה הוא הסקה יישומית מעקרון הבחירה החופשית, לפני בחירת טיפול אונקולוגי או טיפול תומך בלבד (חוק זכויות החולה, סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
"לשם קבלת החלטה בדרך של בחירה מרצון ואי תלות." (סעיף 13(ג), עמ׳ 8)

**א. להמליץ על docetaxel כטיפול סטנדרטי של קו שני.** שגויה, המלצה על טיפול מסוים לפני בירור ההיסוס אינה פותרת את אי־הבהירות לגבי רצון המטופלת. יש להסביר את התועלת, הסיכון והחלופות ולברר מה חשוב לה; אין צורך להכריז שהתרופה אסורה כדי להבין מדוע אינה הצעד המבוקש בשיחה הזאת (הסקה מסעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
**ב. להציע best supportive care בהתחשב בסטטוס התפקודי שלה.** שגויה, בחירה בטיפול תומך בלבד ללא בירור העדפות עלולה לקבוע מטרה שהמטופלת טרם בחרה בה. זו חלופה שיש לדון בה, אך הסטטוס התפקודי אינו מחליף את תהליך המידע והבחירה (הסקה מסעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
**ג. להציע docetaxel עם ramucirumab לתגובה טובה יותר.** שגויה, הוספת תרופה אינה מבררת את הפער בין היסוס המטופלת לבין בקשת הבת. לפני בחירת משלב יש לדון במטרתו, בתועלתו ובסיכוניו במסגרת ההסכמה; אין כאן קביעה בלתי מבוססת על יעילות המשלב לפי גיל (הסקה מסעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).
**ד. לבחון מה המשמעות של 'שייעשה הכל' עבור כל אחד מהם.** נכונה, הבירור מאפשר להבין את העדפות המטופלת ואת חששות הבת, ולהתאים אחר כך את הדיון בחלופות למטרות המטופלת. זוהי דרך ליישם בחירה מרצון ובהבנה, ולא הסכמה אוטומטית לבקשה כללית של בן משפחה (הסקה מסעיף 13, עמ׳ 8).

מקור: חוק זכויות החולה, תשנ״ו־1996, סעיף 13, עמ׳ 8 בעותק שנבדק.
ref: Hazzard Ch 72 — ETHICAL ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: גבר עם דמנציה קלה וסרטן אומר שהוא סומך על בנו. לפני קביעה שאינו מסוגל לתת הסכמה לטיפול רפואי, איזה בירור רלוונטי לפי חוק זכויות החולה?
o: להסתמך על ציון הסקר הקוגניטיבי כדי להעביר סמכות
להסתמך על רצון הבן כדי להחליף את הסכמת האב
לבדוק הבנה וקבלת החלטה לאחר התאמות נגישות
להסתמך על עצם אבחנת הדמנציה כדי להעביר סמכות
explanation:
ההערכה הרלוונטית עוסקת ב**יכולת להבין ולקבל החלטות רפואיות**, ולא באבחנת דמנציה כשלעצמה. בסעיף העוסק במקבל החלטות זמני החוק מתייחס ליכולת להבין עניינים רפואיים, להחליט ולתת הסכמה גם לאחר התאמות נגישות; מסירת מידע באופן מובן נדרשת לצורך הסכמה (עמ׳ 8–9, סעיפים 13 ו-14א).
"המטופל אינו מסוגל להבין בענייניו הרפואיים, לקבל החלטות בקשר אליהם ולתת הסכמה מדעת לטיפול הרפואי, גם בהינתן התאמות נגישות" (עמ׳ 9).
"באופן שיאפשר למטופל מידה מרבית של הבנת המידע לשם קבלת החלטה בדרך של בחירה מרצון ואי תלות." (עמ׳ 8).

**א. להסתמך על ציון הסקר הקוגניטיבי כדי להעביר סמכות.** שגויה, ציון סקר אינו הבדיקה התפקודית של הבנה והחלטה המתוארת בחוק (עמ׳ 8, 9).
**ב. להסתמך על רצון הבן כדי להחליף את הסכמת האב.** שגויה, הסכמה של הבן אינה קובעת שהאב אינו מסוגל להבין ולקבל החלטה (עמ׳ 8, 9).
**ג. לבדוק הבנה וקבלת החלטה לאחר התאמות נגישות.** נכונה, הבירור מתייחס ליכולות הרלוונטיות להחלטה וכולל התאמות לפני קביעה שאינו מבין (עמ׳ 8, 9).
**ד. להסתמך על עצם אבחנת הדמנציה כדי להעביר סמכות.** שגויה, אבחנה לבדה אינה ממלאת את מבחן היכולת המפורט בסעיף (עמ׳ 8, 9).

מקור: חוק זכויות החולה, תשנ_ו-1996.pdf, עמ׳ 8, 9.
ref: Hazzard Ch 72 — ETHICAL ISSUES· Harrison Ch 79 — Infections in Patients with Cancer

q: For a patient receiving osimertinib, which pair appears in Hazzard’s table of adverse effects of targeted lung cancer treatment?
o: Pneumonitis and a shortened QT interval
Pneumonitis and a prolonged QT interval
Reduced pulmonary pressure and a shortened QT interval
Reduced pulmonary pressure and a prolonged QT interval
explanation:
**Pneumonitis** and **QT prolongation** are listed adverse effects of osimertinib. The question asks for the pair in the drug’s adverse-effect row, without inferring which effect an individual patient will develop. (p. 1428)
