ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: A 77-year-old man with hypernatremia and substantial volume depletion presents with hypotension that jeopardizes his cardiovascular status. Which sequence of fluid treatment is described in Hazzard?
o: Give free water initially, then change to isotonic saline
Give isotonic saline initially, then change to hypotonic fluid
Restrict fluid initially, then change to giving isotonic saline
Give free water initially, then maintain restriction of oral intake
explanation:
When cardiovascular status is jeopardized, **isotonic saline** is the initial fluid used to ensure adequate intravascular volume. Once volume status is established, switching to a more hypotonic fluid addresses the water deficit. This sequence follows the source’s distinction between initial volume support and subsequent water replacement. (p. 588)
"If the cardiovascular status is in jeopardy, then the initial fluid of choice is 0.9% saline to ensure adequate intravascular volume." (p. 588)
"Once the volume status is established, switching to more hypotonic fluid is reasonable." (p. 588)

**A. Give free water initially, then change to isotonic saline.** Wrong, the source specifies isotonic saline first when cardiovascular status is jeopardized; free water first omits that initial volume-support step. (p. 588)
**B. Give isotonic saline initially, then change to hypotonic fluid.** Correct, this follows the source’s sequence of establishing intravascular volume and then switching to a more hypotonic fluid. (p. 588)
**C. Restrict fluid initially, then change to giving isotonic saline.** Wrong, initial restriction does not provide the intravascular volume that the source says must first be ensured. (p. 588)
**D. Give free water initially, then maintain restriction of oral intake.** Wrong, this omits the specified initial isotonic saline and does not follow the subsequent water-replacement approach. (p. 588)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 588.
ref: Hazzard Ch 99 — DIABETES MELLITUS · Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: An 86-year-old woman develops hyponatremia with very poor food intake. Evaluation documents low daily solute excretion without evidence of excessive ADH secretion. Which mechanism explains the contribution of low solute availability?
o: Increased water excretion produces a rise in serum sodium.
Increased water excretion produces dilution of serum sodium.
Restricted water excretion produces a rise in serum sodium.
Restricted water excretion produces dilution of serum sodium.
explanation:
**Low solute excretion** can limit the ability to excrete a water load even without excess ADH (p. 586). Hazzard describes hyponatremia as “resulting primarily from the inability to excrete a water load due to excessive ADH presence or due to lack of sufficient solute excretion” (p. 586). Applying this statement, retained water accounts for the dilutional direction of the sodium change.

**A. Increased water excretion produces a rise in serum sodium.** Wrong, The source identifies inability to excrete a water load, not increased water excretion, and the resulting disorder is hyponatremia rather than a sodium rise (p. 586).
**B. Increased water excretion produces dilution of serum sodium.** Wrong, The mechanism stated in the source is restricted water-load excretion; increased water excretion does not express that mechanism (p. 586).
**C. Restricted water excretion produces a rise in serum sodium.** Wrong, Restricted water excretion is the relevant mechanism, but the source links it to hyponatremia, not a rise in sodium (p. 586).
**D. Restricted water excretion produces dilution of serum sodium.** Correct, This combines the source-described limitation in water excretion with the direction of the observed sodium change (p. 586).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 586.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: A 75-year-old man is hospitalized with hyponatremia after diarrhea. Assessment shows weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, and volume depletion without edema. There is no seizure or reduction in consciousness. Which approach targets the mechanism of this hyponatremia?
o: Restore volume with isotonic saline.
Reduce volume with an intravenous loop diuretic.
Reduce volume with strict fluid restriction.
Restore volume with a hypotonic glucose solution.
explanation:
**Volume status** guides treatment of hyponatremia. The patient's findings fit hypovolemia, for which the source recommends isotonic saline; it describes loop diuretics with water restriction for hypervolemic patients (p. 587). "Hypovolemic individuals will respond to 0.9% saline with correction of the hyponatremia." (p. 587).

**A. Restore volume with isotonic saline.** Correct, this treats the volume-depleted category for which correction with 0.9% saline is described (p. 587).
**B. Reduce volume with an intravenous loop diuretic.** Wrong, the source assigns loop diuresis to the hypervolemic pattern, whereas this patient is volume depleted (p. 587).
**C. Reduce volume with strict fluid restriction.** Wrong, water restriction does not replace the volume-restoring approach specified for hypovolemia (p. 587; application).
**D. Restore volume with a hypotonic glucose solution.** Wrong, the source specifies isotonic saline for this category and identifies hypotonic fluid infusion among causes of hyponatremia (p. 587).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 39 — SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY OF AGING AND SELECTED DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTASIS· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders
chapterTitle: Systems Physiology of Aging and Selected Disorders of Homeostasis

q: A woman treated for hypertension develops hyponatremia and hypokalemia. Which drug class is linked to this pattern in Hazzard’s table of antihypertensive medications for older adults?
o: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
Thiazide-type diuretics
Calcium channel antagonists
Angiotensin receptor blockers
explanation:
**Thiazide-type diuretics** are associated with metabolic abnormalities including hypokalemia; the same table flags hyponatremia as a situation requiring avoidance or monitoring. In contrast, the combined ACE-inhibitor and angiotensin-receptor-blocker row lists "Hyperkalemia, cough" (Table 79-4, p. 1226).

**A. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.** Wrong, the table associates this class with hyperkalemia, which does not match the low-potassium pattern described (p. 1226).
**B. Thiazide-type diuretics.** Correct, its row identifies hypokalemia and specifically flags hyponatremia, matching both findings (p. 1226).
**C. Calcium channel antagonists.** Wrong, the table describes an absence of metabolic effects for this class and lists edema, constipation, and heart block rather than this electrolyte pattern (p. 1226).
**D. Angiotensin receptor blockers.** Wrong, the table groups these drugs with ACE inhibitors and lists hyperkalemia, not the low-potassium pattern in the stem (p. 1226).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1226.
ref: Hazzard Ch 43 — FALLS· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: A 78-year-old man with mild Alzheimer dementia and diabetes has become more confused over two days. He lives with his wife, who manages his medications. Serum sodium is 122 mEq/L. She recently gave him additional 'water tablets' for swollen ankles. Which medication-history focus is specifically supported by Hazzard's discussion of hyponatremia?
o: Clarify thiazide exposure as a cause of falsely low sodium without a water-balance disturbance
Clarify thiazide exposure as a cause of high sodium from impaired water retention
Clarify thiazide exposure as a recognized medication-related contributor to low sodium
Clarify thiazide exposure as evidence favoring gastrointestinal rather than medication-related sodium loss
explanation:
**Hyponatremia** commonly reflects inability to excrete a water load, and medications are among its causes (p. 586). In its differential diagnosis, Hazzard explicitly lists "Diuretics, especially thiazides" (p. 587). Identifying the additional tablets is therefore relevant, but the history alone does not establish causation (pp. 586–587; application).

**A. Clarify thiazide exposure as a cause of falsely low sodium without a water-balance disturbance.** Wrong, the source lists thiazides among causes of hyponatremia and discusses impaired water excretion; it does not classify thiazide exposure as pseudohyponatremia (pp. 586–587).
**B. Clarify thiazide exposure as a cause of high sodium from impaired water retention.** Wrong, the drug association being investigated is with low sodium, not high sodium (pp. 586–587).
**C. Clarify thiazide exposure as a recognized medication-related contributor to low sodium.** Correct, thiazides are specifically emphasized in the medication differential, matching the history of additional diuretic tablets (p. 587; application).
**D. Clarify thiazide exposure as evidence favoring gastrointestinal rather than medication-related sodium loss.** Wrong, the table lists gastrointestinal losses separately from diuretics; thiazide exposure points to a medication-related possibility (p. 587).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 586, 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: An 85-year-old nursing home resident with advanced dementia and dysphagia receives thickened liquids. She is less responsive, with sodium 168 mEq/L, BUN 88, creatinine 2.1, and urine specific gravity 1.030. Staff report refusal of thickened water but acceptance of pudding and ice cream. Which mechanism fits the reported intake and a renal concentrating response?
o: Renal water loss accompanied by failure to concentrate the urine
Inadequate water intake accompanied by a concentrated urinary response
Renal water excretion accompanied by appropriately dilute urine in hyponatremia
Preserved water intake accompanied by continued loss of dilute urine
explanation:
**Water deprivation** is a recognized contributor to hypernatremia in dependent older adults (pp. 587-588). Hazzard describes the renal response as "a low-volume, highly concentrated urine" and directs assessment toward inadequate fluid access or extrarenal losses when that response is present (p. 588). Applying that pattern to water refusal and concentrated urine here is an inference, rather than proof that no additional contributor exists.

**A. Renal water loss accompanied by failure to concentrate the urine.** Wrong, Renal water loss from a concentrating defect is associated with polyuria or dilute urine in the source, not the concentrating response asked about (p. 588).
**B. Inadequate water intake accompanied by a concentrated urinary response.** Correct, This connects the observed poor intake with the concentrating response described in hypernatremia (p. 588).
**C. Renal water excretion accompanied by appropriately dilute urine in hyponatremia.** Wrong, The vignette describes hypernatremia and concentrated urine, not the low sodium and dilution described by this option (pp. 587-588).
**D. Preserved water intake accompanied by continued loss of dilute urine.** Wrong, Both preserved intake and dilute urine conflict with the reported water refusal and concentrating response (p. 588).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 587, 588.
ref: Hazzard Ch 31 — DISORDERS OF SWALLOWING · Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss

q: A 73-year-old woman taking warfarin starts using ginkgo biloba extract. Which interaction is described in Hazzard?
o: A lower bleeding risk when ginkgo is combined with warfarin
A lower drug-interaction risk when herbal medicines are added
A higher bleeding risk when ginkgo is combined with warfarin
A lower adverse-event risk when herbal use is left unreviewed
explanation:
**Herbal medicines** can interact with prescribed drugs and cause adverse events. Hazzard specifically links ginkgo biloba with increased bleeding risk during warfarin treatment and recommends routinely asking patients about herbal use (p. 302).
"warfarin in combination with ginkgo biloba extract leading to an increased risk for bleeding" (p. 302).

**A. A lower bleeding risk when ginkgo is combined with warfarin.** Wrong, the documented interaction increases bleeding risk; it does not reduce it (p. 302).
**B. A lower drug-interaction risk when herbal medicines are added.** Wrong, the source explicitly describes adverse interactions between herbal and prescribed therapies (p. 302).
**C. A higher bleeding risk when ginkgo is combined with warfarin.** Correct, this is the adverse interaction specifically described for warfarin with ginkgo biloba extract (p. 302).
**D. A lower adverse-event risk when herbal use is left unreviewed.** Wrong, routine questioning is recommended to identify herbal-drug interactions; leaving herbal use unreviewed does not address this risk (p. 302).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 302.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: An older adult taking spironolactone starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which electrolyte risk does Hazzard emphasize for this combination?
o: Development of significant hyperkalemia during treatment
Development of hypokalemia from the combined medications
A sustained potassium decrease requiring preventive supplementation
Potassium loss that offsets the effect of spironolactone
explanation:
**Hyperkalemia** can reflect reduced kidney function together with medications that impair potassium handling. Hazzard specifically identifies trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in a patient taking spironolactone as a high-risk situation for severe hyperkalemia (p. 1271). The listed combination is "the use of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in patients on spironolactone" (p. 1271).

**A. Development of significant hyperkalemia during treatment.** Correct, the source explicitly identifies this drug combination among high-risk situations for severe hyperkalemia (p. 1271).
**B. Development of hypokalemia from the combined medications.** Wrong, the named risk is potassium elevation, not potassium depletion from the combination (p. 1271).
**C. A sustained potassium decrease requiring preventive supplementation.** Wrong, the source identifies a risk of potassium elevation; a preventive potassium supplement does not address that risk (p. 1271).
**D. Potassium loss that offsets the effect of spironolactone.** Wrong, the combination is described as a high-risk setting for severe hyperkalemia, not a compensating potassium-losing interaction (p. 1271).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: A 76-year-old woman develops postoperative hyponatremia while receiving medication. Evaluation supports SIADH. Which urine finding supports impaired free-water excretion?
o: Dilute urine indicating increased excretion of free water
Dilute urine indicating appropriate suppression of ADH activity
Concentrated urine despite the low serum sodium concentration
Low-solute urine indicating preserved ability to dilute urine
explanation:
**Urine concentration** helps identify failure to excrete a water load during hyponatremia. Hazzard describes "an inappropriately high urine osmolality, that is, an inability to excrete a free water load" (p. 587). Concentrated rather than appropriately dilute urine supports the mechanism asked about.

**A. Dilute urine indicating increased excretion of free water.** Wrong, Increased free-water excretion indicates dilution, not impaired excretion (p. 587).
**B. Dilute urine indicating appropriate suppression of ADH activity.** Wrong, Appropriate dilution does not support excess ADH activity impairing water excretion (p. 587).
**C. Concentrated urine despite the low serum sodium concentration.** Correct, The concentration is inappropriate for hyponatremia and supports impaired free-water excretion (p. 587).
**D. Low-solute urine indicating preserved ability to dilute urine.** Wrong, Preserved dilution is the opposite of the impaired response being assessed (p. 587).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 587.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: An 83-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment and diabetes presents with fatigue and poor oral intake. His daughter manages his metformin and glimepiride. Sodium is 156, glucose 680, and calculated osmolality 348. She has also given him her furosemide for swelling. Which renal mechanism can link uncontrolled hyperglycemia to the water deficit, without establishing its contribution relative to poor intake or diuretic exposure?
o: Enhanced urinary concentration that increases renal water conservation
Osmotic diuresis that increases renal water loss
Extrarenal water loss caused by reduced access to drinking fluids
Suppressed urinary output that accompanies increased water conservation
explanation:
**Uncontrolled diabetes can cause renal water loss through osmotic diuresis** (p. 588). Hazzard describes "renal loss of water due to an osmotic diuresis as is seen commonly with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus" (p. 588). The source contrasts this with a low-volume, concentrated urine response that points toward extrarenal loss or inability to obtain water (p. 588); the stem does not quantify the competing contributions.

**A. Enhanced urinary concentration that increases renal water conservation.** Wrong, enhanced concentration and conservation describe a renal response limiting water loss, rather than the osmotic loss associated with uncontrolled diabetes (p. 588).
**B. Osmotic diuresis that increases renal water loss.** Correct, osmotic diuresis is the source’s stated mechanism for renal water loss in uncontrolled diabetes; the question does not require ranking it against other contributors (p. 588).
**C. Extrarenal water loss caused by reduced access to drinking fluids.** Wrong, difficulty obtaining fluid concerns water intake, not the renal osmotic mechanism requested in the stem (p. 588).
**D. Suppressed urinary output that accompanies increased water conservation.** Wrong, low-volume concentrated urine is the conserving response the source contrasts with polyuria and renal water loss (p. 588).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 588.
ref: Hazzard Ch 99 — DIABETES MELLITUS · Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: A nursing-home resident has inadequate relief of constipation with docusate. What is Hazzard's rationale for considering another treatment?
o: Its frequent use in nursing homes demonstrates established laxative efficacy
Its limited laxative effect favors considering a more effective alternative
It has the highest level of evidence among the agents discussed
It has demonstrated quality-of-life benefits in constipation treatment trials
explanation:
**Docusate** is widely prescribed in nursing homes but has little or no laxative effect. Hazzard recommends discouraging its prescription and using more effective methods of stool softening (p. 1372). "Docusate prescription should be discouraged, and other more effective methods of softening the stool should be prescribed." (p. 1372).

**A. Its frequent use in nursing homes demonstrates established laxative efficacy.** Wrong, common prescribing and clinical efficacy are different; the source explicitly describes little or no laxative effect despite widespread use (p. 1372).
**B. Its limited laxative effect favors considering a more effective alternative.** Correct, the limited laxative effect is the stated reason to favor more effective stool-softening methods (p. 1372).
**C. It has the highest level of evidence among the agents discussed.** Wrong, the evidence summary describes poor published evidence for stool softeners and assigns level 1 evidence to polyethylene glycol (p. 1372).
**D. It has demonstrated quality-of-life benefits in constipation treatment trials.** Wrong, the evidence summary states that the available trials did not include quality-of-life outcomes (p. 1372).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1372.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders

q: A woman with hypernatremia is hemodynamically stable and requires correction of a water deficit. Which principle should guide treatment?
o: Replace water while adjusting treatment and monitoring serum sodium
Prescribe a fixed water volume based on the initial calculation
Restrict water as the main means of lowering serum sodium
Use isotonic saline as the main means of replacing free water
explanation:
**Water replacement** is the cornerstone of hypernatremia treatment. Serum sodium must be monitored because deficit calculations depend on assumptions about body water, fluid distribution, and continuing losses that may not fit the individual patient. (p. 588)
"the cornerstone of therapy for hypernatremia is water replacement." (p. 588)
"Serum sodium should be carefully monitored throughout the therapy as the above calculation is based on several assumptions that may not apply to the individual person" (p. 588)

**A. Replace water while adjusting treatment and monitoring serum sodium.** Correct, this combines replacement of the deficit with the monitoring needed to check the assumptions underlying the initial estimate. (p. 588)
**B. Prescribe a fixed water volume based on the initial calculation.** Wrong, the calculation is an estimate, and the source requires continued sodium monitoring rather than relying on that estimate alone. (p. 588)
**C. Restrict water as the main means of lowering serum sodium.** Wrong, water restriction conflicts with the source’s recommendation to replace the missing water. (p. 588)
**D. Use isotonic saline as the main means of replacing free water.** Wrong, the source uses isotonic saline initially when cardiovascular status is in jeopardy, then switches to a more hypotonic fluid; it is not the principal free-water replacement strategy here. (p. 588)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 588.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION· Harrison Ch 388 — Approach to the Patient with Endocrine Disorders
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: An 84-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 22) presents after 3 days of productive cough, fever and delirium. He has fallen twice that day and missed medications. His usual drugs are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Temperature is 38.8°C, BP 95/60 mmHg, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 28/min and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Chest radiography shows right lower-lobe consolidation; WBC is 16.2, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.2) and glucose 340 mg/dL. Oxygenation and hemodynamic support are being addressed. Which infection-directed strategy accords with Hazzard while microbiology results are pending?
o: Start oseltamivir and reassess before adding antibacterial treatment
Start ceftriaxone plus azithromycin while awaiting microbiology results
Correct hyperglycemia and volume depletion before starting antimicrobial treatment
Obtain viral PCR and use the result to decide on initial antibacterials
explanation:
**Prompt antibacterial treatment** is part of pneumonia management alongside supportive care. Hazzard states, "The first antibiotic dose should be administered as soon as possible" and lists ceftriaxone with azithromycin among inpatient empirical regimens (pp. 1688–1689). If influenza is circulating, the source describes adding oseltamivir rather than substituting it for antibacterial treatment (p. 1689).

**A. Start oseltamivir and reassess before adding antibacterial treatment.** Wrong, The source adds oseltamivir when influenza is circulating; it does not use it to postpone the initial antibacterial regimen for this pneumonia (p. 1689).
**B. Start ceftriaxone plus azithromycin while awaiting microbiology results.** Correct, This is a listed inpatient empirical combination and can begin promptly while microbiology is pending; pathogen risk factors still guide any additional coverage (pp. 1688–1689).
**C. Correct hyperglycemia and volume depletion before starting antimicrobial treatment.** Wrong, Supportive treatment does not replace the instruction to administer the first antibiotic dose as soon as possible (p. 1689).
**D. Obtain viral PCR and use the result to decide on initial antibacterials.** Wrong, Waiting for a viral result delays the initial antibacterial dose, contrary to the source's prompt-treatment instruction (p. 1689).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1689, 1688.
ref: Hazzard Ch 105 — BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA AND TUBERCULOSIS · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: A 79-year-old woman has acute pulmonary embolism, is hemodynamically stable, and has no active bleeding. Creatinine clearance is 22 mL/min. Inpatient treatment is selected, with a need to stop and reverse anticoagulation rapidly if necessary. Which option best fits Hazzard's recommendations?
o: Start oral warfarin and follow INR until the therapeutic range is reached
Start oral dabigatran and monitor renal function and bleeding during treatment
Start an intravenous UFH infusion and adjust treatment using coagulation tests
Start oral rivaroxaban and monitor renal function and bleeding during treatment
explanation:
**Initial VTE treatment** requires rapid anticoagulant action to reduce thrombus extension, recurrence, or embolization (p. 1520). UFH "remains useful in patients with renal insufficiency or high bleeding risk where rapid reversal may be needed" (p. 1520). A therapeutic infusion requires laboratory monitoring, which supports the proposed inpatient approach (p. 1520).

**A. Start oral warfarin and follow INR until the therapeutic range is reached.** Wrong, warfarin has delayed anticoagulant effect and must initially overlap with a parenteral anticoagulant; this option does not provide that overlap (p. 1520).
**B. Start oral dabigatran and monitor renal function and bleeding during treatment.** Wrong, the table says to avoid dabigatran below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min, and initiation also requires prior parenteral anticoagulation (p. 1520).
**C. Start an intravenous UFH infusion and adjust treatment using coagulation tests.** Correct, UFH fits the stated renal and reversibility considerations, with aPTT or anti-Xa monitoring used for the infusion (p. 1520).
**D. Start oral rivaroxaban and monitor renal function and bleeding during treatment.** Wrong, the cited table says to avoid rivaroxaban below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min; monitoring does not change that table recommendation for this clearance (p. 1520).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1520.
ref: Hazzard Ch 7 — DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: An 88-year-old man with falls takes trazodone for sleep and asks to add a sedative. After evaluating his sleep problem, which approach reduces exposure to centrally acting medications?
o: Consider replacing trazodone with zolpidem for sleep
Consider behavioral insomnia treatment and medication review
Consider replacing trazodone with lorazepam for sleep
Consider adding clonazepam to trazodone for sleep
explanation:
**Medication review and nonpharmacologic insomnia care** address exposure to centrally acting drugs. Hazzard identifies these drugs as fall risks and advises against prescribing benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or other psychotropics for insomnia in older people under the described circumstances (p. 639).
"the prescription of benzodiazepines, z-drugs, or other psychotropic medication for the management of insomnia in older persons should be avoided" (p. 639).

**A. Consider replacing trazodone with zolpidem for sleep.** Wrong, zolpidem is a Z-drug, a class the source advises avoiding for insomnia in this context (p. 639).
**B. Consider behavioral insomnia treatment and medication review.** Correct, this considers the nonpharmacologic approach recommended alongside attention to fall-risk medications (p. 639).
**C. Consider replacing trazodone with lorazepam for sleep.** Wrong, lorazepam is a benzodiazepine, another class discouraged for this indication (p. 639).
**D. Consider adding clonazepam to trazodone for sleep.** Wrong, adding a benzodiazepine increases the exposure the question seeks to reduce (inference from the medication-management recommendation, p. 639).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 639.
ref: Hazzard Ch 43 — FALLS· Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: An older woman with influenza develops bacterial pneumonia as a complication. Which pair of organisms does Hazzard specifically identify as infections to which influenza predisposes patients?
o: E. coli and E. faecalis.
P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae.
S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.
M. pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae.
explanation:
**Influenza** predisposes patients to infection with **Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus**, most often causing bacterial pneumonia (p. 1734). Hazzard distinguishes bacterial infection complicating influenza from viral pneumonia among the complications contributing to deaths in older adults (p. 1734).
"Infection with influenza virus predisposes to Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus infection, which most often results in bacterial pneumonia." (p. 1734).

**A. E. coli and E. faecalis.** Wrong, This pair does not identify either organism in the explicit post-influenza association cited by Hazzard: pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus (p. 1734).
**B. P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae.** Wrong, These organisms do not match the pair singled out in the source statement about influenza predisposing to bacterial infection (p. 1734).
**C. S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.** Correct, Both organisms are named in the source statement linking influenza to subsequent bacterial infection, most often pneumonia (p. 1734).
**D. M. pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae.** Wrong, These organisms do not match the pneumococcal and staphylococcal infections named in the source statement (p. 1734).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1734.
ref: Hazzard Ch 108 — INFLUENZA, COVID-19, AND OTHER RESPIRATORY VIRUSES · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock
chapterTitle: Influenza, COVID-19, and Other Respiratory Viruses

q: An 81-year-old man is hospitalized with a complicated urinary tract infection, fever, flank pain, and hypotension. Why should nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin not be selected for this infection?
o: Inadequate penetration into renal tissue for treating complicated urinary infection.
Insufficient antibacterial activity within the bladder during acute simple cystitis.
Limited activity against multidrug-resistant isolates, particularly in the case of fosfomycin.
Excessive penetration into renal tissue, making these drugs unsuitable for older patients.
explanation:
**Complicated urinary tract infection** extends beyond the bladder and includes pyelonephritis (p. 1711). Hazzard advises against nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin for complicated infection because of **inadequate renal penetration**, despite their roles in acute simple cystitis (pp. 1708, 1711).
"Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin should not be used for complicated UTI because of inadequate renal penetration." (p. 1711).

**A. Inadequate penetration into renal tissue for treating complicated urinary infection.** Correct, Inadequate renal penetration is the explicit reason given for avoiding these drugs in complicated urinary infection (p. 1711).
**B. Insufficient antibacterial activity within the bladder during acute simple cystitis.** Wrong, The source includes nitrofurantoin as first-line treatment and fosfomycin as an alternative for simple cystitis. The problem here is penetration for infection beyond the bladder (pp. 1708, 1711).
**C. Limited activity against multidrug-resistant isolates, particularly in the case of fosfomycin.** Wrong, The source states that fosfomycin retains activity against many multidrug-resistant isolates. That activity does not overcome its inadequate renal penetration in complicated infection (pp. 1708, 1711).
**D. Excessive penetration into renal tissue, making these drugs unsuitable for older patients.** Wrong, The stated limitation is inadequate renal penetration, not excessive renal tissue exposure; the proposed mechanism does not explain the source recommendation (p. 1711).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1708, 1711.
ref: Hazzard Ch 106 — URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: A 77-year-old woman is hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia and is receiving ceftriaxone. Legionella infection cannot be excluded, and she has no contraindication to a macrolide. Which antibiotic plan agrees with Hazzard while investigations continue?
o: Add azithromycin as a single 500 mg dose alongside ceftriaxone.
Use amoxicillin-clavulanate instead of combining a beta-lactam antibiotic with azithromycin.
Withhold ceftriaxone temporarily while waiting for identification of the pathogen.
Add azithromycin 500 mg daily while continuing treatment with ceftriaxone.
explanation:
When **Legionella cannot be excluded**, Hazzard recommends a macrolide or respiratory quinolone with a beta-lactam (p. 1689). Its dosing table lists azithromycin 500 mg every 24 hours, and its treatment discussion supports prompt effective antibiotics while evaluation continues. "if it is not possible to rule out infection due to Legionella, a macrolide or respiratory quinolone should be given with a β-lactam." (p. 1689).

**A. Add azithromycin as a single 500 mg dose alongside ceftriaxone.** Wrong, a single dose does not provide the repeated daily regimen listed for azithromycin. Table 105-11 specifies 500 mg per 24 hours, not a one-time course (p. 1689).
**B. Use amoxicillin-clavulanate instead of combining a beta-lactam antibiotic with azithromycin.** Wrong, this replaces the proposed beta-lactam-plus-macrolide regimen with a beta-lactam. It omits the macrolide or respiratory quinolone recommended when Legionella cannot be ruled out (p. 1689).
**C. Withhold ceftriaxone temporarily while waiting for identification of the pathogen.** Wrong, waiting for pathogen identification before continuing treatment conflicts with the source’s recommendation to administer effective antibiotics promptly. The source provides a combination approach while Legionella remains possible (p. 1689).
**D. Add azithromycin 500 mg daily while continuing treatment with ceftriaxone.** Correct, adding daily azithromycin matches the source’s macrolide-plus-beta-lactam approach and the 500 mg per 24 hours dose in Table 105-11 (p. 1689).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1689.
ref: Hazzard Ch 105 — BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA AND TUBERCULOSIS · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: אישה בת 85 מאושפזת עם herpes zoster הפוגע ב-dermatome של V1 ימני. יש לה דמנציה מסוג אלצהיימר מתונה והיא גרה עם בתה. Creatinine הוא 1.3 mg/dL (CrCl של 28 mL/min לפי Cockcroft-Gault), משקל 48 ק"ג. הפריחה הופיעה לפני יומיים. תרופות נוכחיות: memantine 10mg BID, escitalopram 10mg ביום. היא אלרגית לסולפה (פריחה). מהו הטיפול האנטי-ויראלי המתאים?
o: Acyclovir 800mg PO 5 פעמים ביום למשך 7 ימים
Valacyclovir 1000mg PO TID למשך 7 ימים
Famciclovir 500mg PO TID למשך 7 ימים
Acyclovir 400mg PO TID למשך 7 ימים
explanation: התשובה הנכונה היא Acyclovir 400mg PO שלוש פעמים ביום למשך 7 ימים. Acyclovir מעכב את ה-DNA polymerase הנגיפי של herpes zoster לאחר פוספורילציה על ידי thymidine kinase נגיפי. בחולה זו, CrCl של 28 mL/min מחייב הפחתת מינון: לפי עקרונות הגריאטריה (Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine, 8th ed.), עבור CrCl שבין 10 ל-25 mL/min מומלץ Acyclovir 400mg כל 12 שעות, ובגבול העליון של טווח זה כפי שנמצא כאן ניתן לתת שלוש פעמים ביום. אפשרות 0 שגויה כיוון שמינון 800mg חמש פעמים ביום הוא המינון המלא ללא התאמה כלייתית. אפשרות 1 שגויה כיוון ש-Valacyclovir 1000mg TID דורש CrCl תקין; עם CrCl <30 יש להפחית משמעותית. אפשרות 2 שגויה כיוון ש-Famciclovir 500mg TID מיועד לתפקוד כלייתי תקין, ו-CrCl <50 מחייב הפחתת מינון.
ref: Hazzard Ch 3 — IMMUNOLOGY AND INFLAMMATION · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock
retiredReason: Hazzard 8e (marked), p.1727 Table 107-1: famciclovir 500 mg q8h, valacyclovir 1 g q8h and acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days are all listed regimens, and the acyclovir regimen is footnoted 'Adjust acyclovir dosing for renal function' with no adjusted dose given. With CrCl 28 the keyed unadjusted acyclovir conflicts with that footnote, two other options are book regimens, and the explanation's 400 mg TID is not in the book, so there is no single source-supported answer.

q: A 78-year-old man with COPD and impaired kidney function has symptomatic influenza that began one day ago. Which antiviral approach is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Give oseltamivir at a treatment dose adjusted for his kidney function
Give oseltamivir at a prophylactic dose during his symptomatic influenza illness
Give inhaled zanamivir because of its advantage in obstructive lung disease
Give amantadine to treat the influenza A strains circulating in the community
explanation:
**Symptomatic influenza** calls for treatment dosing, which differs from prophylactic dosing. Hazzard specifies renal adjustment for oseltamivir and warns that zanamivir may worsen or provoke respiratory distress in obstructive disease. These two cautions directly relate to the kidney impairment and COPD in the stem. (p. 1736)
"Oseltamivir should be dosed based on renal function." (p. 1736)
"it is important to use treatment doses if a patient is symptomatic." (p. 1736)

**A. Give oseltamivir at a treatment dose adjusted for his kidney function.** Correct, this combines treatment dosing for symptomatic disease with the renal adjustment specified for oseltamivir. (p. 1736)
**B. Give oseltamivir at a prophylactic dose during his symptomatic influenza illness.** Wrong, the source distinguishes prophylactic and treatment doses and explicitly calls for treatment dosing when the patient is symptomatic. (p. 1736)
**C. Give inhaled zanamivir because of its advantage in obstructive lung disease.** Wrong, the source describes obstructive disease as a setting in which zanamivir may worsen or provoke respiratory distress, not as an advantage favoring its selection. (p. 1736)
**D. Give amantadine to treat the influenza A strains circulating in the community.** Wrong, in the source’s account, circulating influenza A strains are predominantly resistant to amantadine, and its use is no longer recommended. (p. 1736)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1736.
ref: Hazzard Ch 108 — INFLUENZA, COVID-19, AND OTHER RESPIRATORY VIRUSES · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock
chapterTitle: Influenza, COVID-19, and Other Respiratory Viruses

q: An 82-year-old woman in a nursing facility for rehabilitation after a hip fracture develops sudden confusion and agitation. She repeatedly pulls at her Foley catheter. She has hypertension, osteoporosis, and mild cognitive impairment. Her medications include amlodipine 5 mg, weekly alendronate, vitamin D, oxycodone 5 mg as needed every 6 hours, and docusate. Vital signs are normal. Urinalysis shows 50–100 white blood cells, positive nitrites, and numerous bacteria. Creatinine is 1.1 and her weight is 58 kg. Which interpretation of the findings is supported by Hazzard?
o: Attribute the acute confusion to urinary infection on the basis of the positive urinalysis.
Exclude an infectious cause of acute confusion because her current vital signs are normal.
Postpone evaluation for other causes of acute confusion while waiting for urine culture results.
Evaluate for infection and alternative causes of acute confusion before attributing it to urinary infection.
explanation:
**Acute delirium** is a warning sign that warrants evaluation for possible infection, but Hazzard also requires consideration of alternative causes before attributing delirium to UTI (p. 1703). Bacteriuria and pyuria are common with chronic catheterization, which makes attribution difficult when symptoms are nonspecific (p. 1707). "In addition, alternative etiologies for delirium should also be considered before attributing it to UTI, especially in the absence of additional signs and symptoms of UTI." (p. 1703).

**A. Attribute the acute confusion to urinary infection on the basis of the positive urinalysis.** Wrong, a positive urinalysis does not resolve the cause of the mental-status change. The source describes common bacteriuria and pyuria in catheterized adults and calls for consideration of other causes before attributing delirium to UTI (pp. 1703, 1707).
**B. Exclude an infectious cause of acute confusion because her current vital signs are normal.** Wrong, acute delirium itself is among the source’s warning signs for possible infection. Normal vital signs therefore do not justify excluding infection on the basis proposed in this option (p. 1703).
**C. Postpone evaluation for other causes of acute confusion while waiting for urine culture results.** Wrong, waiting for a culture does not address the source’s requirement to evaluate alternative etiologies of delirium. That clinical evaluation is needed before attributing the mental-status change to UTI (p. 1703).
**D. Evaluate for infection and alternative causes of acute confusion before attributing it to urinary infection.** Correct, this addresses both parts of the source’s approach: evaluate warning signs for possible infection and consider alternative causes before attributing delirium to UTI. The available findings do not settle that attribution (pp. 1703, 1707).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1703, 1707.
ref: Hazzard Ch 106 — URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: A patient with advanced illness has refractory breathlessness despite optimal treatment of the underlying cause. Which statement is appropriate when considering an opioid trial for relief?
o: Favor morphine in renal insufficiency because its accumulating metabolites are protective
Replace cause-directed treatment with an opioid trial as the initial approach
Weigh relief of breathlessness against deterioration in mental functioning
Expect improved cognitive function to accompany the relief of breathlessness
explanation:
**Opioids for refractory dyspnea** may provide symptom relief after the underlying cause has been treated, although study findings are not consistent. The source emphasizes that decreased mental functioning may be unacceptable to some patients even when breathing improves (p. 1074).
"For some patients, decreased mental functioning will not be acceptable despite its potentially positive impact on breathing." (p. 1074).

**A. Favor morphine in renal insufficiency because its accumulating metabolites are protective.** Wrong, morphine metabolites can accumulate in renal insufficiency and cause neurotoxicity; their accumulation is a safety concern rather than a protective effect (p. 1074).
**B. Replace cause-directed treatment with an opioid trial as the initial approach.** Wrong, pharmacologic treatment should first address the underlying cause; an opioid trial for refractory symptoms does not replace that step (p. 1074).
**C. Weigh relief of breathlessness against deterioration in mental functioning.** Correct, this reflects the source's explicit tradeoff between a possible breathing benefit and decreased mental functioning (p. 1074).
**D. Expect improved cognitive function to accompany the relief of breathlessness.** Wrong, the source describes decreased mental functioning as a potential cost of opioid treatment, not an expected cognitive improvement (p. 1074).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1074.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: An older woman requests an antibiotic despite the absence of a clinical indication. Which statement about treatment risks in older adults agrees with Hazzard?
o: Reduced renal function favors routine dosing because sensitivity to adverse effects is lower
Renal function and polypharmacy require attention to dose adjustment and drug interactions
Polypharmacy makes selection easier because concurrent medications reduce interaction concerns
Increasing age favors routine dosing because antibiotic adverse-effect sensitivity tends to diminish
explanation:
**Renal function and drug interactions** are important when choosing antibiotics for older adults. Hazzard states that dose adjustments are commonly needed because of reduced renal function or increased sensitivity to adverse effects (p. 1670). It also notes, "Polypharmacy can make antibiotic selection and dosing particularly challenging due to drug interactions" (p. 1670).

**A. Reduced renal function favors routine dosing because sensitivity to adverse effects is lower.** Wrong, The source connects reduced renal function with a common need for dose adjustment and describes increased, rather than reduced, sensitivity to side effects (p. 1670).
**B. Renal function and polypharmacy require attention to dose adjustment and drug interactions.** Correct, This combines the two source-described concerns: renal and adverse-effect considerations in dosing, and interactions associated with polypharmacy (p. 1670).
**C. Polypharmacy makes selection easier because concurrent medications reduce interaction concerns.** Wrong, The source says polypharmacy makes antibiotic selection and dosing more challenging because of interactions, rather than reducing those concerns (p. 1670).
**D. Increasing age favors routine dosing because antibiotic adverse-effect sensitivity tends to diminish.** Wrong, The cited discussion identifies increased sensitivity to side effects as a reason for adjustment in seniors, not a reason to assume routine dosing is suitable (p. 1670).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1670.
ref: Hazzard Ch 104 — INFECTION AND APPROPRIATE ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: An older man with COPD has a mild exacerbation suitable for outpatient treatment. What initial adjustment to bronchodilator therapy does Hazzard recommend?
o: Increase short-acting inhaled bronchodilator treatment
Stop bronchodilator treatment during the mild exacerbation
Reduce maintenance treatment during the mild exacerbation
Delay bronchodilator escalation until antibiotic treatment fails
explanation:
**Bronchodilator escalation** is required for COPD exacerbations and may be sufficient in mild cases. The preferred treatment is a short-acting inhaled beta2-agonist, with or without a short-acting anticholinergic, while usual maintenance therapy continues during mild exacerbations (p. 1260).
"Escalation of BD therapy is required for all COPD exacerbations and may be sufficient to treat mild cases." (p. 1260).
"The preferred BD is a short-acting inhaled β2-agonist with or without a short-acting anticholinergic." (p. 1260).

**A. Increase short-acting inhaled bronchodilator treatment.** Correct, Escalation addresses the exacerbation using the preferred short-acting inhaled treatment (p. 1260).
**B. Stop bronchodilator treatment during the mild exacerbation.** Wrong, Stopping treatment would omit the bronchodilator escalation required for an exacerbation (p. 1260).
**C. Reduce maintenance treatment during the mild exacerbation.** Wrong, Usual maintenance therapies should continue during a mild exacerbation, alongside the short-acting treatment (p. 1260).
**D. Delay bronchodilator escalation until antibiotic treatment fails.** Wrong, The source requires escalation for the exacerbation itself; it does not make this contingent on antibiotic failure (p. 1260).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1260.
ref: Hazzard Ch 81 — CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE· Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: An 86-year-old woman with truncal herpes zoster presents 48 hours after rash onset. She is immunocompetent, creatinine clearance is 65 mL/min, and there is no ocular involvement. Which virus-directed treatment is appropriate to reduce acute pain and the duration of chronic pain according to Hazzard?
o: Oral gabapentin adjusted according to tolerability
Oral valacyclovir for a full seven-day course
Topical acyclovir applied over the affected skin
Oral prednisone followed by a gradual dose taper
explanation:
**Oral antiviral therapy** started within the studied early window reduces acute pain and the duration of chronic pain. Hazzard describes a seven-day valacyclovir course and distinguishes antiviral therapy from adjunctive analgesic treatments (pp. 1727–1728).
"valaciclovir (1 g three times a day for 7 days) reduce acute pain and the duration of chronic pain in older patients with herpes zoster" (p. 1727).
"who are treated within 72 hours of rash onset." (p. 1727).

**A. Oral gabapentin adjusted according to tolerability.** Wrong, Gabapentin is discussed as an adjunct for pain inadequately relieved by antiviral and analgesic treatment, not as the virus-directed treatment requested (p. 1728).
**B. Oral valacyclovir for a full seven-day course.** Correct, The source describes oral valacyclovir for seven days; the supplied onset interval lies within the studied treatment window (p. 1727).
**C. Topical acyclovir applied over the affected skin.** Wrong, Topical antiviral therapy is explicitly described as ineffective regardless of when it is started (p. 1727).
**D. Oral prednisone followed by a gradual dose taper.** Wrong, Corticosteroids do not prevent postherpetic neuralgia and, if used, should accompany antiviral therapy rather than replace it (p. 1728).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1727, 1728.
ref: Hazzard Ch 107 — OTHER VIRUSES: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION AND HERPES ZOSTER · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock
chapterTitle: Other Viruses: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and Herpes Zoster

q: אדם עם דמנציה מתקדמת מתקשה באכילה. לפני החלטה על דרך ההזנה מתברר שטרם הושלמה הערכת מצבו, צרכיו ויכולת הבליעה. איזה תהליך החלטה תואם את המלצות הוועדה הארצית?
o: בחירת דרך הזנה לפי משך הירידה באכילה
בחירת דרך הזנה לפי ערך האלבומין שנמדד
בחירת דרך הזנה לפי אבחנת הדמנציה שניתנה
הערכה אישית בשיתוף צוות רב־מקצועי
explanation:
**החלטה על דרך ההזנה** צריכה להתבסס על מצבו וצרכיו של החולה המסוים. ההמלצות דורשות שיתוף צוות רב־מקצועי והתאמה אישית; נתון יחיד אינו מחליף הערכה זו (עמ׳ 5).
"החלטה רפואית צריכה להתקבל בשיתוף פעולה של צוות רב מקצועי" (עמ׳ 5)

**א. בחירת דרך הזנה לפי משך הירידה באכילה.** שגויה, משך הירידה באכילה הוא נתון לבירור, אך אינו מחליף החלטה רפואית אישית לפי המצב והצרכים (עמ׳ 5).
**ב. בחירת דרך הזנה לפי ערך האלבומין שנמדד.** שגויה, ערך מעבדה בודד אינו מספק את ההערכה האישית והרב־מקצועית שנדרשת לבחירת דרך ההזנה (עמ׳ 5).
**ג. בחירת דרך הזנה לפי אבחנת הדמנציה שניתנה.** שגויה, האבחנה לבדה אינה קובעת את הדרך; ההמלצות דורשות התאמה למצב ולצרכים הרפואיים (עמ׳ 5).
**ד. הערכה אישית בשיתוף צוות רב־מקצועי.** נכונה, זהו התהליך שנקבע בהמלצות, ובו משולבים שיקולי מצב רפואי, תזונה ובליעה של החולה המסוים (עמ׳ 3, 5).

מקור: המלצות הוועדה הארצית על הזנה בדמנציה, עמ׳ 5; המלצות הוועדה הארצית על הזנה בדמנציה, עמ׳ 3.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES· Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss

q: An 83-year-old woman develops diarrhea and colitis after antibiotic treatment during hospitalization. Clostridium difficile infection is diagnosed. Which mechanism explains the association with antibiotic exposure?
o: An allergic response to the antibiotic directly damages the colonic mucosa
An osmotic action of the antibiotic draws fluid into the intestinal lumen
An antibiotic-related neural injury disrupts intestinal propulsive activity
Alteration of normal colonic flora permits disease caused by the organism
explanation:
**Altered colonic flora** is the link described between antibiotic exposure and C. difficile disease. The source identifies C. difficile as toxigenic and connects its toxin to antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis (p. 1304).
"Pathogenesis often involves exposure to an agent that alters normal colonic flora such as an antibiotic." (p. 1304).
"the association between the toxin elaborated by this bacterium and antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis was made." (p. 1304).

**A. An allergic response to the antibiotic directly damages the colonic mucosa.** Wrong, the infection mechanism described is disruption of normal flora with toxigenic C. difficile disease, not antibiotic allergy (p. 1304).
**B. An osmotic action of the antibiotic draws fluid into the intestinal lumen.** Wrong, a direct osmotic drug effect does not describe the source's flora-related pathogenesis of the diagnosed infection (p. 1304).
**C. An antibiotic-related neural injury disrupts intestinal propulsive activity.** Wrong, the stated pathway involves altered flora and a toxigenic organism, rather than antibiotic-induced neural damage (p. 1304).
**D. Alteration of normal colonic flora permits disease caused by the organism.** Correct, this expresses the antibiotic-related change in normal flora described in the pathogenesis section (p. 1304).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1304.
ref: Hazzard Ch 104 — INFECTION AND APPROPRIATE ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: בן 78, הסובל מדמנציה מתקדמת מאושפז במחלקה לסיעוד מורכב עקב פצע לחץ דרגה 4 בטרוכנטר. לאחרונה נצפתה החמרה בהפרשה מהפצע, הופיע אודם מקומי ונמדד חום סיסטמי 38.5. מה הגישה הטיפולית לזיהום במקרה המתואר?
o: מתן טיפול אנטיביוטי בהתאם לבדיקת מטוש (SWAB) ממוגלה שיוצאת מהפצע
מתן טיפול אנטיביוטי ראשוני המכסה זיהום ב- PSEUDOMONAS AUROGINOSA
מתן טיפול אנטיביוטי ב- CEFAMEZIN היעיל בטיפול בחיידקי עור כמו STREPTOCOCUS ו- STAPHILOCOCUS
מתן טיפול אנטיביוטי אמפירי רחב טווח
explanation:
A deep pressure injury with fever and local deterioration warrants assessment for **systemic infection**. For suspected bacteremia, the book recommends broad empiric coverage of gram-positive cocci, gram-negative organisms and anaerobes pending appropriate culture results (Hazzard 8e, pp. 695, 697).

**A. Select antibiotics from a swab of pus draining from the wound.** Wrong, cultures of the surface or drainage may reflect only surface contamination and should not alone determine treatment for a deep infection with fever (p. 695).
**B. Give initial treatment directed at Pseudomonas aeruginosa.** Wrong, Pseudomonas-only coverage misses the mixed flora requiring gram-positive and anaerobic coverage in this presentation (pp. 695, 697).
**C. Give cefazolin for skin organisms such as streptococci and staphylococci.** Wrong, coverage directed at skin organisms does not ensure the breadth needed for suspected pressure-injury bacteremia; the source also includes gram-negative organisms and anaerobes (p. 697).
**D. Give broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics.** Correct, fever with wound deterioration raises concern for systemic infection. Broad coverage pending appropriate cultures matches the recommendation, rather than relying on a superficial swab (pp. 695, 697).

Here the infection findings justify appropriate empiric treatment without relying solely on surface drainage. Treatment should be adapted to the clinical findings and appropriate cultures, recognizing that antibiotics also carry risks (pp. 695, 697).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 695, 697.

q: בת 78, אקדמאית בהשכלתה, עצמאית בכל התפקודים אובחנה לאחרונה כסובלת ממחלת אלצהיימר בדרגת חומרה קלה. היא מדווחת על הפרעה בעיקר בזיכרון לטווח הקצר אשר מפריעה לה במשחק ברידג' ובניהול כספים. באבחון הקוגניטיבי שעברה במסגרת הבירור נעשתה בדיקת MOCA המצורפת: המטופלת ובעלה מבקשים לדעת האם מומלץ לבצע תרגול קוגניטיבי ומאיזה סוג. מהי ההמלצה הנכונה?
o: מומלץ לבצע תרגול קוגניטיבי בתחומים שהיו לקויים באבחון כמו הזיכרון והריכוז
מומלץ לבצע תרגול קוגניטיבי בתחומים שנמצאו שמורים באבחון, לדוגמא בתחום השפתי ובתחום התפיסה החזותית מרחבית
מומלץ להימנע מתרגול קוגניטיבי מאחר ואינו יעל והוא עשוי להוביל לתסכול ולדיכאון
מומלץ להמשיך ולהשתתף בפעילות לגירוי קוגניטיבי לצורך עניין והנאה בלבד
explanation:
Official answer: ב.

Encourage **activities using intact cognitive abilities**, tailored to the person’s interests and capabilities. The source describes potential cognitive benefit from appropriate cognitive, physical and social activity. It does not establish that structured training is superior to enjoyable, stimulating activity (p. 915).

**A. Train impaired domains, such as memory and concentration.** Wrong, inference from the source’s example: activity that relies on an impaired domain may be frustrating. Choose activities suited to remaining abilities and interests rather than automatically targeting the weakest domain (p. 915).
**B. Train preserved domains, such as language and visuospatial abilities.** Correct, this matches the recommendation to encourage activities using intact cognitive functions, tailored to the patient’s abilities and interests (p. 915).
**C. Avoid cognitive training because it is ineffective and may cause frustration and depression.** Wrong, the source encourages appropriately adapted cognitive and social activities, so blanket avoidance is not its recommendation (p. 915).
**D. Continue cognitively stimulating activities solely for interest and enjoyment.** Wrong, this was not the officially accepted option. The source describes possible cognitive benefit as well as enjoyment and individual adaptation. The caveat remains that it does not establish superiority of structured training over enjoyable activity (p. 915).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 915.

q: בן 92 הסובל מדמנציה מתקדמת, מאושפז מזה חודש במחלקת קורונה. בקבלתו המוגלובין 12.8. במהלך האשפוז הופיעו פצעי לחץ דרגה 4 בשני הטרוכנטרים. כעת סובל גם מ- MRSA SEPSIS. בבדיקות המעבדה: מדד ויחידות המטופל ערכים תקינים WBC 10e3qµL 12,800 4.0-11.0 HgB gr/dl 9.5 17 - 13.2 MCV fL 80 80-96 PLT 10e3qµL 496,000 140-450 NEU % 82 40-75 LYM % 16 20-40 IRON µg/dL 32 40-150 TRANSFERRIN mg/dL 152 220-400 FERRITIN ng/dL 188 14-163 VIT B12 pg/mL >1000 175-961 FOLIC ACID ng/mL 3.6 2.6-17 BUN mg/dL 24 5-25 CREATININE mg/dL 0.5 0.7-1.3 ALBUMIN g/L 26 35-50 CRP mg/L 158 0.03-5.0 מה האבחנה והטיפול המומלץ לאנמיה?
o: מדובר קרוב לודאי ב- MYELOSYSPLASTIC SYNDROME ומומלץ לתת טיפול ב- ERTHROPOIETIN
מדובר באנמיה מחסר ברזל ומומלץ טיפול בברזל תוך ורידי
לא ניתן לאבחן את סוג האנמיה ללא בדיקת מח עצם ולכן לא ניתן להמליץ על טיפול
מדובר באנמיה של מחלה כרונית. רק שיפור במצבו הזיהומי ישפר את האנמיה
explanation:
The infectious setting, low iron, low transferrin, and non-low ferritin support **anemia of inflammation**. Inflammation limits iron availability for erythropoiesis; ferritin also reflects the inflammatory response and does not exclude concomitant iron deficiency (Weiss et al., Abstract; Diagnosis; inference applying the source to the stem).
"hypoferremia, and hyperferritinemia" (Weiss et al., Abstract).

**A. Likely myelodysplastic syndrome requiring erythropoietin.** Wrong, the fall in hemoglobin in this infectious setting and the laboratory pattern first support inflammatory anemia. They do not prove myelodysplastic syndrome or justify erythropoietin on these facts alone (Weiss et al., Diagnosis; Treatment; inference applying the source).
**B. Iron-deficiency anemia requiring intravenous iron.** Wrong, low iron alone does not prove iron deficiency: inflammation also lowers iron, and transferrin and ferritin help interpretation. Intravenous iron is not automatically justified during infection; coexisting deficiency and benefit versus risk must be assessed (Weiss et al., Diagnosis; Treatment).
**C. The anemia cannot be diagnosed or treatment recommended without bone marrow examination.** Wrong, the article describes diagnosis using the clinical context, inflammatory findings, and iron studies while excluding additional causes; bone marrow biopsy is not a prerequisite for every diagnosis (Weiss et al., Diagnosis).
**D. Anemia of chronic disease; only improvement in the infectious condition will improve the anemia.** Correct, this is the official answer, and treating the underlying inflammatory disease is central. The word only is not an absolute treatment rule: deficiencies, other contributors, or context-specific anemia treatment may also require attention (Weiss et al., Treatment).

**Official answer:** Anemia of chronic disease; only improvement in the infectious condition will improve the anemia (IMA, final answer key, 2020, question 41).

Source versus explanation: "Two therapies have been established for the treatment of AI: iron supplementation and treatment with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs)." (Weiss, Ganz, Goodnough, Blood 2019;133:40–50, Treatment; doi:10.1182/blood-2018-06-856500). The retained sentence does not justify excluding every other treatment in every patient; selection depends on the condition and additional contributors.

The book lists anemia of chronic inflammation among the causes of anemia and recommends iron, ferritin, renal-function, B12, and folate testing. The stem supplies substantial infection, high CRP, and new anemia, but this book passage does not define the iron-transferrin-ferritin pattern as a diagnostic test or state that only improvement in infection improves anemia (Hazzard 8e, p. 1480).

Note: The wording that only improvement in the infectious condition will help is too absolute as a medical rule. The importance of treating infection does not exclude evaluation and treatment of additional anemia contributors (Weiss et al., Diagnosis; Treatment).

Source: Weiss G, Ganz T, Goodnough LT. Anemia of inflammation. Blood. 2019;133:40–50, Abstract; Diagnosis; Treatment. doi:10.1182/blood-2018-06-856500. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6536698/ (full-text HTML sections; PDF pagination not used). Hazzard 8e, p. 1480, for the retained book-source limitation.

q: בן 86, בריא בדרך כלל, שמור קוגניטיבית. לא היה אצל רופאת המשפחה ב- 5 השנים האחרונות ולא עשה בדיקות דם. הגיע למחלקה לרפואה דחופה (חדר מיון) לאחר נפילה ברחוב. בדיקה גופנית ללא ממצא משמעותי. לחץ הדם שמור, ללא חום. בדיקה גופנית תקינה ואין עדות לשבר או חבלת ראש. בספירת הדם: מדד ויחידות המטופל ערכים תקינים WBC 10e3qµL 31.2 4.0-11.0 HgB gr/dl 14.5 17 - 13.2 PLT 10e3qµL 231 140-450 NEU % 11 40-75 LYM % 85 20-40 במשטח דם: המטופל מתמצא בסיטואציה, במקום ובזמן, ללא חסר קוגניטיבי בולט ומעוניין להשתחרר לביתו. מה ההמלצה הטיפולית לגבי הממצא בספירת הדם?
o: אשפוז עם טיפול אנטיביוטי רחב טווח בחשד ל- SEPSIS
אשפוז לצורך בדיקת מח עצם בחשד ל- ACUTE LEUKEMIA
שחרור למעקב מרפאה המטולוגית בחשד ל- CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA
שחרור עם המלצה לטיפול ב- G-CSF עקב נויטרופניה אסימפטומטית ומעקב מרפאה המטולוגית בהקדם
explanation:
The stem describes **absolute lymphocytosis without anemia or thrombocytopenia**, raising suspicion for CLL. Diagnosis requires demonstration of a monoclonal B-cell population by flow-cytometric immunophenotyping. CLL is the most common leukemia in the Western Hemisphere and may be detected as asymptomatic lymphocytosis; early asymptomatic disease calls for observation rather than immediate treatment (Hazzard 8e, pp. 1490-1491).

**A. Admit for broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected sepsis.** Wrong, the stem describes no fever, instability, or infection-directed symptoms. As an inference from the case and asymptomatic CLL presentation, the high cell count alone does not justify sepsis treatment; this does not generally exclude infection in CLL (p. 1490).
**B. Admit for bone marrow examination for suspected acute leukemia.** Wrong, initial assessment of suspected CLL can use peripheral blood and flow cytometry; bone marrow studies are usually unnecessary for diagnosis. Lymphocytosis alone does not establish a need for admission for marrow examination for acute leukemia (p. 1490).
**C. Discharge for hematology follow-up for suspected chronic lymphocytic leukemia.** Correct, for scoring and consistent with the described stable condition. Hematology follow-up permits diagnostic confirmation and staging. This is a clinical inference from observation in early asymptomatic CLL; the blood count alone does not establish the final stage (pp. 1490-1491).
**D. Discharge with G-CSF for asymptomatic neutropenia and prompt hematology follow-up.** Wrong, the neutrophil percentage is relatively low in the setting of lymphocytosis; the data do not imply a low absolute count. Calculating an absolute count applies the stem's data. The source-directed investigation is peripheral-blood assessment for CLL, not colony-stimulating treatment based on the neutrophil percentage alone (p. 1490).

CLL may be found incidentally, and its diagnosis alone does not require immediate treatment; decisions depend on stage and symptoms (pp. 1490-1491).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1490-1491.

q: בת 81, הולכת עם מקל מאז ניתוח החלפת ברך. ברקע יתר ל"ד. נוטלת LERCANIDIPINE (VASODIP). אושפזה במחלקה קרדיולוגית בעקבות NSTEMI שטופל באמצעות צנתור שכלל הנחת תומכן. אקו לב הדגים תפקוד סיסטולי מעט ירוד של חדר שמאל (LVEF 45%). כעת מיועדת לשחרור לביתה. סימנים חיוניים שנלקחו יום לפני השחרור - ל"ד 125/82, דופק 59 ובבוקר השחרור – ל"ד 116/80, דופק 58. בשחרור הומלץ על טיפול ב- ASPIRIN, CLOPIDOGREL (PLAVIX) ו- ATORVASTATIN (LIPITOR). איזו מבין רשימות תרופות הבאות מתאימה להשלמת התרופות המומלצות בשחרור:
o: LERCANIDIPINE (VASODIP), BISOPROLOL (CARDILOC)
LERCANIDIPINE (VASODIP), RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)
RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)
BISOPROLOL (CARDILOC)
explanation:
After myocardial infarction, choose **secondary-prevention treatment** with attention to pulse, blood pressure and tolerability. The source supports considering an ACE inhibitor for coronary disease with reduced ventricular function or hypertension, with renal-function and potassium monitoring (p. 1143). Preferring ramipril without another pulse-slowing or blood-pressure-lowering drug is a clinical application to this vignette; a slightly low pulse is not by itself an absolute beta-blocker prohibition (p. 1179).

**A. Lercanidipine and bisoprolol.** Wrong, this omits an ACE inhibitor and adds a pulse-slowing drug when the pulse is already low. As a clinical inference, it fits secondary prevention and the hemodynamic situation less well; lercanidipine lowers blood pressure but does not substitute for the ACE inhibitor's role here (pp. 1143, 1179; lercanidipine SmPC, sections 4.1 and 5.1).
**B. Lercanidipine and ramipril.** Wrong, ramipril fits secondary prevention, while additional lercanidipine addresses inadequate blood-pressure control. The provided readings do not demonstrate a need for two blood-pressure-lowering agents at discharge; this is inference from the case (p. 1143; SmPC, sections 4.1-4.2 and 5.1).
**C. Ramipril.** Correct, this adds an ACE inhibitor supported in coronary disease with impaired ventricular function without additional pulse slowing. Monitor blood pressure, creatinine and potassium; it is not risk-free (p. 1143).
**D. Bisoprolol.** Wrong, it requires adjustment to pulse and tolerability and does not supply the ACE-inhibitor component of the official choice. This is an individual clinical judgment, not a rule that every pulse below 60 prohibits beta-blockers (pp. 1143, 1179).

Inherited key point for older patients: After NSTEMI with reduced LVEF, avoid iatrogenic bradycardia (pulse below 60 with a beta-blocker) and unnecessary polypharmacy. An ACE inhibitor may provide prognostic benefit after infarction but requires dose adjustment and monitoring of blood pressure, creatinine and potassium; it is not risk-free (p. 1143).

Source versus explanation: In its heart-failure discussion, the source defines a contraindication as "marked bradycardia (resting heart rate < 50/min)" (p. 1179). The inherited caution about a pulse below 60 must therefore not become an absolute prohibition; consider tolerability and clinical context.

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1143, 1179; lercanidipine hydrochloride SmPC, sections 4.1-4.2 and 5.1, https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/102168/smpc.

q: בן 75, עצמאי ב- BADL. ברקע - סכרת ואי ספיקת לב, מטופל ב- DAPAGLIFUZIN (FORXIGA), LINAGLIPTIN (TRAJENTA), METFORMIN, ENALAPRIL ו- DISOTHIAZIDE. התקבל לאשפוז אלקטיבי לניתוח TKR שבוצע ללא אירועים חריגים. ביממה השנייה לאחר הניתוח חלה ירידה במצב ההכרה, החולה נמצא ישנוני ומבולבל. ל"ד 90/60 דופק 100 סדיר, סטורציה תקינה, חום תקין. במעבדה: בדיקה ויחידות ערך לחולה ערכי נורמה BUN mg/dL 80 25 - 5 CREATININE mg/dL 1.7 0.6-1.1 NA mmol/L 145 135-146 K mmol/L 4.5 3.5-5.3 Cl mmol/L 88 95-110 PH 7.0 7.35-7.45 PCO2 mmHg 35 35-46 HCO3 mmol/L 14 21-26 בבדיקת שתן: לויקוציטים +, תאים אדומים -, ניטריט -, קטונים +++ תופעת לוואי של איזו מהתרופות הבאות עשויה להיות הגורם למצבו של החולה?
o: METFORMIN
DAPAGLIFLOZIN (FORXIGA)
LINAGLIPTINE (TRAJENTA)

explanation:
Table 99-11 lists **diabetic ketoacidosis** among adverse effects of **SGLT2 inhibitors**, including dapagliflozin, and notes that it is rare in type 2 diabetes. This supports the official selection; the table does not specify a preoperative withholding interval (Hazzard 8e, p. 1578).

**A. Metformin.** Wrong under the official key, its listed adverse effect is lactic acidosis, whereas urinary ketones distinguish this stem (pp. 1577–1578; inference).
**B. Dapagliflozin (Forxiga).** Correct, dapagliflozin belongs to the SGLT2-inhibitor group in which the table lists ketoacidosis (p. 1578).
**C. Linagliptin (Trajenta).** Wrong, it is a DPP-4 inhibitor; the table links ketoacidosis to SGLT2 inhibitors. Dapagliflozin is therefore the supported drug explanation, without implying that linagliptin has no adverse effects (pp. 1577–1578).
**D. Disothiazide.** Wrong, the thiazide profile includes metabolic and electrolyte abnormalities but does not provide the explicit ketoacidosis link given for SGLT2 inhibitors (pp. 1226, 1578).

Inference: The combination of acidosis and urinary ketones points to the listed SGLT2-associated adverse effect; this applies the table to the case and does not prove normal glucose (p. 1578).

Inference applied to the question: postoperative confusion, hypotension, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and urinary ketones support suspected SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis. Glucose was not provided, so this episode cannot be called euglycemic (p. 1578; examination paper, p. 25, as cited in the existing explanation).

Inference: The comparison favors dapagliflozin; ketones do not exclude concurrent lactic acidosis from metformin (pp. 1577–1578). The thiazide option is less consistent with the ketones in the question (pp. 1226, 1578).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1226, 1577–1578.

q: הממשלה מעוניינת לבדוק כדאיות חיסון לקורונה בקרב אנשים בני פחות מ- 60 שגרים עם קשישים באותו בית. על פי הפרסום "בני 65+ בישראל" מה אחוז הקשישים שגר עם ילדיו בבית?
o: 0.5% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 0.5% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים
2% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 1% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים
12% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 5% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים
24% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 12% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים
explanation:
## סידורי מגורים של בני שישים וחמש ומעלה

**א. 0.5% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 0.5% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים.** שגויה, שיעורים זעירים בשתי קטגוריות הילדים אינם מתארים את שתי הקבוצות בלוח. זו השוואה לשנתון המאוחר, ולא אימות ישיר של מהדורת הבחינה (עמ׳ 118).
**ב. 2% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 1% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים.** שגויה, גם צמד שיעורים זה ממעיט באופן מהותי בשתי קבוצות משקי הבית עם ילדים המתוארות בלוח המאוחר (עמ׳ 118).
**ג. 12% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 5% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים.** נכונה, נכונה לפי המפתח הרשמי. צמד השיעורים תואם בקירוב את שתי קטגוריות הילדים בלוח המאוחר; הסתייגות התיארוך בפתיח נשמרת (עמ׳ 118).
**ד. 24% מהקשישים גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים, 12% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים.** שגויה, צמד זה מייחס לשתי הקבוצות משקל גדול בהרבה מזה שבלוח, ולא נובע מהבדל בין ילד קטין לילד בוגר, שכן שניהם נכללים (עמ׳ 118 והערה 2).

על פי הפרסום "בני +65 בישראל" של הלשכה המרכזית לסטטיסטיקה, כ-12% מהקשישים בישראל גרים במשק בית של זוג עם ילדים וכ-5% גרים במשק בית של הורה יחיד עם ילדים. נתונים אלו חשובים לתכנון מדיניות בריאות הציבור, במיוחד בהקשר של חיסונים והגנה על אוכלוסיות פגיעות. אימות מאוחר: שנתון 2024, לוח 1.34, עמ׳ 118, נתוני 2022 — 11.6% ו־4.9% בהתאמה, מקרב בני 65+ במשקי בית; אוכלוסייה מוסדית אינה כלולה. אין זה אימות ישיר של מהדורת הבחינה.

הלוח כולל ילדים בכל הגילים, גם מעל גיל 18; אין להסיק ממנו לבדו שיעור מגורים עם ילדים קטנים (שנתון 2024, לוח 1.34, הערה 2).

מקור: בני 65+ בישראל, שנתון 2024, עמ׳ 118, לוח 1.34 (עמוד PDF 120).
referenceNote: Brookdale yearbook: בני 65+ בישראל. Examined on an earlier edition; figures may differ from the required 2024 edition.

q: בת 82, מאושפזת מזה כשבועיים בטיפול נמרץ באבחנה של דלקת ריאות, כשהיא מונשמת ומטופלת באנטיביוטיקה וסטרואידים IV.תחת הטיפול נצפה שיפור קליני במצבה. בשל הופעת פרפור עליות במהלך האשפוז נלקחה בדיקה לתפקודי בלוטת התריס. להלן התוצאות. מדד ויחידות ערך לחולה ערכי נורמה TSH mU/L <0.01 0.4-4.7 T4 ng/dl <0.1 0.7-1.8 T3 pg/ml <0.01 1.71-3.71 מה ההסבר לשינוי בבדיקות וההמלצה הטיפולית?
o: מדובר בהיפותירואידזם מרכזי, יש להשלים בדיקות מעבדה לשלול מחלה היפופיזרית נוספת, ולהתחיל בהקדם טיפול ב- IV LEVOTHROXIN
מדובר ב- Non thyroidal illness syndrome ויש להתחיל טיפול ב- IV LEVOTHYROXINE
היות ובמצב זה תיתכן גם פגיעה באדרנל המשך טיפול בסטרואידים יתרום לעליה ב- TSH
אין השלכה קלינית לתוצאות בשלב זה, יש להמליץ על בדיקה חוזרת לתפקודי תריס בעוד כחודשיים
explanation:
Official answer: ד

Severe illness can produce **nonthyroidal illness syndrome**: T4-to-T3 conversion falls first, followed in more severe illness by lower T4 and TSH. High-dose corticosteroids may profoundly suppress TSH. Thyroid replacement provides no benefit in this syndrome; clinical improvement favors reassessment after recovery (p. 1548).

**A. Central hypothyroidism: investigate pituitary disease and urgently start IV levothyroxine.** Wrong, the biochemical pattern can be identical, but does not establish central disease or justify immediate IV treatment. Further testing need not be pursued when the clinical picture supports nonthyroidal illness (p. 1548).
**B. Nonthyroidal illness syndrome: start IV levothyroxine.** Wrong, the diagnosis fits, but T4 or T3 treatment provides no benefit in this syndrome (p. 1548).
**C. Possible adrenal injury means continued steroids will raise TSH.** Wrong, high-dose steroids may suppress TSH. Thyroid results alone do not establish adrenal damage (p. 1548).
**D. No clinical implication now; repeat thyroid tests in about two months.** Correct, officially accepted. The source supports deferring levothyroxine and repeating outpatient tests after improvement, but does not specify two months. The wording does not negate the association with severe illness (p. 1548).

Low TSH with low T4 and T3 fits nonthyroidal illness in this context but does not alone exclude central hypothyroidism. Reassessment after recovery remains necessary (p. 1548).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1547, 1548.

q: בת 78, פנתה למרפאה עקב חולשה וירידה במשקל של 5 ק"ג בשנה האחרונה. בן זוגה מדווח על ירידה מסויימת בזיכרון. לחץ הדם 128/62 עם ירידה ל- 102/45 בעמידה. בבדיקות המעבדה: בדיקה ויחידות ערך לחולה ערכי נורמה WBC 10e3qµL 6700 4.0-11.0 HgB gr/dl 10.8 17 - 13.2 PLT 10e3qµL 496,000 140-450 CREATININE mg/dL 0.5 0.7-1.3 BUN mg/dL 24 5-25 Na mmol/L 124 135-146 K mmol/L 5.4 3.5-5.3 מה סביר שיימצא בבדיקות המעבדה האנדוקריניות שלה?
o: רמת CRTISOL בשתן מעל מהנורמה
רמת TSH מתחת לנורמה
תגובה מופחתת למתן ACTH
תגובה מופחתת ל- LOW DOSE DEXAMETHASONE SUPRESSION TEST
explanation:
Weakness, weight loss, postural hypotension and electrolyte abnormalities suggest **adrenal insufficiency**. Mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency explains the possible accompanying hyperkalemia. These findings can be nonspecific in older adults and should be interpreted together (Hazzard 8e, pp. 587, 1531; application to the stem).

**A. Urinary cortisol above normal.** Wrong, elevated cortisol indicates glucocorticoid excess, whereas this presentation suggests deficiency; it is not the expected finding when investigating this hypothesis (pp. 1530–1531).
**B. TSH below normal.** Wrong, an isolated low TSH does not explain the combination pointing to glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. The source distinguishes pituitary hormone deficiency from primary adrenal insufficiency (pp. 1529, 1531; inference).
**C. Reduced response to ACTH.** Correct, corticotropin stimulation tests the adrenal capacity to increase cortisol; an impaired response fits the suspected hormonal deficiency (p. 1531).
**D. Reduced response to the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test.** Wrong, failure of cortisol suppression does not demonstrate the impaired stimulated response expected in adrenal insufficiency; the source describes corticotropin stimulation for this suspicion (p. 1531).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 587, 1529–1531.

q: בן 82, מתגורר בביתו עם מטפל זר. ברקע - דמנציה מתקדמת, מרותק לכיסא גלגלים, נזקק לעזרה בכל צרכי ה- ADL. בנוסף, סוכרת, אי-ספיקת לב ופרפור פרוזדורים. לאחרונה קיבל טיפול אנטיביוטי ממושך עקב זיהום בדרכי השתן. התקבל למחלקה למלר"ד עקב ירידה במצבו הכללי, אירועי שלשול מימי מרובים עד 5 ליום וחום. בקבלתו למלר"ד לחץ דם 82/45, דופק 105, סטורציה 91% באוויר חדר, חום 37.8. בבדיקת צואה- CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE TOXIN חיובי. בבדיקות המעבדה: מדד ויחידות החולה ערכים תקינים WBC 10e3qµL 18,700 4.0-11.0 HgB gr/dl 13.2 17 - 13.2 MCV Fl 78 80-96 PLT 10e3qµL 300,000 140-450 Na mmol/L 148 135-146 K mmol/L 3.2 3.5-5.3 CREATININE mg/dL 2 0.7-1.3 מה הטיפול האנטיביוטי המומלץ?
o: METRONIDAZOLE (FLAGYL) פומי
VANCOMYCIN פומי
METRONIDAZOLE (FLAGYL) פומי בשילוב עם LOPERAMIDE (IMODIUM) אחרי כל שלשול
VANCOMYCIN פומי ו- METRONIDAZOLE (FLAGYL) תוך ורידי
explanation:
The patient has severe **Clostridium difficile infection with hypotension**. For very ill patients, the source recommends oral vancomycin combined with intravenous metronidazole (p. 1305).

**A. Oral metronidazole (Flagyl).** Wrong, the source favors oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin over oral metronidazole and recommends combination treatment in very ill patients. Oral metronidazole alone does not match this pathway (p. 1305).
**B. Oral vancomycin.** Wrong, oral vancomycin alone treats many patients, but the severe illness here points toward adding intravenous metronidazole (p. 1305).
**C. Oral metronidazole plus loperamide (Imodium) after each diarrheal episode.** Wrong, symptomatic diarrhea treatment does not supply the missing recommended antimicrobial regimen for a very ill patient. Oral metronidazole remains different from the recommended combination (p. 1305).
**D. Oral vancomycin plus intravenous metronidazole.** Correct, this is the combination recommended for very ill patients; hypotension in the stem is the decisive clinical feature supporting this pathway (p. 1305).

The stem gives blood pressure 82/45, leukocytes 18,700, hypernatremia (Na 148), hypokalemia (K 3.2), and creatinine 2; it does not show hyponatremia (inherited question-paper locator: p. 37).

In older adults, metronidazole treatment carries a high risk of failure and recurrence; severity guides selection of the antimicrobial regimen (p. 1305).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 1305.
